en: Citing Tiantai and Xianshou, [the Master] taught the Dharma according to what was appropriate. Those who speak of the Tiantai and Xianshou teachings do not realize this themselves;

later generations give rise to such thoughts that they immediately create a separation between them as two distinct parts. By overemphasizing Tiantai, one loses Tiantai; by overemphasizing Xianshou, one loses Xianshou.
Thus it is. To cling to appearances and become mired in names, or to divide the river and set up banners—this is a great malady of the Dharma-ending age.

Those of comprehensive understanding should not, among such matters, engage in the biased selection of elevating one side while disparaging another. The *Wujiaoyi* (The Ritual of the Five Teachings) was missing from the Xianshou school;

Master Bai Ting composed it to supplement it. This is like using poison to counteract poison, or using a wedge to extract a wedge. For now, rely on paper and ink to bestow equality; do not [discriminate] toward...
Placing right and wrong upon the tips of one's eyebrows—this is likely not merely the meritorious achievement of the Xianshou school alone.
As for those who have caught a glimpse of the "tigers of meaning" from the southeast, those who take sides between the two schools should simply refrain from casting their eyes upon this.

On the day of the commencement of autumn in the Gengshen year of the Kangxi era, Dai Jingzeng, Vice Governor of the Capital Prefecture (Shuntianfu), Qiantang, inscribed this preface to the *Wujiao yi* (The Ritual of the Five Teachings) by Xianshou.
The *Avataṃsaka* is called the Fundamental Wheel of Dharma; it is not only the basis for opening the gradual [teachings], but also serves to subsume the derivative ones.
This fundamental text is most highly revered throughout India and China. From the successive Buddhas and patriarchs down through the generations of masters and disciples, it has been transmitted.
Based upon it, Nāgārjuna distinguished the two types of Prajñāpāramitā; based upon it, Vasubandhu elucidated the perfect fusion of the six aspects;
based upon it, Dushun expounded the three contemplations; and based upon it, Yunhua opened up the ten mysteries. As for the Great Master Xianshou, he likewise relied upon this [text].
In establishing their fundamental tenets and judging the teachings, [Zhiyi] departed from the four divisions of the Tiantai school to establish five;

furthermore, he followed the model of Qingliang (Chengguan), opening ten gates to harmonize the two teachings of Nature and Characteristics. Guifeng (Huiyuan) followed in his lineage, enumerating five meanings to distinguish between the two schools of Emptiness and Nature.

All of these masters possessed divine intelligence granted by Heaven and were profoundly learned and versatile; thus, they were each able to display their eloquence and widely propagate the subtle [Dharma].

Whether composing treatises or commenting on the sūtras, the essential principles of the Dharma-realm were brilliantly elucidated and fully prepared; thus, the teachings for the Great Vehicle’s single period were exhausted without any remaining storehouse.

Although there have been wise individuals from generation to generation who followed after Guifeng, none could surpass him in comprehensive synthesis and systematic organization, such that no one can add another word of praise. Yet those who merely taste [his work] fail to examine it closely when they read...
First, they do not read [the texts] themselves; they neglect their eyes and rely solely on their ears. They condemn those who differ to form factions with their own kind.
Some criticize them for being devoid of both cessation and contemplation, while others point out that they have lost both the teachings and the contemplations.

The various masters of the Tiantai and Huayan schools from former times feared that the descendants of these two houses would indiscriminately blend the principles of Xianshou (Fazang) into their own traditions; therefore, they did not spare effort in their clarifications, offering critiques and refutations.

How could those of later generations have gone so far as to seize upon mere fragments of his teachings to indulge their own madness and blindness, recklessly leveling slanders and launching unprovoked attacks, refusing to stop until they had divided the river at the drinking well? Alas! Who else would have known that there were such profound and manifest errors?
Our late master, the Great Master Baolun, had plumbed the depths of all schools of thought; he was especially bound by a karmic affinity with the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, having cultivated its essence...

He studied with profound penetration, grasping the essence through his mind and attaining realization through his spirit. He often lamented that the lineage of Xianshou, which had not yet fallen, was as fragile as a single thread;
he thus vowed to revitalize this extinct enterprise to continue the past and open the way for the future. After elucidating the Dharma, he exerted himself to propagate this school.

Regarding the Five Teachings and the Ten Profundities, there was no time or place where he did not loftily proclaim the perfect teaching (*yuan-chang*). He authored the *Wujiao jie* (Exegesis on the Five Teachings) and the *Xiao lun* (Treatise on Refutation), in which he critiqued the teachings of Xian.

The first section, "On the Unknown Meaning of the Perfect [Teaching]," and the second section, "On the Interpretation of the Two [Families]," state that the general principle is that Great Master Xianshou’s division of four into five was not in opposition to Tiantai; rather, it truly fulfilled what Tiantai had not yet fully provided.

That Qingliang succeeded and promoted this—regarding Great Master Qingliang as a great foundational merit for Tiantai—is likewise not an error. In the interim, the two schools were clearly distinguished.
The divergent paths [of the two schools] are as distinct as a suspended mirror; their ultimate convergence is as seamless as a pair of joined jade disks.

Furthermore, with not a grain or a fraction of discrepancy and no partiality in the slightest detail, they are like a perfectly balanced scale. Had those who harbor resentment seen this, they would have had no place to insert their tongues.
My late teacher said that Tiantai should regard the Great Master Qingliang as its great foundational merit; I, [Lì], likewise say so.
The late Master was truly a primary pillar of the Tiantai school; he was not merely the direct successor of Qingliang.

(Li) had served his master for many years, yet because he was late in "dislocating the shoulder joint" [of awakening], his wisdom remained dust-covered and his intellect fettered, leading to a heart-stricken realization upon gazing at the sea and empty-handedness upon entering the mountains.

Meanwhile, Dharma Master Bǎixiōng of Cíyún possessed a talent for comprehension that was peerless, having personally received the instructions and guidance of his teacher as he traveled back and forth seeking counsel.
He reached a definitive resolution and, beneath a single word, finally attained the marrow. Yet, he remained as deeply concealed as a skilled merchant.

For years, he had closed his door and withdrawn from the world, spending his days and nights in solitary companionship with Jingman. Beyond his meditative contemplation, he took up this scripture and the treatises of the various patriarchs, grinding them over and correlating them.
He observed extensively and extracted the essentials; first, he categorized and itemized the branches, analyzing them into their constituent streams.

Thereafter, he thoroughly investigated the origins and synthesized them into a single work. It is divided as follows: first, the section on Time; second, the section on Rituals; third, the section on Teaching;
followed by the section on Doctrinal Schools; and finally, the section on Contemplation. Regarding Time, there are distinctions of priority and sequence, as well as general and specific aspects.

Regarding Rituals, there are primary and secondary forms, as well as manifest and esoteric dimensions. Regarding Teaching, there are beginnings and endings, as well as sudden and perfect modes. Regarding Doctrinal Schools, there are small and great, as well as nature and characteristics. Regarding Contemplation, there are various methods.
There are causes and conditions; there are phenomena with opposition; there are gates of contemplation; there are the six characteristics; there are the ten mysteries.

The words are concise yet the meanings are detailed; the principles are harmonious and the purport is manifest. Faith, understanding, practice, and realization are clearly arrayed like hairs upon one's eyebrows.

To read this and still claim that it contains only teaching without contemplation—is this possible? To claim that it provides no instruction regarding the subduing and severing of afflictions, nor cultivation and realization—is this possible? From this day forward...
The fundamental principle of the Dharma-realm will surely not remain forever suppressed. Thus, this work ensures that the Dharma Master truly does not fail his late teacher as a legitimate heir;
tracing it further back, it shall serve as the standard for Guifeng, Qingliang, and Xianshou.
Even the great achievements of masters such as Nāgārjuna do not surpass those of Tiantai. As for those who harbor resentment and seek out the faults of Xianshou, they have no place to interject;
one should simply observe with an impartial mind. Thus he titled his work *The Ritual of the Five Teachings of Xianshou*.
The Dharma Master himself claimed that he had secretly modeled it after the Korean master [Wonhyo], having received his profound principles (*xuanyi*).

Thus it is recorded in the *Sijiao yi* (The Ritual of the Four Teachings). Who would say otherwise? Now, as this work is being prepared for publication, I have been entrusted with composing a preface.
I am deeply rejoiced that the fundamental Dharma-wheel of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra stands majestically revealed like the sun and moon in the heavens.
Consequently, with palms joined in praise, I have disregarded my own meanness and composed these words accordingly.
Preface composed by the Dharma-brother Zhenli of Meiwu Xingfu Monastery, respectfully saluting.
Confucius could not have been without Mencius; Laozi could not have been without Zhuang Zhou; and the Buddha Śākyamuni could not have been without Nāgārjuna.
Zhiyi was indispensable to the Dharma as its necessary transmitter; Nanyue could not have lacked Zhiyi, and Śīlabhadra could not have lacked Xuanzang.
Bodhidharma could not have lacked Huik'e as the necessary person for the transmission of the teaching.
Furthermore, Zhiyi could not have lacked Zhanran, Xuanzang could not have lacked Ci'en, and Huik'e could not have lacked Sengcan to serve as the recipients of his transmission.
Having its source, it does not exhaust; transmitted through successive generations, it is inexhaustible.
How could this be otherwise for the Great Master Xianshou? Speaking of his teachers, Du Shun and Yunhua opened the way before him;
speaking of his disciples, Qingliang and Guifeng succeeded him afterward. In establishing his teachings, he possessed both beginning and end, and both sudden and gradual approaches.

In its perfect severance, it cuts through both the thick and the thin; in its realization, it rectifies both the shallow and the deep. Regarding stages, it grades their high and low; regarding practices, it determines their far and near.
It reveals the characteristics of dharmas as clearly as a candle’s bright light, and its selection of capacities and benefits is like the carving of firewood.
In its discernment of the schools, there are the small and the great, and the nature and the characteristics. As for characteristics, they are false characteristics.
When characteristics are empty, then even true emptiness is empty. "Sudden" means there is nothing that is not severed, like a shadow detached from the sun in the sky.

"Round" means there is nothing that is not integrated, like images contained within the sea. When these aspects are distinguished, there is a sequence of before and after, and a distinction between the particular and the universal.

It is not because there is no "before" that one knows it to be the suddenness of gradual opening; it is not because there is no "after" that one knows it... [to be the gradualness of sudden realization].
To grasp the root of the branches, there is nothing other than this; to perceive the sequence of the Dharma teachings, there is nothing other than this.
To see the perfect integration of doctrine and principle, there is nothing other than this. In its exposition of ritual, there is the root and the branch, the manifest and the esoteric.
Without the root, one cannot realize the sudden reality of the One Vehicle; without the branch, one cannot recognize the provisional gradualism of the Three Vehicles; without the manifest...
To resolve its certainty, one must certainly not rely on the secret; to fathom its indeterminacy, one must rely on clarity.

Its clear contemplation possesses expedient means, causal conditions, corresponding dharmas, contemplative gateways, the six aspects, and the ten mysteries. Without expedient means, there is no way to distinguish cultivation and realization;
without causal conditions, there is no way to manifest the function of luminosity; without corresponding dharmas, there is no way to understand non-existence.
Without the gates of contemplation, there is no way to enter the Dharma-realm; without the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*), there is no way to manifest perfect penetration;

and without the ten mysteries (*daśamithuna*), there is no way to reveal non-obstruction. Why is this? Because ordinary people perceive form as real form and perceive emptiness as nihilistic emptiness;

therefore, the gate of "True Emptiness Beyond Characteristics" is opened to lead them to contemplate that form is not real form, but that its entire substance is true emptiness, and to contemplate emptiness...
That non-interruption and emptiness are, in their entirety, illusory form—this is seen in principle (*li*), yet not yet in fact (*shi*).

To further open the gate of the non-obstruction between principle and fact, one contemplates that the indivisible principle is perfectly encompassed within a single atom, and that the limited fact likewise pervades the entire Dharma-realm. In this way, it may be so when viewing principle from the perspective of fact.

To regard phenomena through phenomena alone is still insufficient; therefore, the "Gate of Universal Inclusivity" is further opened to enable one to contemplate the principle within each phenomenon such that it is visible in every instance, and the phenomena within the principle such that they are harmoniously integrated in every instance.

Only then will the non-obstruction of the one and the many and the mutual containment of the large and the small emerge, whereby the divine function of manifestation and concealment becomes unfathomable. This is the teaching and contemplation.
Once the ritual protocols of the Zhou dynasty were fully established, [this work] definitively explained the ceremonial procedures for the Buddhas’ preaching of the Dharma;

it is ultimate and exhaustive, with nothing further to be added. By means of this, one cultivates oneself such that there is no Dharma not understood; by means of this, one teaches others such that no capacity is left unreached.
Therefore, three emperors honored and revered it, and the two courts submitted with joy. Master Li offered his discourses and praises in the past, and Cui Xuezhi transmitted it.
Its beauty extended from later generations throughout the land and beyond the seas, such that there were none who did not extol its transformation;
from the heavens above to the earth below, all looked up to its sublime character. When verified against the sages and worthies of antiquity, it was without error;
when awaited by the geniuses of future centuries, it remained beyond doubt. Consequently, the Dharma-gate flourished, with wise men appearing in every generation, like a long-flowing river.
It was spread throughout Eastern Wu; Mount Cang rose majestically in Western Shu; Yuniqi propagated it in the South Seas; and Jiaoguang elucidated it on the Northern Peaks.
How magnificent and auspicious! Alas, how regrettable that today’s scholars of the Yogācāra school fail to find the door through which to enter.
Upon seeing that the doctrinal sections are vast and their underlying principles profound and subtle—just as in the case of the writings of the Great Master Xianshou—[they become discouraged].
There are over one hundred fascicles currently circulating from the time of National Teacher Qingliang;

the commentaries and sub-commentaries by Grand Master Guifeng total approximately ninety fascicles. Those who are frivolous and reckless disparage them as mere "entanglements," while those who are dull-witted regard them as "gravel and stones.
Who, then, can explore their subtleties or peer into their profundities? Fortunately, our Master Rulung has [attained this]...
Since the Great Master [Kūkai] first propagated the Dharma, he has exhorted us morning and evening and performed recitations for us on special occasions;

yet, he had not yet disseminated these throughout the various regions so that all might see and hear them. (Continuation of the Dharma) Although I am an unworthy disciple under his wheel, my nature is extremely dull and ignorant;

through following him day and night, I have gradually become matured by his influence. I humbly consider that these are the mind-teachings transmitted within the House of the Sages, and that if they were not transmitted...
In later times, if one harbors parsimony regarding the Dharma within oneself, how can others possibly receive the benefit of the correct eye?
Therefore, I have recorded what my late teacher frequently delighted to expound and further compiled the most essential points from among the great treatises.

After examining them two or three times over more than ten years, and only after reaching the fourth stage of profound contemplation, these six volumes were completed and titled: *The Great Commentary on the Meaning of the Mahāyāna Sūtras* (Dacheng yizhang).

I have set forth these Fivefold Rituals for Instruction so that the essential tenets of the *Avataṃsaka* may spread further throughout the mundane world, and the Heart-Seal (*dharmacitta-mudrā*) may shine once more as it did in ages past, with the lamps passed one to another in succession and the transformations unfolding endlessly. I have recorded these details in the hope that you will perceive my sincere intentions;
as for whether others will understand me or condemn me, I have no leisure to concern myself with such matters. At this time—
On the full moon day of the middle month of autumn in the year of Yimao, the fourteenth year of the Kangxi era,
this "Diagram of the Rituals and Contemplations of the Xianshou School" was inscribed by the practitioner Ganding Xufa of Ciyun Monastery in Ancient Hangzhou.

The *Diagram of the Universal Integration and Infinite Extent of the Realm of Phenomena as the Object of the Dharma-Realm Contemplation* by Great Master Xianshou. The classification and interpretation of the Tathāgata’s teachings throughout his single lifetime do not exceed these three contemplations in the aforementioned diagram.
The First Patriarch, Dushun, compiled the Five Teachings; the Second Patriarch, Yunhua, drafted the *Rituals* and other works; and the Fourth Patriarch, Qingliang, completed the final additions.
Regarding the patriarchs and so forth: although the Five Patriarchs and Guifeng added further distinctions, the present diagram designates only the Third Patriarch Xianshou as a single master.

This is because the perfection of both teaching (*jiao*) and contemplation (*guan*) was achieved through the Third Patriarch, and the establishment of the ritual protocols of the school (*zongyi*) was inaugurated by him;

his merit in exposition and composition is uniquely exalted, and for this reason, the other patriarchs are not mentioned here. Those who study the Dharma in the future should strive to understand how he opened the school and established the teaching.
The Master of the Lineage. The remaining patriarchs are naturally included herein and made manifest.

Compiled by the Qing Dynasty Chan Monk Guanding Xufa of Ciyun on the banks of the Zhe River. Volume One of the *Wujiaoyi* of Xianshou.
The Great Master Xianshou’s doctrinal classification of the Tathāgata’s teachings throughout his single lifetime does not exceed three periods, ten modes, five teachings,
six schools, and three contemplations.
Regarding these "three periods," there are both specific and general interpretations.
The three distinct periods are: first, the time when the sun first shines; second, the time when the sun rises and shines further; and third, the time when the sun sets and still shines.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "One may enter during the first part of the day, or during the middle part of the day, or during the latter part of the day.
This refers to what the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* calls being "good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end."
Regarding "the time when the first sun rises and shines": The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "For example, when the sun rises, it first illuminates Mount Sumeru and other great high mountains;

likewise, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, having accomplished the wheel of wisdom that pervades the boundless Dharma-realm, constantly emits the unimpeded light of wisdom, which first illuminates the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
[And so forth with] all the great kings of mountains. △ If we consider the characteristics of the teachings expounded therein:

△ The Sūtra states that at the time when the World-Honored One first attained perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, he universally beheld all sentient beings attaining perfect enlightenment, and even universally beheld all sentient beings entering parinirvāṇa. He universally beheld all sentient beings...
Within the afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, and pride, there exists the body of the Tathāgata, whose wisdom is eternally unstained and whose marks and attributes are fully perfected.
There is not a single sentient being who does not possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata; it is only because of deluded thoughts and attachments that they do not realize it.
I wish to instruct them through the Noble Path so that they may forever leave behind deluded thoughts within their own bodies.
They shall behold the vast wisdom of the Tathāgata as being no different from my own.

△ Within these three weeks, I shall then, for the sake of these sentient beings, at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), proclaim the causes of the myriad practices according to the Great Vaipulya Dharmadhātu;
by adorning their original nature with these flowers, I shall cause them to achieve the fruit of Buddhahood endowed with the myriad virtues. △ As for those who, in past kalpas, were equal to me—
Those who have planted roots of goodness and were once gathered by me through the four methods of attraction throughout oceans of kalpas—
upon first seeing my body and hearing what I say, they all immediately believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata. Even within the Jeta Grove,
when I enter the Lion’s Stretching Samādhi, the great assembly all realizes the inexhaustible dharma-realm.
At this time, for sentient beings of the great root of the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching], he turns the unsurpassed fundamental wheel of Dharma, which is called the "Direct Manifestation Teaching.
For those who follow the Identical One Vehicle (Samaya-yāna), it turns the identical into the distinct;
that is to say, it is the "Initial Goodness," or the first portion of the day. Thus, the *Expedient Means* chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "When I first sat upon the seat of enlightenment..."
He then reflected to himself: "If I were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle, sentient beings submerged in suffering would be unable to believe this Dharma;
they would reject it and lack faith. Thus, the verse on faith and understanding says: "At that time, the elder sat upon the lion throne, surrounded by his retinue and attended by his servants.
He brought out his property and recorded it in deeds and contracts. When the impoverished son saw his father, he fled in haste."
He immediately commanded his messengers to pursue and seize him; the impoverished son was startled and cried out in distress, falling prostrate upon the ground.
△ The sutras he spoke of are the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Brahmajāla*, and others.
Regarding the second point, "the rising sun shines sequentially," there are two meanings: first, the general, and second, the specific. △ First, the general explanation:
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "It is simply because the mountains and lands have elevations and depressions that the illumination occurs earlier or later;
the wheel of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise so, manifesting various kinds of light of wisdom according to the differing faculties and inclinations of sentient beings."

The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* also says: "Just as the rising sun shines equally upon those of inferior, middling, and superior capacities, so does the Tathāgata illuminate the world by classifying all dharmas.
△ If we consider the characteristics of the teachings expounded therein, △ the sūtra states:

"Except for those who previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna, those who are attached to signs and arrogant, those who do not believe in the Dharma, and those who are submerged in the waters of craving and attachment to the five [desires]."
"Those who are deeply immersed in various false views and the perilous paths of birth and death—such sentient beings as these have all their faculties rendered dull and darkened;
blinded by attachment to pleasure and ignorance, how can they be delivered? △ For twenty-one days, I contemplated such matters:
if I were to encounter sentient beings and teach them all the Buddha-way, they would immediately sink into the sea of suffering and slander it."
Because they lack faith, they would quickly enter the evil realms; if I were to convert even a single person by means of the Hīnayāna, I would fall into stinginess and greed.

This matter is impossible, for it is difficult to proceed or retreat. Then, reflecting upon the skillful means practiced by the Buddhas of the past, he first realized that all past Buddhas had led beings through the three vehicles before finally causing them to awaken and enter the ultimate [truth].
Because the One Buddha Vehicle is ultimate, the path I have attained should also be taught as three vehicles.

While I was reflecting thus, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared and comforted me with Brahma-sounds, saying: "Excellent, Śākyamuni! You, the foremost guide, have attained this unsurpassed Dharma;
you follow the example of all Buddhas by employing the power of skillful means. Having heard these words of consolation, I followed [their instruction].
In accordance with the intentions of all Buddhas, he first proceeded to Vārāṇasī to turn the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths;
he praised and revealed the Dharma of Nirvāṇa to Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the other five, and gradually traveled to various places, even to thousands and tens of thousands of others,

preaching the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination for those seeking the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddha, and the Six Pāramitās for those seeking the Mahāyāna, while in the interim he preached the Vaipulya sūtras.
The profound *prajñā* dharmas refine those above—the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the provisional vehicle practitioners among the lesser bodhisattvas.

During this single period, for the sake of the three classes of sentient beings—lower, middle, and upper—he turns the wheel of Dharma that takes the fundamental as the beginning and the derivative as the end;
this is called the teaching of skillful means (*upāya-śāsana*). It causes those three classes of people to transform the three into one, namely, the middle.
It may be that he entered [parinirvāṇa] at midday. △ Thus, the *Upāya* chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states in verse:
"I further formed this thought: 'I have emerged from this turbid and evil world; as all Buddhas have taught, I too shall practice accordingly.

By the power of skillful means (*upāya*), I preached for the five bhikṣus, and for the various classes of sentient beings, I distinguished and taught the three vehicles (*triyāna*). Although I have thus taught three,"
The vehicle is intended solely for the instruction of bodhisattvas.

Regarding the subsequent distinct explanation, during the middle portion of the day, the illumination has three revolutions: namely, the first revolution, the middle revolution, and the final revolution.

Regarding the time of the first turning: the *Avataṃsaka* states that next the Tathāgata’s wheel of wisdom illumines the Black Mountains, and subsequently it illumines the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

This refers to when the Buddha first turned the Dharma-wheel of the Hīnayāna at the Deer Park for sentient beings of dull faculties and inferior class, teaching that all phenomena arise through causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in order to refute the non-Buddhists' doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and further explaining dependent origination.

The teaching of "no-self" reverses the non-Buddhists' attachment to a real self; at this first turning, it clarifies that the dependent nature is substantially real solely from the perspective of its objective referent.
Yet, it has not yet explained the Mahāyāna Dharma of the wondrous principle of True Suchness (tathatā) and emptiness.

For this reason, it is called the "teaching that conceals reality," intended to lead ordinary beings and non-Buddhists to transform from the mundane to the sacred. Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "The elder knew..."

The son, being foolish, narrow-minded, and base, was immediately sent by [the father] using skillful means with another person—one who was one-eyed, short, ugly, and lacking in majesty—with these instructions:
"You may say to him: 'We shall look after you and remove all the filth and excrement; we will give you double the wages.
When the impoverished son hears this, he will come gladly to follow you and clear away the filth, cleaning the rooms and halls. The sutra he preached was precisely the *Dharmapada*.
This refers to the Āgamas and so forth.
Regarding the "intermediate turning," the *Avataṃsaka* states: "Next, the Tathāgata’s wheel of wisdom shines upon the high plains;

next, it shines upon sentient beings with determined roots of goodness, manifesting vast wisdom according to their mental capacities. This means that the Buddha, during the intermediate period, [taught] for those of medium faculties.

A class of sentient beings turns the wheel of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, teaching that all phenomena are manifestations of consciousness alone, thereby refuting the Hīnayāna view that phenomena exist externally to the mind and arise from causes and conditions;
furthermore, they teach that dependently originated things are merely conventionally existent, overturning the Hīnayāna attachment to phenomena as substantially real.
At this first turning, one begins by explaining that the pervasive imagination is entirely empty based on the mind, yet at this stage, [the nature of emptiness] has not yet been fully explained.

The sublime principle of the single vehicle’s true emptiness and dharma-nature is called the "teaching of attraction and inclusion" because it causes those of the two vehicles to turn from the small toward the great.
Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "The wise elder gradually leads [his children] in and out for twenty years, having them manage the household affairs.
The sūtras he speaks of are those such as the *Vaipulya* and the *Gambhīra-guhyaka*.
Regarding the subsequent turning [of the wheel], the *Avataṃsaka* states: "Thereafter, the Tathāgata’s wheel of wisdom universally illumines the entire earth;
thereafter, it universally illumines all sentient beings, even those fixed in error, so as to provide the causes and conditions for their future benefit and bring them to maturity.
This means that the Buddha, at a later time, acts for the sake of sentient beings of superior faculties and highest class.
He turns the wheel of the One Vehicle (ekayāna), teaching that the fundamental nature of all phenomena is the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous true suchness (tathatā).

This is done to shatter the provisional vehicles' failure to realize that both mind and objects are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature. Furthermore, he teaches that dependent origination is itself emptiness, overturning the dualistic clinging to selflessness found in those provisional vehicles.
At this turning of the wheel, he directly relies upon the nature to manifest the Middle Way and return to the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva); yet, he has not yet fully expounded it.

Because the wondrous principle of the ultimate, true, and eternal *dharmatā*—the Buddha-nature of the One Vehicle wherein the Buddhas and sentient beings are equal—is thoroughly integrated, it is called the "Teaching of Interfusion.
It causes those of the three vehicles to transform their provisional [attainments] into the real. Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"At that time, the elder, knowing for himself that [his end] was near, showed him gold, silver, pearls, and crystal; all the goods coming in and going out..."
This is intended to make it known that the sūtras he preached are those such as the *Prajñāpāramitā*, which is the sublime wisdom.
Regarding the phrase "on the third day, when the sun sets, it shines again," this takes its meaning from the intent of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, stating:
"Just as when the sun sets, it shines again upon the high mountains, so too does the wheel of the Tathāgata’s wisdom finally shine upon the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."

Regarding the various great mountain kings: the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* (Ten Stages Chapter) states, "For example, the Sun Deva-son travels around, illuminating and shining without ceasing day or night;

the rising of the sun is called 'day,' and its setting is called 'night. The Bodhisattva is also like this. The *Dharmadhātu-parivarta* (Chapter on the Dharma-realm) states, "For example, the solar orb has no distinction between day and night;
merely when it rises is it called 'day,' and when it sets is it called 'night. So too is the wheel of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom."
It is likewise thus: there is no discrimination, but rather [the teaching] manifests according to the mind to transform sentient beings.

△ If we consider the characteristics of the teachings as they are expounded: △ The Sūtra says that after more than forty years have passed, as their faculties gradually matured, those of middling and inferior capacities became of the highest grade; such persons I now also cause to hear this sūtra and enter into it.
The Buddha’s wisdom then led him to proclaim to the great assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa: "O World-Honored Ones, after a long time, the Dharma must ultimately reveal the truth.
You all should with one mind believe and understand it; there is no other vehicle, for there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle.
It reveals, awakens, and leads others into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, universally bestowing upon all the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
He manifested that sentient beings of the three and five vehicles possess the nature of the Dharma-body and enter the path of the One Vehicle in equality;

even at the time he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, while between the twin śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara, he let out a great lion’s roar and definitively proclaimed the eternally abiding Dharma, saying:
"All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; all who have a mind [possess it]."
They shall certainly attain Buddhahood and ultimate *nirvāṇa*, and all shall be established in the Secret Treasury of permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
this is no different from the sudden realization attained by the great assembly of the Lion’s Stretching at the Sea-Gathering of the *Avataṃsaka*.
This single period of time is when the Dharma wheel for beings of the highest capacity is turned, subsuming the branches back into the root; it is called the "Opening of the Assembly."
The teaching instructs those who were previously limited to the five vehicles to transform their partiality into perfection;
this is what is meant by "excellent in the end," or entering during the latter part of the day. Thus, the *Expedient Means* chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra* states in verse:
"When I see sons of the Buddha whose resolve seeks the path of the Buddha, I immediately think: 'The Tathāgata has appeared for the sake of preaching the Buddha-wisdom. Now is precisely the time."

At that time, [the father] directly abandons expedient means and speaks only of the unsurpassed Way to teach and transform the various bodhisattvas, with no śrāvaka disciples who possess faith and understanding.
The verse says: "The father knows the son’s mind has gradually become expansive; he then gathers his kinsmen and declares, 'This is my son.
Whatever I possess—house, residence, people, and all else—I entrust it all to him, allowing him to use it as he pleases. The son reflects...

"In the past I was poor, but now, at my father's place, I have obtained great treasures," he said with immense joy. △ The sutras he refers to are the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, and others.
Question: According to the interpretation above, do the names and meanings of the three periods not rely on multiple sutras and śāstras? Answer: They are derived from various sutras.
Because it is the ultimate conclusion of logic. △ Question: Since there is no mention of "shining back" in the sutra, why is this now established and judged?
△ Answer: There are two meanings for establishing [this]. △ First, taking the intent of the sutra: when the sun first rises, it first shines upon the high mountains;
likewise, when the sun is about to set, it should also shine back upon the various mountain kings. Therefore, as in that Tiantai school, they also establish [this].

The level ground constitutes three to complete five (the three being dawn, mid-morning, and noon; adding the deep valley and the high mountain to correspond to the five flavors makes five). Taking the deep valley as two to combine with four (the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

"For example, when the sun rises, it first illuminates the great kings of mountains, next it illuminates all other mountains, then it illuminates the diamond treasure mountains, and finally it shines universally upon the entire earth—this is four.

Yet it is said to be 'two combined with four' because, as the *Miaoxuan* states: 'Just as when the sun rises, it first illuminates the high mountains, next it illuminates the deep valleys, and finally it illuminates the level ground'; thus, combining the four illuminations results in three illuminations").

Therefore, the *Shuchao* states: "Our Buddha appeared in the world for the sake of a single matter; though forty-odd years passed without revealing the ultimate truth, we now divide the teachings of his entire career into periods.

How could this hinder our judgment of what precedes and follows, or our analysis of the provisional and the real, the empty and the existent, what is to be accepted or rejected, and the partial and the perfect, the gradual and the sudden?
Only then will one know the subtle, profound, and mysterious nature of the Buddha-dharma, which is like not drifting aimlessly upon a great [ocean]."

How could the ocean know its own boundaries? Not being familiar with wood or stone, how could it recognize true treasures? Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*), stating:
"To extensively develop principles based upon and following the sūtras and śāstras, and to establish names and designations for them—all these are called the gift of Dharma.

II. Regarding the Teaching and Principle: The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* relies on the root to give rise to the branches; thus, there is a hidden flow but no subsequent illumination. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* encompass [all things].

Because the branches ultimately return to the root, there is a convergence of the flowing waters but no prior illumination; now, by taking both root and branch together, they are unimpeded, and the sequence of before and after is perfectly complete.

It is not without the root that the branches can be extended downward; thus, within the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* sūtras, the meaning of the sun’s emergence and its hidden flow is illustrated through metaphor:
"For example, when the sun rises, it first illuminates Mount Sumeru and other great high mountains. Furthermore—
It is like the great ocean, whose waters flow secretly beneath the lands of the four continents and the eight hundred million minor islands;

there is no way for them to return to their source except through the mouths [of rivers]. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* provide a shadowy manifestation of this principle, while the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clarifies the meaning of the "converging streams at sunset.
It says: "When the sun sets over Jambudvīpa, sentient beings do not see it because it is obscured by the Black Mountains (*Kṛṣṇaparvata*); yet it is so."
The nature of the sun truly has no setting, yet sentient beings perceive it as setting; the Śrāvaka disciples are likewise thus.
Because they are obstructed by the mountains of various afflictions (*kleśa*), they do not see my body.

Because they do not see it, they conceive the notion that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, whereas in truth I have never undergone ultimate extinction. Furthermore, just as the Son of Heaven, the Sun, is able to...
This sutra is also like this, for it can destroy all the darkness of unwholesome states. It is like the four rivers that flow from Lake Anavatapta;
if any devas or humans, or even Buddhas, were to say that these rivers do not enter the great ocean but instead return to their source, such a thing is impossible.
The mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) is also like this: for those who possess the Buddha-nature, [it likewise cannot turn back].
Whether one hears it or not, whether one practices it or not, all shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, just as among all the waters of streams, rivers, and great rivers, the ocean is foremost, so too is this sutra;
among all sutras, it is the most profound and vast. If it were otherwise, then the sun would only rise and never set or enter [the horizon]. Therefore, it is universal.

Once the earth has been illuminated, the great high mountains cannot be further illuminated; therefore, after the midday illumination has passed, it would be like the onset of twilight, as the world would fall into total darkness.

Why, then, does the sutra say: "Now I shall again turn the most wondrous, unsurpassed Great Dharma Wheel, so that you may also hear this sutra and enter the Buddha-wisdom"? Furthermore, among the hundred rivers, there is no ocean that remains hidden.
Since a current must originate from a source, those who seek it through mere excavation will ultimately fail to gain benefit;

furthermore, when rivers and streams dry up, there should subsequently be no water to enter their currents. Why, then, does the Sūtra say that within the single Buddha-vehicle, one distinguishes and teaches three vehicles—just as from a cow comes milk, and from milk comes curd? Therefore, one should know that it is improper to cling exclusively to a single passage.

This is a doubt and difficulty regarding a single principle. △ However, within the sūtras and śāstras, there are cases where names exist but meanings do not, cases where meanings exist but names do not, cases where both name and meaning are complete, and cases where both name and meaning are missing.
Now, from among the first three of these categories, we further distinguish six phrases for examination: 1. partial names; 2. complete names; 3. partial meanings; 4. complete [meanings].
There are five [types of] partial meanings and six [types of] complete meanings. Regarding the term "partial meaning," as stated in the "Ten Samādhis" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"The rising of the sun is called day; the setting of the sun is called night. The first fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The light of the sun of noble wisdom shall from now on perish forever; the unsurpassed Dharma-ship sinks here. The latter section states: "The sun of wisdom has set and vanished."

On the mountain of Great Nirvāṇa, all sentient beings have lost their true father of compassion. The *Caturvargika-vinaya* states that it is like when the sun sets and the world becomes entirely dark and gloomy.

Regarding the names of the complete sections: as the *Benqi jing* (Sutra on the Original Arising) says, when the Bodhisattva was dwelling in the womb, he preached the Dharma to the devas of the Form Realm in the morning, to those of the Desire Realm at midday, and to the spirits and ghosts in the evening; this is also described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The *Daśadhyāya-parivarta* states: "Whether in the first part of the day, the middle part of the day, or the latter part of the day. The *Prajñāpāramitā* states:
"In the first part of the day one gives away one's body; in the middle part of the day and the latter part of the day, one likewise gives away bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
△ Regarding the meaning of "a small portion": as stated in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* in the analogy of the initial formation of fifty worlds:

"For example, when a trichiliocosm first begins to form, it is first the realm of the Form Heavens (*rūpa-deva*), then the realm of the Desire Heavens (*kāma-deva*), then the human abodes and other sentient beings.
Likewise, when a Tathāgata appears, he first transforms Bodhisattvas, next transforms those of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*), and finally reaches all other sentient beings. (51)

The analogy for the arising from the *dharmadhātu* is as follows: Just as the *dharmadhātu* constantly gives rise to the liberations of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, yet the *dharmadhātu* itself neither increases nor decreases;

so too, the Tathāgata’s wisdom constantly gives rise to all kinds of mundane and supramundane wisdom, yet the Tathāgata’s wisdom neither increases nor decreases. This clarifies the meaning that [the teaching] is sudden first and gradual later. (4)

Seventeenth, it says: "At times he may preach the differentiated Three Vehicles, and at times he may preach the perfect One Vehicle, universally delivering all so that they may transcend birth and death.
This clarifies the principle of first employing the gradual and subsequently the sudden. Fifty-fourth, the *Yiqi yu* (Metaphor of the Supporting Wheels) states:
"For example, a forest depends on the earth-wheel; the earth depends on the water-wheel; the water depends on the wind-wheel; and the wind depends on..."
The wheel of emptiness is empty and has no basis; all Buddha-dharmas rely upon compassion, and compassion relies upon skillful means;

skillful means rely upon the four great wisdoms, and wisdom relies upon unimpeded insight (*prajñā*); insight has no basis. Regarding the analogy of the production of the four jewels from the fifty-one [elements], it is said:
"For example, the great ocean contains four precious jewels endowed with immeasurable virtues, which are able to produce one [jewel] within the sea."
Within the great ocean of wisdom of the Tathāgata Sarvaratnakośa, there are four great jewels of wisdom that are fully endowed with immeasurable merit and wisdom.

From these, the jewels of wisdom for all sentient beings—those in the stages of śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha, both those in training and those beyond training, as well as the bodhisattvas—are produced. This is the meaning of how the derivative arises based upon the fundamental. (52)

Regarding the analogy of being encompassed by letters: it is like written characters which universally enter into all things, all speech, all calculations, and all mundane and supramundane realms, yet they abide nowhere.
Likewise, the voice of the Tathāgata universally enters into all places, all sentient beings, all phenomena, all karmas, and all retributions, yet it abides nowhere.
Abiding in the various languages of all sentient beings, they never depart from the Dharma-wheel of the Tathāgata. Why is this?
Because the true reality (*dharmatā*) of vocal sounds is itself the Dharma-wheel. Regarding the analogy of all rivers entering the ocean:
"O Son of the Buddha, the wisdom of the Buddhas is infinite, boundless, and inconceivable. In this Jambudvīpa, there are two thousand five hundred rivers that flow into [the ocean]."
To the west of the great ocean, in Aparagoyānī, five thousand rivers flow into the great ocean;
to the east, in Pūrvavideha, seven thousand five hundred rivers flow into the great ocean; and to the north, in Uttarakuru, ten thousand rivers flow into the great ocean.
Son of the Buddha, these twenty-five thousand rivers of the four continents flow continuously and without interruption into the great ocean.
In the *Sāgara-parivarta*, these all represent the principle of subsuming the branches back into the root. At the end of the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter in the *Lotus Sūtra*, it says:

"The causes and conditions by which I have revealed and shown [the truth] are my skillful means; now, for your sakes, I speak of the most ultimate reality. This indicates that what came first was the provisional (*prajñapti*) and what follows is the ultimate (*tattva*).

In the "Parable of the City of Transformation," the Brahmās from the eastern direction request: "We only pray that you will deliver us and open the path to Nirvāṇa. The Brahmās from the southeastern direction... [text fragment].
The Brahmās of the Southern Quarter requested, saying: "We pray that you turn the Wheel of Dharma and reveal the characteristics of all phenomena.

The Brahmās of the Upper Quarter requested, saying: "We pray that you turn the Unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma. The Brahmās of the Highest Quarter requested, saying: "We pray that you reveal the path of Great Nirvana.

This represents the sequence from the partial to the complete. The teachings of Jñānavijaya and Bhīṣmagarjitasvara represent the sequence from the three to the one. These are illustrated by the metaphors of the well-digging and the crest-jewel.
This means starting with the small and ending with the great. Even the royal cuisine reveals the ultimate truth (*tattva*), while the skilled physician opens the provisional (*upāya*).
In the third fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it says: "For example, from Lake Anavatapta flow four great rivers; the Tathāgata is likewise, giving rise to all life from the root to the branches.
In the eighth fascicle, it says: "For example, as all streams flow back to the ocean, so do all sūtras converge in the Mahāyāna."
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* returns to its fundamental source. Section Five states: "For example, suppose there is an elder who has only one son.
Out of affection, he diligently teaches him the 'half-syllables' day and night, but does not instruct him in the *Vyākaraṇa* (grammar).
Why is this? Because the child is young and his strength is not yet sufficient. Once the son has grown up and is capable of reading and studying, at that time the elder..."
Having taught the half-syllables, he next expounds the Vyākaraṇa treatises; the Tathāgata is likewise.
Because the śrāvakas lack the power of wisdom, the Tathāgata teaches them the "half-syllable" ninefold canon but does not teach the Vyākaraṇa treatises or the Vaipulya Mahāyāna.
If the śrāvakas possess the capacity for such tasks, I shall likewise [teach them] at that time.

Having taught the "half-syllable" ninefold canon to his disciples, he next expounded the Vyākaraṇa-śāstra and the Mahāyāna sūtras—namely, that the Tathāgata eternally abides and is immutable—which represent the "full" teaching following the "half. Seventh, it is said:
For example, suppose a woman gives birth to an infant son who falls ill; this woman, distressed and troubled, seeks out a physician. The physician...
Once the teacher had arrived, he prepared a compound of three substances—ghee, milk, and honey—and gave it to him to drink. He then instructed the woman, "Do not give him milk for the time being;
only after the medicine has been digested may you give it to him. At that moment, the woman immediately smeared bitter substances upon her breasts.
When the medicine was fully digested, the mother washed her breasts clean with water and called her son, saying, "Come here!"
"Give this milk to your child. Upon hearing this, the child gradually returned to drinking it. The Tathāgata is likewise;
in order to deliver all beings, he teaches sentient beings to practice the Dharma of non-self. For the sake of cultivating emptiness, he says that all dharmas are entirely devoid of self.
By thus cultivating emptiness, they forever sever the mind of "I," enter nirvāṇa, and at that time, I speak of the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Therefore, bhikṣus should not give rise to fear, but should discern for themselves that the Tathāgata’s secret treasury must necessarily involve first employing provisional means and subsequently revealing the ultimate reality.
Regarding the full meaning [of this], the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the "Parable of the Dragon King Raining" (Chapter 51), states:
"For example, when the Dragon King Anavatapta raises great dense clouds that pervade Jambudvīpa, he pours down sweet [rain] everywhere."
It rains upon the hundred grains and all crops, which all attain growth; the rivers, streams, springs, and ponds are all filled to overflowing. The Tathāgata is likewise:

he raises the cloud of great compassion that pervades the worlds of the ten directions, universally raining down the unsurpassed Dharma-rain of ambrosia, causing all sentient beings to give rise to joy, increase their wholesome dharmas, and fulfill the various vehicles. He is also like the dragon Mānasa.
When a king intends to send down rain, he first raises a great cloud that completely covers the void, remaining suspended for seven days while waiting for all sentient beings to finish their labors;
after the seven days have passed, he sends down a fine rain that universally moistens the great earth. The Tathāgata is likewise:
when he intends to send down the rain of the Dharma, he first raises the cloud of the Dharma to bring sentient beings to maturity, desiring to ensure that their minds are not struck with alarm.

He awaits their full ripening before universally bestowing the nectar-like rain of the Dharma, expounding the profound, subtle, and excellent teachings to gradually lead them to fulfillment in the supreme flavor of the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*). This is like the rain of the *Avataṃsaka* and the clouds of the *Saṃghāṭa Sūtra*.
The turning of the light of the three teachings is the gradual process of maturation; thereafter, he bestows the rain of the Dharma—the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, regarding the analogy of the ocean-treasures that drink and contract [water], it is said: For example, within the great ocean there are four great jewels of blazing radiance spread across its floor;
their nature is extremely fierce and hot, and they are constantly able to drink up and contract the immeasurable waters poured into it by the hundred rivers.
First, when the radiance of the Great Treasure of the Sun’s Treasury shines upon the seawater, it entirely transforms the water into milk. Second, the Great Treasure of Separation from Moisture...

The light of the Great Jewel illuminates and touches the milk, and it all transforms into curd; the light of the Great Jewel of the Three Blazing Flames illuminates and touches the curd, and it all transforms into cream;

the light of the Great Jewel that Exhausts All Without Remainder illuminates and touches the cream, transforming it into clarified butter (ghṛta), blazing like fire until it is entirely exhausted without remainder.
Sons of the Buddha, if these four jewels did not exist within the great ocean, [the world would be deprived of these products].
From the four continents up to the pinnacle of existence (*bhavāgra*), all that exists therein is swept away and submerged by the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
This ocean of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom is fully endowed with four kinds of great jewels of wisdom and possesses immeasurable majesty, virtue, and radiance.

When the light of these jewels of wisdom touches the bodhisattvas, it causes them to attain the great wisdom of the Tathāgata; thus do the sons of the Buddha, the bodhisattvas, cultivate and accumulate it.
At all times, when immeasurable waves of distracted wholesome states arise as auxiliary factors for the path,
they cannot be destroyed by any worldly beings, devas, or asuras. The Tathāgata, through the light of the jewel of great wisdom that extinguishes all waves of distracted wholesome states,
touches those bodhisattvas, causing them to abandon all such waves and abide with the mind fixed on a single object.
Furthermore, the great jewel-light of wisdom that removes attachment to all dharmas touches those bodhisattvas,

causing them to relinquish their attachment to the flavor of samādhi and to give rise to vast supernormal powers. Moreover, the great jewel-light of wisdom that universally illumines with the light of insight touches those bodhisattvas,
causing them to relinquish the vast supernormal powers they have produced and to abide in the functional power of great illumination.
Furthermore, by means of the touch of the light of the great jewel of wisdom— which is equal to that of the Tathāgata, boundless, and effortless—
that bodhisattva is caused to abandon all exerted practices of great illumination, until they attain the ground equal to that of the Tathāgata,
where all effort is stilled without remainder. O Son of the Buddha, if it were not for these four jewels of wisdom of the Tathāgata, [the bodhisattva would not reach this state].
The light shines and touches, yet it is impossible for even a single bodhisattva to attain the stage of a Tathāgata;
this is the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* of the great ocean of wisdom. It possesses the four jewels of wisdom, and within the fundamental wheel, it fully contains the teachings of the latter two periods.
It drinks in and contracts the great waters of the hundred rivers, drying up the water of greed and attachment cultivated within the nature of the hundred realms. The Sun-Treasury shines forth.

The touching of the ocean water so that it transforms into milk refers to the *Āgama* teachings extinguishing the waters of craving— the mundane and heterodox precepts, the wholesome states of humans and devas, the wholesome dhyānas,
and all other [afflictions] of the three miserable realms— and thereby transforming them into the emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

The separation from moisture and the illumination such that the milk transforms into curd refers to the *Saṃdhinirmocana* teachings extinguishing the attachment to the Dharma within the partial truth samādhis of all the two vehicles, and thereby entering into the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and giving rise [to the wisdom of the Middle Way].

The various supernatural powers and transformations adorn the land; that the flames illuminate the curd so that it all becomes ghee signifies that through wondrous wisdom one teaches the cessation of all attachments to signs in the three vehicles, the clinging to the practice of the two kinds of emptiness, and the various cravings for dharmas, thereby achieving universal emptiness, giving rise to the practice of great illumination, and entering into the *prajñāpāramitā* of true reality.
That the remaining light transforms the ghee into clarified butter (*sarpis*) signifies the Dharma.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* teaches the extinction of all provisional vehicles—the various attachments to phenomena such as cultivation, realization, Buddhas, and birth—thereby attaining the perfection of Bodhi through non-attainment.
One enters the equality of the Buddha and sentient beings, the single vehicle-nature, and the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
In the "Burning House" parable of the *Lotus Sūtra*, if I were to rely merely on wisdom...

If one relies on the power of wisdom and spiritual penetrations while abandoning skillful means to praise for the sake of sentient beings the Tathāgata’s powers of knowledge and fearlessness, those sentient beings will be unable to attain deliverance through this;
it is like that elder who, although possessing strength in his body and arms, does not employ them.
This is the teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*. Rather, by means of the skillful means of wisdom, one delivers [beings] from the burning house of the triple world.
The Tathāgata preaches the three vehicles—the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the buddha-vehicle—to sentient beings;

by these skillful means, he entices and advances sentient beings, just as that elder preached of the goat-cart, deer-cart, and ox-cart to his sons, who immediately vied with one another to escape from the burning house.
This refers to the illumination of the three intermediate teachings. If the Tathāgata perceives immeasurable sentient beings through the Buddha’s teaching...
Upon emerging from the gate of the three realms of suffering, he then forms this thought: "All these sentient beings are my children;
I shall bestow upon them equally the Great Vehicle and not allow anyone to attain extinction alone, but shall cause them all to attain extinction through the extinction of the Tathāgata.
This is like that elder who, seeing his children safely emerge from the burning house, reflects upon his own immeasurable wealth and resources.

Bestowing great carriages upon the sons refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. In the "Parable of the Poor Son" (*Śraddhāparivarta*) and the "Emergence from the Earth" (*Bhūmyutsarpaṇa-parivarta*), they enter the Buddha-wisdom at the beginning and end [of the teaching].

In the "Expedient Means" (*Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*), at the very commencement of sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), he praises only the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*), which is non-dual and non-triple.
He went to Vārāṇasī and, within the single Buddha-vehicle, taught the three vehicles through differentiation; seeing those who sought Buddhahood, he preached the Buddha-wisdom for them.
The absence of any other vehicle and the existence of only the Single Buddha Vehicle all signify the meaning of the "Three Illuminations.
Furthermore, in the Parable of the Knot in the Garment within the *Vyākaraṇa-parivarta*, the priceless jewel tied inside one's clothing represents the teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*.

Wandering about in search and being satisfied with obtaining only a small amount represents the illumination of the Middle Teaching (*madhyama-deśanā*). Pointing out the jewel and exchanging it for things that fulfill one's wishes represents the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
In the Parable of the City of Illusion, sixteen princes requested that Mahāśravaṇa and Mahāpraticchanna preach the Great Sūtra;
each of those transformed—beings numbering six million billion nayutas of Ganges-sands—was taught the Buddha-wisdom of the Avataṃsaka.
Those who currently abide on the level of the Śrāvaka should enter the Buddha-way gradually by means of this Dharma. Why is this so?
The Tathāgata’s wisdom is difficult to believe and difficult to understand; it is the teaching of the Āgamas, Vaipulya, and Prajñāpāramitā.
Knowing for himself that the time for his parinirvāṇa had arrived and that the assembly was pure, he gathered the multitude of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas and preached this sutra for them.
In the world, there are not two vehicles by which one attains extinction; there is only the single Buddha-vehicle by which one attains extinction. Thus is the Dharma.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* is the teaching of the Flower [of the Dharma]. In the "Parable" chapter (*Upamā-parivarta*), the Buddha told Śāriputra:

"In the past, I taught you to set your aspirations on the Buddha-way; this was the first illumination. Now you have completely forgotten it and instead claim that you have already attained extinction (*nirvāṇa*);

this is the second illumination. I now cause you to remember your original practice of the Way by preaching the Mahāyāna sūtras; this is the third illumination. Among the eight [aspects of] *Nirvāṇa*, these correspond to the latter three illuminations.

The analogy of the medicinal juice flowing from a single flavor is as follows: For example, on Mount Himavat there is a medicinal herb called "Delightful Flavor" (*rasa-rati*), whose taste is exceedingly sweet.
In a past age, a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) fashioned a wooden vat to catch this medicine.
When the medicine flowed from the earth during its heated season, it collected within the wooden vat, and its flavor was pure and authentic. After the king had passed away, subsequently...
This medicine may be sour, salty, sweet, bitter, pungent, or bland; though it is of a single taste, it manifests various differences according to where it flows.
The true essence of this medicine remains in the mountain like the full moon.
Beings of meager merit, despite exerting effort through digging and excavating until they reach great hardship, are unable to obtain it. Yet, there shall appear a holy king.

In this world, through the causal conditions of merit, one immediately attains the true flavor of this medicine; this is the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka* when the Wheel-Turning King constructs a vessel to receive the medicine.
After the King has passed away, it flows along with the current and becomes the provisional teaching (*upāya-śāsana*);

this is the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* when the Sage-King appears once more and one again attains the true flavor. Ninth: It is like a great ship departing from this shore of the ocean.

Reaching the other shore and returning from there to this shore, the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, boards the precious ship of the Great Vehicle of Mahāparinirvāṇa and travels back and forth to ferry sentient beings across.
Wherever there are those who should be saved, he causes them all to behold the body of the Tathāgata; first he shines upon this shore of the sea, and then he shines upon the other shore.
Returning to this shore, it shines once more; it is also said that, like the *āmra* tree and the *jambu* tree, they undergo three transformations in a single year:
at times they produce flowers, their radiance and colors flourishing; at times they produce leaves, lush and verdant;
and at times they wither and fall, appearing as if dead. The Tathāgata is likewise; within the triple world, he manifests three kinds of bodies. At times, first...
There is the time of birth, the time of growth, and the time of parinirvāṇa; yet the body of the Tathāgata is truly not impermanent.

The initial stage is like the sudden blooming of flowers; the middle stage is like the gradual growth of leaves; and the final stage is like the withering and falling away. Regarding the metaphor of the five flavors within this middle stage, it is said:
"For example, from a cow comes milk; from milk comes curd; from curd comes fresh butter; from fresh butter..."
From clarified butter comes cream of clarified butter, and from cream of clarified butter comes ghee; the Buddha is also like this. From the Buddha come the twelve divisions of the scriptures;
from the twelve divisions of the scriptures comes the Sūtra; from the Sūtra comes the Vaipulya (Extensive) Sūtra;
from the Vaipulya Sūtra comes the Prajñāpāramitā; and from the Prajñāpāramitā comes the Mahāparinirvāṇa, just as [ghee is produced].

*Mahāmṛta* (the finest essence). From the cow comes milk, which is the initial *Avataṃsaka*. From that, curd and fresh butter arise, which correspond to the phenomena with and without marks (*nimitta*) in the *Madhyama Āgama*.
*Mahāmṛta* (Nirvāṇa) returns to illuminate the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa*. △ Regarding the meanings of these partial names:
the fifty-fascicle *Avataṃsaka* says, "For example, when the sun rises over Jambudvīpa, immeasurable sentient beings all..."

It brings about benefit by dispelling darkness and creating light, transforming moisture into dryness, causing grasses and trees to grow, bringing grain crops to fruition, clearing the void of space, and causing lotus flowers to bloom.
For those who travel, it reveals the path; for those who dwell at home, it clarifies their karmic affairs. Why is this?
Because the solar disc universally radiates immeasurable light, so too does the Tathāgata’s sun of wisdom universally benefit sentient beings through immeasurable deeds.
That is to say: extinguishing evil and generating good; breaking through ignorance to attain wisdom; protecting with great kindness and delivering with great compassion;

causing the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment to increase; engendering deep faith and causing one to abandon turbid minds; enabling the seeing and hearing of the non-destruction of cause and effect;
obtaining the divine eye to see the places of death and rebirth; making the mind unobstructed and the roots of goodness indestructible; and [attaining] wisdom.
By cultivating clarity, one causes the flowers of awakening to bloom, enabling the arousal of the bodhicitta and the fulfillment of fundamental practices. Why is this?
Because the sun-body of the Tathāgata’s vast wisdom emits immeasurable light that shines everywhere; thus, this refers specifically to the meaning of "first illumination.
As stated in [the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*] 59: "The sun of the Bodhisattva's True Dharma appears in the world, its wheel of precepts perfectly complete."

Moving with swift feet, he illuminates all with the light of wisdom; he increases the medicinal power of the faculties, extinguishes the darkness of afflictions, and dries up the ocean of craving and desire.

Regarding the sequence from the fifty intermediate [mountains] onwards: first he illuminates the King of Mountains (Sumeru), then the Black Mountains and the high plateaus, and finally the great earth.
Both the phenomena and the metaphors are clear; "first illumination" and "successive illumination" refer to their names and meanings. The sixty [fascicle version] says: "It is like space."
The sun and moon move without ceasing for even a moment; the Tathāgata is likewise, his spiritual transformations constantly continuing.

This metaphor illustrates the meaning of "successive illumination. The fifty-second [chapter] states: "Just as when the sun spreads its light over the dharma-realm, if the vessel is destroyed and the water leaks away, the reflection is extinguished accordingly;
so too is the sun of supreme wisdom: when sentient beings lack faith, they perceive nirvāṇa, yet this is merely a reflection cast back upon them."
This refers to the meaning of the name. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 19, states: "The Buddha-sun is about to set behind the mountain of Great Nirvāṇa.
When the Great King, the Buddha, departs from the world, there will be no one left to cure the heavy evils of the king; thus, [the light] shines back upon this single point alone.

△ Regarding the meaning of the name in its entirety, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, fascicle 50, says: "For example, as the sun and moon appear according to the seasons, they shine universally upon great mountains and deep valleys."
The Tathāgata Wisdom of Universal Illumination without Partiality shines universally upon all things without discrimination;
according to the differences in the faculties and desires of sentient beings, the light of his wisdom appears in various ways to illuminate them all.

Just as when the moon sets and the sun rises, it first illuminates the great mountains, and when the sun sets and the moon rises, it likewise illuminates the great mountains, so too does this wisdom shine universally at all times, turning its light to illuminate all.
The "deep valley" represents the differing capacities of those to be taught across the five assemblies; the "light" represents the differing teachings bestowed during the three periods.
Furthermore, it is said: "For example, when the sun rises, although blind sentient beings have never seen it before, they are nonetheless benefited by its light.
Why? Because by means of this light, they can discern day and night, the seasons, and enjoy appropriate regulation and comfort."

Because it is free from all afflictions, the sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise: sentient beings who are born blind due to their violation of precepts and views and lack of the eye of faith do not see the solar orb of the Buddhas’ wisdom. Although they do not see the Buddha, they are nonetheless benefited by the sun of wisdom.
Why is this? Because, through the majestic power of the Buddha, all the sufferings of those sentient beings are [extinguished].
Because [ignorance] is extinguished, there are the divisions of day and night: the first part of the day, the middle part of the day, and the latter part of the day.

One partakes of food during these three periods. "By the power of the Buddha" means that, through the solar orb of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, one is first able to hear and know the teachings—whether they concern the initial, middle, or final illuminations—and furthermore, causes those beings to be freed from suffering.
"Attaining bliss," section seventy-three, states: "For example, when the solar disc rises it is called day, and when it sets it is called night;

the wheel of a Bodhisattva’s wisdom is likewise. In teaching and transforming sentient beings, its abiding through prior kalpas and subsequent kalpas—within the *Avataṃsaka*’s direct manifestation of the teaching—it awakens the latent roots of goodness from past lives in sentient beings, causing those not yet planted to be planted; this is precisely what is meant [by 'abiding']."

In the past, during the preceding kalpa, when the sun first appeared, it was called "day"; at that time, those who had already planted seeds within the teachings of the *Phased* (turning and spreading) were caused to grow, which is termed the "intermediate kalpa of the present," like the sun rising to midday and being called "noon.

Within the teachings of the *Lotus Sūtra’s* Assembly for the Opening [of the One Vehicle], those who have already grown are caused to reach maturity; moment by moment, immeasurable sentient beings are led [to this state].
To attain non-retrogression in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is what is meant by saying that in future kalpas, when the sun has set, it is called "night";
thus, it is clear that the preceding and succeeding kalpas are defined in relation to the three periods of the present. As stated in section 46:
"All Buddhas, within a single moment, know all times; possessing pure roots of goodness, they enter the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*)."
Without abiding in or clinging to anything, he is able to manifest day and night, the beginning, middle, and end of time,
and even until the exhaustion of future kalpas, constantly turning the wondrous Wheel of Dharma for sentient beings without interruption,
without retreat, and without rest. The manifestation of day and night, beginning, middle, and end specifically clarifies the three periods within the Tathāgata’s entire dispensation.
"Exhausting the future" summarizes the three types of time within inexhaustible transformation. As stated in the second [chapter] of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
"For example, when the sun first rises, its radiance is exceedingly brilliant; it can both illuminate itself and dispel all darkness.
The light of the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers can likewise eliminate my suffering and afflictions while he dwells amidst the great assembly, like Mount Sumeru. Now I hear this.
When the Buddha enters *nirvāṇa*, the sun falls to the earth and the waters of the Dharma all dry up; we shall surely die.
When the Tathāgata passes into *parinirvāṇa*, sentient beings suffer extreme distress. It was first emitted to shine forth, and when the sun fell, it returned to shine;
turning its light back upon itself, it gathers [all] within. (The twenty-fourth fascicle states: "World-Honored One, if one generates *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the Buddha-nature..."
Why is it that the Tathāgata extensively expounds the twelve divisions of the sūtras for the sake of sentient beings?

World-Honored One, it is like the sun rising from Mount Udayana and reaching due south; if the sun were to think, "I shall not go to the west, but shall return to the east," such a thing is impossible.
The Buddha-nature is also like this: if one does not hear [the Dharma], does not observe the precepts, does not practice giving, and does not cultivate [virtue]...
"It is impossible that one who possesses wisdom should not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; such a thing cannot exist. The Buddha praised him, saying, "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
There are two kinds of people in the world: first, those who are skilled at posing questions; second, those who are skilled at answering.

You are the one who is skilled at posing questions, and the Tathāgata is the one who is skilled at answering. Son of good family, because of this skillful questioning, you shall immediately attain the turning of the unsurpassed [Dharma-wheel]."

If the Wheel of Dharma arises from the Buddha-nature to produce bodhicitta, it is the *Avataṃsaka*; if it is like the sun rising in the east to preach the twelve divisions of the scriptures, it is the *Vaipulya* and so forth;
if it is like the sun at its zenith in the south, such that even those who have neither heard nor practiced shall all attain bodhi and turn the unsurpassed wheel, it is the *Nirvāṇa*;
and if it is like the sun setting in the west. Section Nine says: "For example, when the sun rises, there are three [aspects]."
"Different times" refers to winter, spring, and summer. In winter days are short; in spring they are moderate; and in summer they are at their longest.
The Tathāgata is likewise: for those of short lifespan and for the śrāvakas within this trichiliocosm, he manifests a short lifespan, just as in winter;
for the bodhisattvas, he manifests a moderate lifespan, whether it lasts for one kalpa or slightly less.
