at the first of the thirty practices (*caryā*), both conceptual and innate seeds of the self-grasping (*ātmanirgraha*) are suppressed. The coarse portion is equal to the Initial Teaching...

In the Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi), one attains parity with the second stage of practice; within the two types of grasping, one truly subdues the coarse portions of the seeds of both conceptual and innate grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).

In the Wondrous Enlightenment (Prativedhabodhi), one attains parity with the third stage of practice; within the two types of grasping, one truly subdues the subtle portions of the seeds of both conceptual and innate grasping at self (*ātman-grāha*).
From this point onward, the stage of initial teaching (*ādikarmika*) is transcended; in the ten stages of practice, one fully subdues both [types of grasping].

In the forty preparatory stages (*prayoga*) leading to the first stage (*bhūmi*), one suppresses the coarse divisions of the seeds of both the conceptual and innate grasping at a real self and phenomena;

in the ten stages leading to the first stage, one suppresses the subtle divisions of the seeds of both the conceptual and innate grasping at a real self and phenomena; and in the five and four preparatory stages, one fully suppresses them.
Subduing the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the two attachments constitutes the "similar awakening" within initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*).

At the beginning of the sixth stage—the first stage—one exhausts the manifest activity and seeds of both the conceptualized and innate aspects of the two attachments; furthermore, one portion of their habitual tendencies is severed.

Throughout the ten stages, the habitual tendencies of the two attachments are severed in ten portions. At the seventh stage, equal awakening (*samyak-sambodhi*), the habitual tendencies of the two attachments are severed in eleven portions, proceeding until the Buddha-stage is reached.

A portion of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) constitutes the "partial awakening" within initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*). From the moment of first generating the resolve for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), one proceeds toward the causes of initial awakening until their completion.

When the eight kinds of wondrous awakening are perfected and the two types of grasping—both manifest and latent seeds as well as habitual tendencies—are exhausted, one attains ultimate awakening (*niṣṭhā-gata-bodhi*), which signifies the fulfillment of the fruit.
Within the *saṃbhogakāya* realm, one becomes a *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha; seated upon the Vajra Throne, one expounds the Great [Dharma].
By means of the Dharma that stores the mind of the vehicle, it causes those bodhisattvas of provisional teachings, persons of the two vehicles,
as well as a class of ordinary people and non-Buddhists of middling faculties, to transform the provisional into the real.

Within the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao), from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no severance or realization; yet, from the perspective of delusion, it is said that there are stages of affliction.
Furthermore, while this teaching originally possesses no gradations, when contrasted with what precedes and follows it, it appears to have levels of superiority and inferiority.

First, we clarify the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*). Within the first level of faith, there are also three stages: 1. **Non-awakening (abodha) and awakening (bodha), abiding in the nature (*dharmatā*):** This refers to the fundamental nature itself.

2. **Arousing the mind (*cittotpāda*):** In this stage, one suddenly suppresses the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*). Having already suppressed the coarse portions of the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of both discriminative (*vikalpita*) and innate (*sahaja*) grasping, this stage—from the beginning of the ten transferences (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) through the end of the seventh faith—attains the third [stage] of faith. Within the sudden suppression of the two graspings, it is completed.

First, regarding the subduing of the coarse and subtle portions of the active manifestations of both conceptual and innate grasping at a self: from the stage of small preparatory effort up to the end of the "Worldly Supreme Dharma" (laukikāgradharma), and from the beginning of the ten stages of faith (śraddhā) up to the seventh stage of faith, one simultaneously subdues the two types of grasping, first eliminating the coarse portions of the active manifestations of both conceptual and innate grasping at a self.

Furthermore, regarding the simultaneous subduing of the two types of grasping from the beginning of the first fruit (srotāpanna) up to the end of the first ground (bhūmi), and from the beginning of the first dwelling (vihāra) up to the tenth stage of faith, one first eliminates the coarse portions of the active manifestations of both conceptual and innate grasping at a self.
Excluding the coarse and subtle manifestations of the innate and discriminative grasping at a self, this is the "name-only awakening" of ordinary beings within the context of initial awakening;

it corresponds to the beginning of the Small Vehicle’s three fruits and the end of the fifth stage (pañcamī-bhūmi) up to the fifth dwelling (pañcama-vihāra). At the first of the twenty dwellings, one suddenly severs the two types of grasping;

among these, one first eliminates the manifestations of the innate and discriminative grasping at a self, and subsequently eliminates the manifestations of the innate and discriminative grasping at phenomena.

The manifest activity [of the path] is aligned with the beginning of the four small fruits; the initial seven stages (*bhūmi*) and final seven dwellings (*vihāra*) are aligned with the seventh dwelling, wherein one suddenly severs the coarse portions of the seeds of both conceptual and innate dualistic grasping, having first suppressed them;

the initial stage of wondrous enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*) and final two practices (*caryā*) are aligned with the tenth dwelling, wherein one suddenly severs the subtle portions of the seeds of both conceptual and innate dualistic grasping, having first suppressed them; and the final ten practices are aligned with the end [of the path].
Thirty stages. In the first stage, one suddenly severs the coarse portions of both the discriminative and innate seeds of the two attachments;

this is equal to the final portion of the ten faiths and the initial portion of the ten abidings. In the ten practices, one suddenly severs the subtle portions of both the discriminative and innate seeds of the two attachments, while simultaneously suppressing the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*);
this is equal to the final portion of the ten abidings and the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*). In the ten directions, the first direction suddenly...

6. By severing both the dualistic grasping and the innate [grasping], along with their manifest seeds and further severing a portion of their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), one attains parity with the end of the first stage (*bhūmi*).
By suddenly severing the ten portions of the habitual tendencies of the dualistic grasping during the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), one attains parity with the end of the tenth stage.

Through the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) of the fifth and fourth [stages], one exhausts the aforementioned habitual tendencies and advances to subdue the habitual tendencies of the first stage, thereby achieving the "initial awakening" (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) which constitutes the semblance-awakening prior to the middle stages.
In the first of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one suddenly severs eleven portions of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), which is equal to the final stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

In the second stage, one suddenly severs twelve portions of habitual tendencies, which is equal to the final stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*pratyakṣa-bodhi*). From the third stage onward, the names for these are not known in the Final Teaching (*paryantavāda*);
in the tenth stage, one suddenly severs twenty portions of habitual tendencies, and at the seventh stage of Equal Enlightenment, one suddenly severs twenty-one portions.

Advancing to sever one portion of the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of the Buddha-ground constitutes the "commencement of awakening" (*ārambha-bodhi*) within the "awakening according to stages" (*bhūmi-anupūrva-bodhi*).

From the initial generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*) onward, these all serve to draw forth the "inherent nature" (*prakṛti*) through the commencement of awakening. [The preceding section on] the perfection of causes is concluded.

The eighth, "wondrous awakening" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), involves the sudden severance of the two attachments (*dvaya-grāha*), the exhaustion of both manifest seeds and their habit-energies, and the realization of the Tathāgata’s ultimate awakening (*atyanta-bodhi*), thereby attaining the "attained nature" (*prāpta-prakṛti*). This occurs within the *dharmatā*-realm (*dharmatā-kṣetra*).
The Buddha of the Dharma-nature Body (dharmatākāya-buddha), seated upon the throne of empty space, preaches the Dharma of the true nature of the One Vehicle (ekayāna),

so that those bodhisattvas of gradual teaching, those of the two vehicles (dvayayāna), as well as various types of ordinary people of superior faculties and non-Buddhists (tīrthika), may gradually transform their gradual practice into the sudden (sudden enlightenment).

In the Fivefold Perfect Teaching (Wu yuanjiao), the stages of practice and their causes and fruits are none other than the Dharma-realm; as the Dharma-realm is perfectly interfused, the stages of practice are without obstruction.
Here, in contrast to the Final and Sudden Teachings, we clarify the characteristics of sequential progression (xingbu); yet in reality, from beginning to end, all are entirely interfused.

First, the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are clarified; within the first level of faith, there are also three stages: (1) non-enlightenment, which is the defiled *dharmadhātu* of sentient beings as opposed to original enlightenment;

(2) the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), in which stage one completely subdues the two types of grasping and has thoroughly suppressed the coarse and subtle manifestations of both conceptual and innate [afflictions], being equal to the beginning of the first level of faith—which corresponds to the initial stage of the "small" preparatory application (*prayoga*) up to its culmination in the "worldly supreme dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*). (3) The accomplishment...

When the fifth faith is perfected, having thoroughly subdued the two types of grasping, one has already eliminated the coarse portions of the manifest activity of both the conceptual and innate forms of self-grasping;

this is equal to the beginning of the Small Vehicle’s third fruit, the end of the fifth stage (*bhūmi*), and the initial attainment of the first dwelling (*vihāra*) during the sudden seven stages of faith.

When the fifth faith is perfected, having already eliminated the subtle portions of the manifest activity of both the conceptual and innate forms of self-grasping, it corresponds to the beginning of the Small Vehicle’s third fruit and the end of the fifth stage.

The fifth dwelling (*pañcama-vihāra*) is simultaneous with the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). Within the seventh stage of faith, one has fully suppressed the two types of grasping (*dvividha-grāha*);

among these, the afflicted grasping of self (*ātma-grāha*)—both its conceptual (*vikalpita*) and innate (*sahaja*) forms—is already eliminated, and its manifest activity (*samudācāra*) is further exhausted. One thus attains equality with the Small Vehicle’s four fruits (*catur-phala*), from the beginning of the seventh ground (*bhūmi*) up to the end of the seventh dwelling (*vihāra*).

At the initial dwelling, this is simultaneous. Within the ninth stage of faith, one has fully suppressed the two types of grasping; among these, the conceptual and innate [afflicted grasping] have been suppressed.
The coarse portion of the seeds [of the two attachments] is equal to the initial "subtle awakening" (ādikṣayabodha) at the end of the ten practices (daśacaryā) and the seven dwellings (saptavihāra).

Within the ten faiths (daśaśraddhā), one has already subdued the seeds of both the conceptual (vikalpita) and innate (sahaja) attachments; this subtle portion is the "awakening by name" (nāmabodhi) within initial awakening, which is equal to the final stage of the ten practices and the ten dwellings.
At the beginning of the twenty dwellings, the first dwelling completely severs the two attachments, and within this state, they have already been eliminated.
The coarse portions of the seeds of both the discriminative and innate [afflictions] are equal to the initial stages of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*),
while the subtle portions of the seeds of both the discriminative and innate [afflictions], along with the suppression of their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*),

are equal to the final four preparatory stages (*prayoga*) and the initial stage of the ten practices (*daśaprayoga*). At the beginning of the thirty [stages of practice], one completely abandons the manifest seeds of both the discriminative and innate [afflictions].

Furthermore, the partial severance of habit-energies (*vāsanā*) at the end of the ten stages of practice (*prayoga-mārga*) is equal to the initial stage of the ten stages of dedication (*adhimukti-caryā*).
The complete severance of the ten parts of habit-energies at the end of the ten stages of practice is equal to the ten stages of dedication at the end of the ten stages of the bodhisattva path.

The complete severance of the eleventh part of habit-energies at the beginning of the first stage of the forty stages of dedication is equal to the initial stage of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*). The complete severance of the twelfth part of habit-energies at the second stage of dedication...

Ultimately, the two stages of Wondrous Enlightenment (*miàojué*) and Sudden (*dùn*) are equal. At the tenth stage of Dedication (*shíxiàng*), the twenty parts of residual habituation (*xìqì*) in the Perfect-Sudden [practice] are equal to the ten stages of the Sudden.

At the fifth and fourth stages of Preparatory Application (*jiāxíng*), one exhausts the aforementioned habituations and advances to subdue the habituations of the first stage, thereby achieving the "similar enlightenment" (*xiāngsì jué*) within initial awakening (*shǐjué*).
At the sixth stage, the first stage [of the Perfect-Sudden], one perfectly severs the twenty-one parts of residual habituation, becoming equal to the Perfect Awakening (*děngjué*) of the Sudden.
Equal. At the second stage (*bhūmi*), the complete severance of the twenty-second portion of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) is equal to the sudden, wondrous enlightenment (*sadyo-abhisambodhi*).
From the third stage onward, the names for this are unknown in the Sudden Teaching (*tongjiao*). At the tenth stage, the complete severance of the thirtieth portion of habitual tendencies;

at the Equal Enlightenment (*samabhisambodhi*), the complete severance of the thirty-first portion of habitual tendencies; and by further severing the one portion of habitual tendencies of the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*), one achieves the partial realization of initial enlightenment (*ādikṣānti-anubodha*).

From the initial arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) onward, all belong to the stage of the Bodhisattva of Initial Enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*), which is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of both defilement and purity.

Having completed the section on the perfection of the cause, the eighth stage is the Perfect Enlightenment of the Wondrously Awakened One (*miàojué yuán*). Here, the two types of grasping—the manifest and the latent seeds—are severed and exhausted, resulting in Ultimate Enlightenment.
This is the Tathāgata’s purely pure Dharma-realm. Abiding within the land of the unobstructed Dharma-realm, one manifests as the Buddha-body of the unobstructed Dharma-realm.
Sitting upon the lion throne, he expounds the Dharma of the One Vehicle of the Dharma-realm, so that those bodhisattvas of partial teachings,

all those of the two vehicles who have turned their minds toward Buddhahood, and a certain class of ordinary people and non-Buddhists of the highest faculties may transform their partiality into perfection.

If one distinguishes the specific characteristics of the various capacities for benefit according to their sequence and circumstances, there are four types of capacities benefited within the initial Hīnayāna teachings. Within the first, the lineage of human beings (*manuṣya-gotra*), there are further two:

first, those of the *icchantika* lineage who lack roots of goodness; second, those of the lineage possessing roots of goodness, who are ordinary worldlings or non-Buddhists—namely, only the non-Buddhists.

These are the two lineages of the celestial beings: those who are rightly virtuous and those who are wrongly virtuous ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). Furthermore, within the wrongly virtuous, there are two types: first, the non-Buddhist celestial beings such as the Non-conceptualizers (*asaṃjñin*);
second, the celestial beings of the Māra kings, namely the two sovereigns of the Peak of Desire (*kāmadhātu*) and the Peak of Form (*rūpadhātu*).

As for the rightly virtuous, these are the ordinary person celestial beings: the six classes of gods of the desire realm, the gods from the Sphere of Infinite Space up to the Vast Fruit (*bṛhatphala*), and the four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). III.
The śrāvaka lineage and the pratyekabuddha lineage—each of these two has two types: first, those who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment] after coming from the realms of humans and devas;
second, those who proceed directly without passing through those [lower realms]. These four types of faculties are identical to those described in the *Taidi* (Skt. *Taitira*) Āgama.

In the assembly of the *Upadeśa*, they see the Buddha of Inferior Response (*hīna-nirmāṇakāya*), dwell in a defiled transformation land (*saṃkliṣṭa-nirmāṇabhava-kṣetra*), and for a short duration, conceal the ultimate truth while manifesting expedient means. They hear [the teaching].
The exposition of the precepts is based on the truth of the dependent origination of all phenomena.
Among those four classes of persons, each has two types: first, those of dull faculties who, whether through understanding or realization, abide within their own level and do not advance further;
they are termed "those of fixed nature" (niyata-gotra), as they merely accomplish the causes and effects of their current teaching and are thus subsumed under that teaching.
Second, those with sharp faculties—whether through understanding or realization—who transcend their own stage and advance forward are called "those of indeterminate nature" (*aniyata-gotra*).
This refers to those who penetrate the causes and fruits of other teachings and are subsumed by them. Furthermore, within this category of the indeterminate, three types are distinguished:

first, those who possess both transcending and sequential progression, entering the *dharmadhātu* after traversing all five teachings; second, those of the indeterminate type who transcend within the five teachings.
Because these three are incomplete and indeterminate, one directly transcends them by entering the Dharma-realm through any single teaching.

Now, first we shall discuss the precepts and virtues of humans and devas. Those who hear the teachings of humans and devas, cultivate various precepts and virtues, and give rise to the contemplation of the six practices, yet seek only worldly happiness and do not aspire for Nirvana, are termed those of dull faculties; they are subsumed under the Vehicle of Humans and Devas and achieve only the mundane.

There are two types of those who attain liberation from suffering within the realm through the wholesome discipline of outflows (*sāsrava-śīla*). First, there are those who, having attained pleasure, rest and do not advance further;
these are people of fixed nature among gods and humans, the most dull among the dull, and are included among those to be taught according to the *Śrāvaka-yāna*;

even if they encounter the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*), it serves merely to nourish them. Second, there are those who loathe the suffering of the three realms and joyfully seek *nirvāṇa*; these are called "indeterminate" (*aniyata*).
Among those of human and celestial nature who are dull, middling, or sharp, those who later encounter various teachings will necessarily be subsumed by them and transformed into other fruits.

If they understand that the wholesome merit of their precepts arises from causes and conditions, and they cultivate the contemplation of the emptiness of self while seeking liberation from birth and death and aspiring for the bliss of nirvana, they will be subsumed by the Two Vehicles and attain supramundane, untainted [attainments].
If they possess coarse and defiled wholesome merit of the precepts, they will obtain coarse and defiled liberation. If...

If one perceives the precepts and wholesome deeds as merely manifestations of consciousness and practices the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) for the sake of all sentient beings, practicing this for kalpas, one is subsumed under the Hīnayāna (Initial Teaching) of the Characteristics School (*lakṣaṇavāda*).

If, however, one realizes that the precepts and wholesome deeds are empty, signless, and true emptiness, and gives rise to the contemplation of true emptiness to practice the path of signlessness for the sake of all sentient beings, one is subsumed under the Hīnayāna (Initial Teaching) of the Emptiness School (*śūnyatāvāda*). Both of these result in the pure and wondrous state within the supramundane.

If one attains pure and wondrous liberation through the wholesome precepts by knowing that the treasury of wholesome precepts is inherently possessed within the mind and practicing the contemplation of "mind-only," then for the sake of all sentient beings, one proceeds from the nature toward cultivation;

this is the inclusion of the Final Teaching (Niṣṭhā-naya), whereby one immediately achieves untainted liberation that is both coarse and wondrous, wherein the wholesome precepts are themselves both coarse and wondrous.
If one understands that the wholesome precepts are solely the One True Nature and practices the contemplation of the True Nature...

If one contemplates for the sake of all sentient beings the practice of non-substantiality and is gathered by the Sudden Teaching, one immediately accomplishes the supramundane dharma of precepts that are neither coarse nor subtle,

and attains liberation that is neither coarse nor subtle. If one understands the dharma of virtuous precepts as the dependent origination of the dharma-realm and practices the contemplation of the dharma-realm universally for the sake of the entire dharma-realm,
being gathered by the Perfect Teaching which cultivates the perfect according to its nature, one immediately accomplishes the untainted (anāsrava).
Within the realm, they are universally integrated and inexhaustible; through the excellence of their precepts, they well attain all unobstructed liberations.
Since the time of the Lesser Vehicle, they have all been termed those of keen faculties, possessing directness and equal transcendence, yet even this is not fixed.

Next, regarding the exposition of the Four Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination: upon hearing the teachings on the truths and conditions of the Two Vehicles, one understands that these truths and conditions are the dharma of cause and effect.

One then gives rise to the sixfold contemplation (*ṣaḍākāra-bhāvanā*), yet remains attached to a self and what belongs to a self, seeking the pleasures of various realms of existence. This constitutes falling into the vehicles of the former [teachings] for humans and devas;

it results in mundane, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) truths and conditions, whereby one merely attains the cessation of suffering within the various evil realms of the world, but does not attain [ultimate liberation].
Regarding the true bliss of supramundane *nirvāṇa*, there are also two types of dispositions (*gotra*) among those suited for it:

first, those who do not turn back—namely, the aforementioned class of people of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) among devas and humans; second, those who go directly forward, possessing their own distinct lineage.

Therefore, these truths and conditions serve as auxiliary moisture for them. Although this remains so for the time being, they will ultimately enter [the path]. If one knows that these truths and conditions are the cause.

Taking as their object the arising of what is truly existent external to the mind, they cultivate the contemplation of self-emptiness (*ātmaśūnyatā*), desiring to swiftly escape the three realms and joyfully seek the bliss of *nirvāṇa*.
This constitutes the vehicle of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha; compared to the subsequent teachings, they are also termed those of dull faculties.

Having achieved only the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), they realize through the conditions of the truths of arising and ceasing—which are finite and conditioned—entry into *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*). This also has two types: the first is...
First, those of the indeterminate nature among humans and devas who turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna]; second, those whose lineage is established as naturally progressing in this way.

Within these two, there are again two types: first, those who, having already entered cessation, rest and no longer advance, being called the "determined-nature" (niyata-gotra) of the Two Vehicles—the most dull among the dull—who are only to be gathered by the teaching and, even upon reaching the initial stage, merely receive further nourishment; second, [those who do advance].

Those who are not yet satisfied with their own state and seek further advancement are called those of "indeterminate nature" (*aniyata-gotra*). Among those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), those who are dull but relatively sharp are gathered by various teachings and subsequently enter [the Mahāyāna];

thus they are "indeterminate" from beginning to end. If they recognize that all objects of consciousness are manifestations of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and practice the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra-darśana*), they universally cultivate for three great eons (*tri-kalpa-asamkhyeya*) for the sake of both themselves and others; they are then gathered by the teachings of the *Abhidharma* and *Yogācāra* schools and thereby become Great Vehicle practitioners.

If one realizes that the immeasurable marks of the truths and their conditions enter into non-abiding *nirvāṇa*, and understands that these conditioned phenomena are all like illusory manifestations and are thus empty by nature, then although sentient beings are empty, one cultivates illusory practices;
this is subsumed within the Emptiness School (*śūnyatāvāda*) of the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*), which constitutes the Mahāyāna of the markless truth of non-arising.
If one knows that the truths and their conditions are fundamentally the *tathāgatagarbha*, [one enters the true emptiness *nirvāṇa*].

If one gives rise to the contemplation of mind-only, accords with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and performs various meritorious deeds, being subsumed by the teaching of reality, one immediately achieves the Mahāyāna of immeasurable nature, truth, and conditions, entering true and eternal *nirvāṇa*.

If one awakens to the fact that these conditions of truth are solely the nature of *tathatā*, and gives rise to the contemplation of *tathatā*, then although knowing quiescence, one cultivates the practice of self-realization; being subsumed by the sudden teaching, one immediately achieves the Mahāyāna of non-arising.
If one realizes that the nature of reality, the truths, and their conditions lead into the quiescent nirvana, and understands these truths and conditions as the arising of the Dharma-realm,

then by performing the contemplation of the Dharma-realm throughout the ten Dharma-realms and cultivating the practices of Samantabhadra, one is encompassed by the Perfect Teaching (Paryanta-yāna) and becomes the One Vehicle (Ekayāna)—
the effortless, inconceivable, universally harmonious, and inexhaustible realization of the truth and conditions that enters into the Tathāgata’s ultimate, unobstructed Great Parinirvāṇa.
In the teachings of our own tradition, all are referred to as having "sharp faculties" (*tīkṣṇendriya*), being "straightforward" (*ṛjukāya*), and so forth;

yet these categories are also not fixed. Question: At what stage does one enter [the path], by which teaching is one subsumed, and by what means is one introduced and led forward? Answer: Regarding those first subsumed and entered:

among humans, those with superior faculties (*uttamendriya*) enter when they hear the Dharma and attain faith and understanding (*śraddhādhimukti*); those with middling faculties (*madhyendriya*) enter when they have practiced for a long time and attained power (*balaprāpta*); and those with inferior faculties (*mṛdvindriya*) [enter]... [text fragment ends].

Regarding the faculties (*indriya*): during the stage of maturation and subduing delusions, within these three positions, one attains entry into the Small, Initial, Sudden, or Perfect [vehicles] according to the magnitude of the understanding and practice that arise.

Next, among the two vehicles (*śrāvaka-yāna*), those of superior faculty do so at the stage of skillful means (*upāya*); those of middling faculty, during the paths of seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-mārga*);
and those of inferior faculty, at the stage of the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*). This is likewise according to the depth of their understanding and practice.
"Deep" means that one attains entry through the gradual and sudden, from the beginning to the end, reaching the Perfect. Second, regarding the capacity to encompass and enter the teachings:

first, within the Human and Celestial [vehicles], according to the Path of Teaching (*jiao dao*), it begins with the stage resembling [the path of seeing] and the Small Worldly First Dharma, and ends with the Sudden and Perfect at the Ten Directions; those below the Ten Faiths are included.

According to the Path of Realization (*zheng dao*), the True Stage Small [Vehicle] begins with the First Fruit and the First Ground, and ends with the Sudden and Perfect at the First Abode and above; all [stages] from this point upward are included.
It is capable of guiding those of indeterminate nature among humans and devas to progress toward the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), the Initial [Vehicle], the Sudden, or the Perfect.

Furthermore, regarding the second category—those within the Two Vehicles—it guides those at the stage of semblance, such as the Ten Directions of Dedication (*daśa-praṇidhāna*), and those at the true stage, such as the First Ground (*prathamā-bhūmi*), to progress from the Small Vehicle and enter the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*).
Question: By what teachings and principles is this subsumed? Answer: There are cases where it provides instruction by relying on the teachings of others, such as when subsuming humans.

The heavens likewise rely on the precepts and virtues; the Hīnayāna likewise relies on the truths and conditions, as explained above. There are those who rely on their own teachings to achieve awakening:
for example, those among humans and devas who seek supramundane discernment of the partial truth employ the Four Truths to encompass them;
if they awaken to suffering and emptiness and delight in solitary tranquility, they employ Dependent Origination to encompass them—just as the followers of the Two Vehicles realize all phenomena.

The abandonment of the two attachments is subsumed under the *Phenomenal Teaching* (Phenomenology) school; the realization that all phenomena are empty and the attainment of the two kinds of selflessness are subsumed under the *Initial Teaching* (Emptiness) school, as explained below.
Question: What is meant by "possessing the direct, the indeterminate, and the transcendence of characteristics"? Answer:

Knowing that the roots of all precepts and virtues are fundamentally without a self transcends the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*); furthermore, knowing that there are no phenomena (*dharma*) transcends the Initial Teaching.

Furthermore, the fact that this *ālayavijñāna* (the storehouse mind) transcends the ultimate signifies its transcendence of the final; that its nature is fundamentally beyond words signifies its transcendence of the sudden; and that dependent origination is inexhaustible signifies its transcendence of the perfect.

That it possesses these marks of transcendence and realizes that the wholesome dharmas of the precepts are empty and devoid of marks signifies its transcendence of the initial; that there is only the single true nature signifies its transcendence of the sudden;

and that its nature gives rise to successive layers of phenomena signifies its transcendence of the perfect. These indeterminate marks are the realization of the mutual interfusion of the precepts and wholesome dharmas.

Pervasive, fused, encompassing, and detached—apart from this Dharma-realm, there is no other dharma; this is precisely how the precepts and virtues of humans and devas directly transcend the characteristics of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
This may be understood by analogy with the Truth and Conditions (Diyuan).

Second, regarding the capacities and suitability benefited within the Initial Teaching (Shijiao), they are briefly divided into three categories: first, the class of those lacking the nature for enlightenment (wuxing chanditi).
Second, those of fixed nature comprise three categories of the five vehicles; third, those of indeterminate nature encompass the preceding two categories.
Within these three natures, each further possesses two types: first, those who have previously [attained realization]; second, those who advance in the present.

These are identical to what was taught in the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and *Prajñāpāramitā* assemblies, wherein one beholds the supreme Nirmāṇakāya Buddha dwelling in the Pure Nirmāṇarati realm, and—according to the duration of their cultivation—hears both the provisional and the ultimate teachings simultaneously revealed.
Regarding the teaching on the true emptiness of the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*):

if one hears the Mahāyāna *vijñaptimātra-lakṣaṇa* (the characteristic of consciousness-only) and, identifying these characteristics, gives rise to the three realms through the six modes of contemplation (*ṣaḍākāra-bhāvanā*),

mixing this with the afflictions while practicing various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), this likewise falls into the teachings of the previous vehicles of humans and devas, and thus becomes mundane.
The characteristics of the dharma of cause and effect can only suppress karma but cannot sever delusions.

If one knows that these dharmic characteristics are phenomena of arising and ceasing that exist in dependence upon the six consciousnesses and the three poisons, and thus gives rise to a partial realization of ultimate truth (*tathyatā*), seeking with delight transcendence and solitary liberation—this still falls within the previous teachings of the Two Vehicles.
It constitutes the dharma-characteristics of the world-transcending, untainted (*anāsrava*) state, which severs the afflictions within the realm.

The hindrance of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) also has two types of dispositions (*yogyatā*), which likewise comprise two categories: first, those who do not turn back, namely those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) mentioned in the preceding teaching;

second, those who proceed directly, as this category of lineage (*gotra*) exists by its very nature (*dharmatā*). Therefore, these characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) also serve to provide nourishment and moisture.

If one realizes that these characteristics of phenomena exist based upon the eight consciousnesses, one practices the contemplation of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra-darśana*); through three great aeons (*tri-kalpa*) and a hundred eons (*śata-kalpa*), one extensively cultivates [this practice].
The myriad practices herein constitute the characteristics of the Mahāyāna according to the Dharma-characteristics (Faxiang) school.

Compared with the subsequent teachings, this is also termed the "dull-rooted" [path], which achieves only the *vijñaptimātra* dharma-characteristics and severs the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) beyond the realms. This also has two types:

first, those who turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], namely those of indeterminate nature within the aforementioned teaching; second, those who proceed directly [to the goal], who originally possess such a spiritual lineage (*gotra*). Among these two:

Furthermore, regarding the two categories: first, those who enter the Dharma-realm after the latter three teachings, or after passing through two teachings, and only then attain the perfect fruit—these individuals of the three vehicles who are the "dullest among the dull" are categorized within the present teaching as having a "fixed nature" (*niyata-gotra*) even amidst the Sudden Teaching.

Second, those who, upon hearing the final teaching, immediately seek higher advancement—these individuals of the three vehicles who are "sharp among the dull" and possess an "unfixed nature" (*aniyata-gotra*) are for that [Sudden Teaching].

Regarding the inclusion through teaching: if one realizes that all phenomena are empty and practices the contemplation of non-arising, then although all phenomena are empty, one does not abandon anything;

this is subsumed under the Initial Teaching (Śrāvakayāna) and the Emptiness School (Mādhyamika), whereby one achieves true emptiness and signlessness (*animitta*), yet only severs the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

If, however, one understands the characteristics of phenomena as the dependent origination of mind-only and practices the contemplation of the *ālayavijñāna*, deeply penetrating the true reality (*dharmatā*) where the three natures are non-differentiated, [this constitutes the final teaching].

If one is subsumed under the *xingzong* (Nature School) *shijiao* (Teaching of Reality), one realizes the true aspect of *tathatā* (*zhenshi xiang*) and gradually severs the seeds of the two obstacles;

if one penetrates the *faxiang* (Dharma Characteristics), this is the reality of the true nature, and by giving rise to the contemplation of true nature, one realizes that the characteristics of all phenomena are quiescent in every respect.

If one is subsumed under the *xingzong* *dunjiao* (Sudden Teaching), one realizes the aspect of eternal quiescence and suddenly severs the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the two obstacles; if one clarifies the *faxiang*, [the same result follows].
Universally fusing the inexhaustible, one performs the contemplation of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong guan*); all phenomena are pervasive and all matters are unobstructed.
From the perspective of the Perfect Teaching of the Nature School (*xingzong yuanjiao*), they are subsumed and thus become the marks of the inexhaustible Dharma-realm;
from the perspective of the Final Teaching (*zhongjiao*), they are all termed "sharp faculties" who possess direct transcendence and so forth, yet this is also not fixed.

Furthermore, one may hear of the Mahāyāna’s true emptiness and signlessness, yet upon understanding that emptiness, merely transcend the sufferings of the various realms of existence by giving rise to the contemplation of the six aspects (*ṣaḍākāra-bhāvanā*), ceasing evil conduct, practicing good, and seeking happiness in the present and future.
This too falls within the teachings of the vehicles of humans and devas; it constitutes the emptying of worldly, outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) dharmas.

Such a person only understands the emptiness of annihilation (*prahāṇa-śūnyatā*) and does not penetrate the emptiness of principle (*tattva-śūnyatā*). If one knows true emptiness, there is no self and nothing belonging to a self (*anātman-anātmīya*).

To practice the contemplation of suffering and emptiness, to feel weary of and distressed by [saṃsāra], and to abide in cessation and the path—this also falls within the preceding Small Vehicle teachings of the Two Vehicles, whereby one achieves the supramundane, outflow-free emptiness of sentient beings and the extinction of the realm of internal, delimited death. Furthermore, these two types of roots also have two aspects:

first, those who do not turn back, namely the aforementioned fixed-nature [śrāvakas] and others; second, those who go directly, which exists as a natural law (*dharmatā*). Therefore, this [latter category] does not [belong to the former].

Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are also further moistened; if one awakens to true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) such that no characteristics of dharmas arise, and one practices the three contemplations of emptiness (*trividha-śūnyatā-darśana*), and furthermore bestows non-characteristic giving for the sake of sentient beings—this constitutes the Mahāyāna school of Emptiness (*śūnyatāvāda*).
This is the Initial Teaching (*ādikāya*), which, when contrasted with the subsequent teachings, is also termed "for those of dull faculties.

It achieves only the single flavor of true emptiness and extinguishes the death of transformation (*nirmāṇa-cyuti*) outside the realms. This also has two aspects: first, the turning of the mind (*citta-parāvṛtti*).
Regarding those of the previously mentioned indeterminate nature who progress directly—among these two types of innate lineage, there are further two subcategories:

first, those who pass through the three subsequent teachings; second, those who attain the perfect fruit after the [second] teaching. These are termed those of "determined dull" nature within the dull. Those of the "dull-dull" type are subsumed under the present teaching.
Those of the "dull-sharp" type encounter the subsequent final teaching and immediately enter it; they are termed those of "indeterminate sharp" nature. As for those...

If one follows the teachings to subsume [the view] within the True Emptiness (śūnyatā), this merely negates the existence of external objects and gives rise to the contemplation of the eight consciousnesses;

by abandoning the two types of self-grasping, one awakens oneself and awakens others—this is subsumed under the Teaching of Characteristics (Lakṣaṇayāna). Once this is achieved, one realizes the emptiness of the two non-selves; furthermore, one merely cuts off the death of transformation (nirmāṇa-maraṇa).
If one penetrates that True Emptiness is but the functioning of the One Mind, and practices the contemplation of the One Mind according to the various dispositions, one will achieve self-realization.

If one is subsumed under the teachings of the Final Vehicle (Niṣṭhā-yāna), it results in the emptiness of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-śūnyatā*), wherein birth and death are severed through both partial and transformative means;

if one awakens to the true emptiness whose nature is originally beyond words, one practices the contemplation of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā-dhyāna*) and transforms all sentient beings from the place that is fundamentally without origin.

If one is subsumed under the teachings of the Sudden Vehicle (Aksara-yāna), it results in the emptiness of non-arising (*anutpāda-śūnyatā*), wherein birth and death are severed neither partially nor through transformation; if one realizes the principle of true emptiness...
The true dharma-realm constitutes the unimpeded contemplation wherein the one and the many enter simultaneously; this is fully present in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

When subsumed [by this], it becomes the ultimate dharma-realm (*paramārtha-dharmadhātu*). From the Final Teaching (*zhongjiao*) onward, both the emptiness of the realm and the cutting off of the internal and external realms are called the two kinds of inconceivable and inexhaustible birth-and-death;
these are naturally terminated. All are termed those with sharp faculties who possess direct transcendence, and they are likewise not fixed.

However, regarding those categorized within the initial stage [of the Separate Teaching], those of superior faculties enter during the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) and the three stages of worthiness (*kṣānti*); those of middling faculties enter during the four stages of application (*prayoga*) and the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*);

and those of inferior faculties enter during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) and the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). According to their respective understanding and practice, they provisionally or ultimately transition into the subsequent three teachings.

As for the capacity to include them within the teachings, this refers to the provisional positions up to the end of the ten stages of faith in the *Sudden*, *Gradual*, and *Perfect* teachings, as well as the true positions.

From the final stage of the Sudden Teaching up through the first abode of the Perfect Teaching, all are able to lead those of the three vehicles forward into the latter three teachings; the rest may be understood by analogy with what precedes.
Within the third, the Final Teaching, the capacities and conditions of those benefited likewise do not deviate from the five natures; among these, there are also two types within the three vehicles.

The first refers to those who have come before, and the second refers to those currently advancing. Together, they witness the Buddha of the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) abiding in the Land of Enjoyment at the assembly of the Wondrous Wisdom Nirvana;

according to the duration of time—whether long or short—they set aside provisional teachings to establish the ultimate reality, expounding the Dharma of the *tathāgatagarbha* as the source of dependent origination.
If one hears of the *tathāgatagarbha*, one immediately recognizes that the essence of the *garbha* is the six consciousnesses giving rise to the six [objects].

If one practices contemplation by turning away from defilement toward purity and performing tainted meritorious deeds, this also falls within the teachings of the previous vehicles of humans and devas;
it is still called the "mind-nature pure while enmeshed," for it does not yet achieve liberation from entanglements or the purity that is free from defilement.

If one knows that the *tathāgatagarbha* mind is solely the *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness) and performs the contemplations of suffering and emptiness, forever abandoning craving and removing all objective obstacles, this also falls within the previous two vehicles.
The Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) involves entering the empty *tathāgatagarbha* to achieve the realization of non-self and formlessness;

if one penetrates the *garbha*-mind, it becomes the *ālayavijñāna*, through which one performs the contemplation of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only), transforming the defiled basis into the pure and accomplishing the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*).

This also falls within the categorized teachings of the preceding *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic) school. If one understands the *garbha*-mind as being like an illusion or a dream and performs the contemplation of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), all consciousnesses are extinguished.
The contemplation that severs the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) also falls within the aforementioned Emptiness school’s Initial Teaching;

these two types of practitioners both enter the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha* to achieve the stainless, unarisen Bodhi of Perfect Enlightenment. Among the four superior types of persons mentioned above, there are two categories for each:
first, those who turn their minds (referring to those of determinate or indeterminate nature within the preceding teachings); second, those who proceed directly in the present dharma.

Because you possess these four natures, this *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse mind) serves as their supportive moisture. If one awakens to the *tathāgatagarbha* (womb of the Tathāgata) as being unchanging despite following conditions, and practices the contemplation of "mind-only" (*cittamātra*), its essence and function will constantly permeate [the mind], causing the *dharmakāya* to manifest. This constitutes the True Teaching of the Mahāyāna Nature School;

compared to the subsequent Sudden and Perfect [teachings], it is also called the teaching for those of dull faculties, wherein one enters only into the *tathāgatagarbha* which is both empty and not empty. Thus is it accomplished.

The perfect and universal knowledge of enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), which is neither impermanent nor subject to annihilation, is also of two kinds: first, those who turn their minds [toward awakening], namely those of the "definite" and "indefinite" types mentioned in the preceding teaching;
second, those who proceed directly and enter [the path] immediately, as described in the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*). Within these two, there are again two sub-categories:

first, those who proceed directly to the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*) and subsequently enter the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which also encompasses the gradual passage through the Sudden Teaching (*tathatā-yāna*); and second, those who are ultimately included within the Real Teaching (*bhūta-yāna*).

This is called "the dull among the dull. Second, those who encounter the subsequent Sudden Teaching, or who redirect themselves toward the Sudden, or who enter the Perfect—being encompassed by these teachings—are called "the sharp among the dull.

If one understands that the nature of the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) is fundamentally quiescent, gives rise to the contemplation of the single nature, and, through its total cessation and lack of dependence, achieves the realm of self-awakening, one is encompassed by the Sudden Teaching and immediately enters it.
The Tathāgatagarbha is neither empty nor non-empty; it constitutes the unconditioned realm of practice for the sages, the supreme and wondrous Perfectly Complete Enlightenment (Samyaksaṃbodhi).

If one realizes this mind of the Garbha, which universally encompasses all phenomena, one gives rise to the Indra-net contemplation. This realization penetrates from cause to fruit, attaining the Ten Mysterious Gates.
When the Perfect Teaching (Ekayāna) comes to encompass and integrate all, there is no obstruction whatsoever. Thus, the Tathāgatagarbha becomes the basis for inexhaustible dharmas.

The unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) is termed "sharp faculties" following the Sudden Teaching; it is characterized by directness, equality, and transcendence, yet it is also indeterminate.

△ However, in the ultimate reality, those who enter are categorized as follows: those of superior faculties during the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), those of middling faculties during the stage of the three worthies (*tri-puṇya-kṣetra*), and those of inferior faculties during the stage of the ten sages (*daśa-ārya*).
According to the superiority or inferiority of their understanding and practice, they successively enter the latter two stages.

The teaching can also encompass those who enter through the semblance stage (*sadr̥śa-avasthā*)—the sudden perfection from the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) downward—and those who enter through the true stage (*bhūta-avasthā*)—the sudden perfection from the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) upward; all are able to be led into the sudden perfection.

Within the capacities benefited by the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao), there are two categories: first, those of the aforementioned five vehicles' dispositions; second, those currently progressing toward the nature of existence or non-existence.
This is identical to the *Awakening of Faith* (*Yuanjue*) and the assembly at the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, wherein one perceives the Dharma-nature body Buddha dwelling in the Dharma-nature land.
According to the breadth or narrowness of their respective temporal capacities, the provisional is set aside and the real is praised, as they hear the teaching of the tranquil true nature.

The Dharma of Extinction. △ If one hears of the *tathatā-dharmatā* (the true nature of reality) and immediately understands that this true nature is the arising-nature of the six consciousnesses, yet gives rise to views of longing for and aversion toward them—reforming evil and transforming toward good in order to seek the rewards of humans and devas—this falls into the teachings of the previous vehicles of humans and devas.

One remains within the originally existing true nature, but because the perfectly luminous nature has not been realized, if one awakens to this true nature as a partial truth, the birth [of delusion] arises.

If one uses the contemplation of emptiness to sever the afflictions of views and thoughts and attains the selflessness of persons, this falls within the preceding Small Vehicle teachings of the Two Vehicles;
one enters the true suchness and dharma-nature of the emptiness of self, thereby achieving the pure wisdom of the Small Vehicle.

If one recognizes that true nature is the nature of consciousness-only and practices the contemplation of consciousness-only, thereby distancing oneself from the parikalpita (imagined) nature and entering the pariniṣpanna (perfected) nature, this then falls within the preceding categorized teachings of the Characteristics School (Xiangzong). If...

To realize the true nature as the nature of true emptiness, to give rise to the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*), and to extinguish all existence by entering the three non-natures—this belongs to the preceding school of Emptiness, the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*).
Those who follow these two teachings both enter into the dharma-emptiness, true suchness (*tathatā*), and the dharma-nature, thereby accomplishing the Great Vehicle’s omniscience.

If one knows that the true nature is the nature of dependent origination, one gives rise to the contemplation of the *ālayavijñāna* (store-consciousness), turning away from sense objects and merging with [the source].

Awakening to the entry into the Tathāgatagarbha means falling into the final teaching of the Nature School (Xingzong), whereby one enters the non-empty *tathatā* (suchness) and the dharma-nature to achieve the Great Vehicle’s Perfect Universal Wisdom (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Among the aforementioned five types of persons, there are two categories:

first, those who turn their minds, which refers to those of the "fixed" and "unfixed" types within the previous teaching; second, those who proceed directly, which refers to those who advance from this lineage within the present teaching.

This true nature serves as the moisture that assists them. If one realizes that this true nature is the nature of non-arising (*anutpāda-dharmatā*) and practices the contemplation of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-bhāvanā*), remaining as it truly is by being free from subject and object, this constitutes the sudden teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Compared to the subsequent Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), this is also termed "dull faculties," yet by entering into ineffable true suchness (*nirabhilāpya-tathatā*) and the nature of phenomena, one attains the immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) of the One Vehicle. This also has two types: first, [the dull-facultied].

Regarding those who turn their minds, there are two types within the aforementioned teaching of the fixed and unfixed natures: first, those who proceed directly in the teaching of immediate advancement;

second, among these two, there are again two sub-types: first, those who, having heard the subsequent Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇa-yāna*), still remain hindered by the Sudden Teaching, waiting until their practice and realization are exhausted before finally returning to the Perfect;
these are called the "dull among the dull. Second, those who, upon hearing the Perfect Teaching for the first time, immediately...

Entering into this perfection is what is called "the sharp among the dull. If one realizes that the true nature is the nature of the *dharmadhātu* and performs the ten mysterious contemplations (*daśa-gūḍha-vipaśyanā*), then delusion is exhausted and one returns to the source;

the nature of the source is inexhaustible. When one is subsumed by the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), one enters the Great Universal Characteristic of the Single Dharma-realm, the True Suchness of the Dharma-nature, and achieves the inconceivable wisdom of the One Vehicle. In contrast to the Original Sudden Teaching, this is termed...
Those of sharp faculties. △ However, among those included within the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao), those of superior faculties do so during the stage of the Ten Faiths (shixin);

those of medium faculties do so before the stages (dixian); and those of inferior faculties do so from the stages onward (dishang). All are able to turn the Sudden toward the Perfect (yuan). Furthermore, regarding the teachings that can include them:

the semblance stage of the Perfect (simwei yuan) corresponds to the stage of faith (xinwei), while the true stage of the Perfect (zhenwei yuan) corresponds to the stage of abiding (zhuiwei). In all cases, one is able to use the Perfect to lead the Sudden.
Within the Fivefold Perfect Teaching (*pañca-pūrṇa-yāna*), there are likewise two classes of practitioners who benefit: first, those of the aforementioned three and five vehicles;

second, those currently advancing who possess or lack the Buddha-nature (*gotra*). This is identical to the assemblies at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Avataṃsaka* sūtras, where one beholds the Buddha’s body of the inexhaustible Dharma-realm dwelling in the land of the unobstructed Dharma-realm, according to all those times and occasions that are both "all" and "not-all."

Kuan Hsien heard the teaching on the inexhaustible Dharma-realm. △ If one hears of the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm and understands that this Dharma-realm is itself the phenomena of the world, they will give rise to the contemplation of joy and aversion, abandon all evil karma, and swiftly obtain wholesome benefits;

yet this merely falls within the teachings of the vehicles of gods and humans, remaining within the entanglements of the intrinsically pure Dharma-realm without having emerged from obstructions to achieve perfect clarity.
Therefore, if one perceives the dharma-realm as a supramundane dharma, giving rise to contemplation based on the truths to loathe old age, sickness, death, and to exhaust the limit of all suffering—
this then falls within the preceding Lesser Vehicle teachings of the Two Vehicles, wherein one realizes the unconditioned dharma-realm and returns to the nature of pure,

boundless quiescence. If, however, one understands the dharma-realm as comprising a hundred dharma-gates, giving rise to the contemplation of dharmic characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and single-mindedly cultivating various practices for the sake of the Buddha-way...

To practice in this way is to fall into the preceding category of the Characteristics School (Lakṣaṇayāna). If one realizes that the Dharma-realm is the eighteen emptinesses and gives rise to the contemplation of the destruction of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-bhaṅga*), with a mind free from attachment and seeking unsurpassed wisdom, this then falls into the preceding category of the Emptiness School (Śūnyatāvāda), the Initial Teaching (Ādikarmika-yāna).
Those of these two schools both realize the conditioned Dharma-realm and return to the boundless without losing its nature; if one penetrates the Dharma-realm, it is these two gates.

To contemplate the nature of conditions through the principle [of dependent origination], to thoroughly understand all dependent arisings, and to seek the Supreme Vehicle— this falls within the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao) of the Nature School (Xingzong),
which realizes that there are both conditioned and unconditioned dharmas within the Dharma-realm, and that one accords with the infinite nature.
If one understands that the Dharma-realm is the single nature of mind and practices the contemplation of emptiness, abiding in the Dharma-nature as if it were empty space— this then falls into...
The preceding Nature School’s Sudden Teaching—that realization is neither conditioned nor unconditioned—converges upon the single nature of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which is uninterrupted.
Among the six types of persons mentioned above, each contains two categories: first, those who turn their minds, whose natures are either fixed or unfixed within the previous teaching;
second, those who proceed directly, whose seed-nature advances through the present teaching. Thus, this dharma-realm serves as an aid for them.

If Run were to know that the dharma-realm arises through ten sets of ten gates, and by practicing the "master-and-retainer" contemplation (*shobun-kwan*) throughout the realms of the finite and the infinite, he would preach the Dharma to benefit sentient beings;
this constitutes the Perfect Teaching (*enkyō*). When compared with the preceding teachings, all of those are termed "dull," while only this is "sharp.

It is able to realize the unobstructed dharma-realm and return to the nature of infinite adornment. This also has two types: the first is the turning of the mind, which refers to the aforementioned [stage].
Regarding those within the Teaching who are either fixed or unfixed: there are two types of those who proceed directly to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) in both the present and the future.
Question: When do the aforementioned six types of persons enter the Perfect [Teaching]? Answer: Their progress is varied in terms of speed, yet they will ultimately all return to the Perfect.

Why is this? Because they possess the diamond-seed nature; because the Buddha never abandons them; because they will ultimately attain awakening; and because they all abide in their inherent nature. The Perfect is the ultimate.
Therefore, the remaining points regarding the transcendent characteristics and the principles of inclusion can be understood from the preceding examples.

Question: Why does the teaching not establish a vehicle for humans and devas? Answer: Because there are no distinctions such as stages of abandonment and realization, it is not established as a separate teaching;
rather, it serves as a skillful means for gradual entry into the Hīnayāna, and is thus subsumed within the Hīnayāna teachings.

Question: Within the benefits for subsequent capacities, why is there yet another opening? Answer: Because the benefits of worldly and world-transcending dharmas differ, its teaching vehicle is explained again prior to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Question:

Regarding the Śrāvaka’s teaching and practice of the Four Noble Truths, which establishes the four stages of progress (*pratipannaka*) and fruits (*phala*), does it merely sever the manifest afflictions (*kleśa*), or does the teaching and practice of the Pratyekabuddha’s Dependent Origination establish partial fruits that also invade the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*)?

Answer: [The Śrāvaka] merely severs the manifest afflictions; the Pratyekabuddha, through the teaching and practice of Dependent Origination, establishes partial fruits that concurrently invade the habit-energies. Practice...
Question: Since their characteristics are distinct, how can they be combined into a single teaching? Answer: Although the teachings and practices differ, the principle and the fruit are the same;
for they equally realize the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), and they equally attain the fruits of *sopadhiśeṣa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa* nirvāṇa.

Although the stages of abandonment differ, their wisdom is one, as both constitute the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). Because they are collectively termed "Hīnayāna," one discards the differences and takes up the commonality.
Because they are identical, they are unified. Furthermore, the teachings regarding the opening and closing of the contemplation of the truths (*satya*) are likewise the same.

Since they equally practice the contemplation of the emptiness of persons, equally sever the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), and equally attain the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle, their practice, severance, and fruits are entirely without distinction;

therefore, while the Buddha was in the world, he subsumed the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas under that of the Śrāvakas, naming it the Śrāvaka-piṭaka—the "half-syllable" Lesser Vehicle—and for this reason, it was not separately classified.

Question: What distinguishes this from the *zàngjiào* (Tripitaka Teaching) of Tiantai? Answer: That *zàngjiào* is for the sake of Bodhisattvas who practice the six perfections through concrete phenomena (*sīshì*);
the present "Lesser Teaching" (*xiǎojiào*) does not include Bodhisattvas, as it classifies the teachings based on the six perfections practiced through concrete phenomena. Question:
Why do the commentators (*shūjiā*) both state that the Lesser Teaching is identical to the Tiantai *zàngjiào*? Answer: Regarding the dharma-gates subsumed within the Lesser Teaching...
Because it is not different from that, it is designated as being the same. Question: Since it is not different from that, why is there no Bodhisattva? Answer:

Although the characteristics of the phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are the same, their meanings and intentions differ. Why? Because, in order to lead those of the Lesser Vehicle toward the Mahāyāna meaning, it is explained in a shallow manner similar to that of the Lesser Vehicle.
In reality, the two vehicles have no share [in this], and it exists only in the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-śāsana*). Therefore, in this Lesser Teaching, there is no Bodhisattva.

[Sāya. Question: It may be that the "Small" (Hīnayāna) does not include the "Great" (Mahāyāna). However, since the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna is identical [to the Mahāyāna], why is it further changed from "Tripiṭaka" and renamed "Small"?
Answer: Because establishing the name "Tripiṭaka" for them would invite many difficulties; by now establishing it as "Hīnayāna," there is no error of conflating it with the Mahāyāna.

△ Question: The Śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa (Destruction of Characteristics) Initial Teaching explains the ten stages, such as the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*), and establishes the teachings on the division of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-bheda*).

Question: The teachings on the five stages beginning with the "provisional equipment" (*sambhāra*) teach the severance of *dṛṣṭi-heya* (afflictions abandoned through vision) and *bhāvanā-heya* (afflictions abandoned through cultivation) and the realization of true emptiness;

the teachings on the "characteristics of the realization of true suchness" (*tathatā*) teach the severance of the two attachments and the realization of true suchness. Since these characteristics are distinct, why are they not divided into two? Answer:

Although the fifteen stages (*bhūmi*) differ, the characteristics of the paths of vision (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) are identical. Moreover, since it is accepted that all three vehicles share a single sequence of abandonment and realization, there is no distinction [between them].

Since they are distinct, how can they be divided into two? Furthermore, while the attachments of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) appear to differ in that those of *dṛṣṭi* (view) are abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*) and those of *vitarka* (conceptualization) are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), there is no difference between them in their innate nature (*sahaja*). As for the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), they likewise consist of the views and conceptualizations of the supramundane realm;
even the ultimate reality of emptiness and suchness is nothing other than the principle of the two-fold selflessness. Because these are all identical, they are combined [into one].
First: Question: Is this initial division of teachings (shifun-jiao) the same as or different from the two schools of Nature (xing) and Characteristics (xiang)? Answer: There is a slight difference.
In that [initial division], the two natures are combined with emptiness; here, they are judged as three natures by opening up emptiness within emptiness.

Since both the schools of Characteristics and Emptiness agree that those of fixed nature and those without nature do not all become Buddhas, it is established as the Initial Teaching (chujiao), wherein the determination of nature (*xingding*) reveals only the manifest.

Because all [beings] of the One Vehicle attain Buddhahood, it is established as the Final Teaching (*zhōngjiào*). Question: How is the School of One Nature (*yīxìngzōng*) judged to comprise both the Initial and the Final Teachings?

Answer: Because its meanings include the provisional and the real; because its scriptures include the primary and the auxiliary; because its characteristics are taught provisionally based on the nature with the intent that characteristics are empty;

and because its emptiness is taught provisionally based on the nature with the intent that the nature is empty—none of these are the definitive meaning (*lìoyì*), but are rather provisional. The nature, however, is directly revealed.

Only the Middle Way *dharmatā* is called the definitive meaning and the reality (*tattva*). Regarding the aspect (*lakṣaṇa*), it is precisely the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, while the *Vaipulya* is supplementary;

regarding the nature (*svabhāva*), it is precisely the *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā*, while the *Prajñāpāramitā* is supplementary. The *Saṃdhinirmocana* explains the aspect, and the *Prajñāpāramitā* discusses emptiness;

this marks the initial division. The *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā* reveals the nature, which is the final reality. Based on this, two [schools] are distinguished. Question: Since emptiness and nature are distinct, how can those schools combine them into one?

Yes. The answer is: because their teaching through the wondrous wisdom of *prajñā* is identical; furthermore, while the School of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇavāda*) establishes characteristics, that school (the School of Nature) discourses on emptiness and manifests nature, neither establishing characteristics, and thus they are unified.
Question: Within the three periods of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, two periods clarify emptiness and both allow for the attainment of Buddhahood, whereas the third period clarifies non-emptiness.
Does this mean there is a distinction between those who attain Buddhahood and those who do not? Answer: In the School of Nature (*dharmatāvāda*), [all] possess the nature [of Buddhahood].

Regarding the three periods of the *Sūtra of Profound Wisdom* (*Xianzhong san shi*), it clarifies that during two [periods] there is non-emptiness and the establishment of both success and failure, while during one period it clarifies emptiness, all of which allow for the attainment of Buddhahood.
If this is so, how can the characteristics of the teachings be distinguished according to their meaning? Answer: This is based on the time of the preaching of the sūtras.

First, the *Prajñāpāramitā* clarifies the principle of mere emptiness; it also allows that those of fixed natures do not attain Buddhahood, while simultaneously revealing the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (the Profound and Secret) explains that the principle of the Dharma-lakṣaṇa (phenomenal characteristics) is such that those of fixed natures and so forth do not attain Buddhahood; this is the second and third periods of the School of Characteristics (*xiāngzōng*).

Subsequently, the *Sūtra of the Profound Wisdom* (the *Prajñāpāramitā*) clarifies that within the Middle Way of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which is ultimate emptiness, even those of no-nature (*aniyata-gotra*) all attain Buddhahood;

this is the second and third periods of the School of Nature (*xìngzōng*). Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Saṃdhinirmocana* correspond respectively to the second and third periods of these two schools.

Furthermore, according to the second [period] of the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* and the second period of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, which clarify that the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) are merely empty and that the meaning of their existence is not established, these are judged to belong to the initial stage.

According to the third period of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, which clarifies that the emptiness of the nature of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu-śūnyatā*) leads to the fulfillment of Buddhahood, these are judged to belong to the final reality.
Moreover, the establishment of the teachings by our own school primarily relies upon the meaning of the Dharma, and does not depend solely on [the chronological periods].

Regarding the principle of "time," while a single sūtra may contain multiple teachings—wherein the provisional and the ultimate, or the sudden and the gradual, are simultaneously revealed—the temporal sequence of these teachings is fixed or unfixed, making it difficult to distinguish their beginning and end;

this is explained in detail elsewhere. Question: The three periods and five stages established by the Nature School (Xingzong) in its Final Teaching are also the same as those categorized by the Characteristics School (Xiangzong).
Why are they separately established as a distinct teaching? Answer: This concerns the temporal teaching of the Characteristics School.

Regarding the distinction between the Provisional and the Real: when the *Yicheng* (One Vehicle) school takes the One Vehicle as provisional and the Three Vehicles as real, it is a school of Nature (*xingzong*);

when the *Shijiao* (Teaching of the Ages) school takes the Three Vehicles as provisional and the One Vehicle as real, it is a school of Characteristics (*xiangzong*). In the five stages of the school of Characteristics, the various phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) follow one another with vast intervals;

in the five stages of the school of Nature, the gradations are manifested based upon a single Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). Furthermore, from the arousal of practice, the subduing of delusions, and the severance of hindrances, all aspects differ and are not the same.

Therefore, it is established separately. △ Question: Since the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao) distinguishes only the single nature and does not establish stages of severance and realization, why is it divided separately as a distinct teaching?

Answer: Because the "stage of no stage" constitutes the stages of this teaching; it differs from the preceding Gradual Teaching and differs from the subsequent Perfect Teaching, and is thus divided separately.
Question: Why is it that within the Sudden Teaching, severance and realization are also explained? Answer: It is for the sake of...
Because it clarifies the superiority and inferiority of the preceding and succeeding [teachings], it also reveals that while there is no "sudden" position, yet in every position there is no position;

this is because its ineffable meaning transcends words. Question: Since the four teachings of Tiantai all possess the "transcendence of words," and these four teachings already encompass them, why is the "Sudden" not established therein?
What is the significance of establishing it separately here? Answer: Tiantai does not establish it because within those four teachings, all...
There was one instance where all words were cut off precisely so that [the practitioner] might forget linguistic expression and realize the ultimate meaning.

Now, this [teaching] is opened because it reveals that beyond the four aforementioned instances of cutting off words, there is yet another principle of sudden expression where words are transcended; it is established as a distinct category for those with faculties characterized by the detachment from thought.
Without this door, it would be insufficient to accommodate such faculties. Furthermore, this Sudden Teaching is not the "Perfect-Sudden" (yuan-ji-dun) of the Tiantai school.
Meaning. △ Question: The *Huayan shu* states that there are two types of One Vehicle: first, the "Teaching-Common" (tongjiao) One Vehicle, which is identical to the Sudden and the Real;
second, the "Teaching-Specific" (biejiao) One Vehicle, which possesses only the virtue of perfect interpenetration (*yuanrong*).

Since it is identical to the Sudden and the Real, how does it differ from them such that a separate "Perfect Teaching" (yuanjiao) is established? Answer: Within this very commonality, there must necessarily be a specific meaning. It is like [the distinction between] phenomena and principle being non-dual...

If there is obstruction, it must be precisely the non-obstruction of phenomena within phenomena; just as when the waters of a river enter the sea they become salty, the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is established by distinguishing the different from the identical.

Moreover, while the preceding four teachings are not subsumed within the Perfect Teaching, the Perfect Teaching necessarily subsumes the four—just as the hundred rivers do not contain the great ocean, yet the great ocean necessarily contains the hundred rivers. Thus, the preceding four are limited, whereas the Perfect Teaching is universal.

How can that which is universal and that which is restricted be combined? Question: Since the single Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) is divided into the Identical and the Distinct, should it not constitute two teachings rather than one, making six in total?
Answer: Although it is divided into the Identical and the Distinct, it remains but a single teaching; there are merely two gates based on the principles of exclusion and inclusion.
Because of its Distinct aspect, it is utterly distinct from other schools; because of its Identical aspect, it universally includes all things. Thus, it is established as one.
5. Question:
It has been said in the past that these five teachings and the four teachings of Tiantai differ only in their expansion and contraction, while their general outline is the same.
Is this so, or is it not? Answer: Since it is said they are "largely the same," there are indeed minor differences; however, in principle, there is none.

They are identical in their non-difference; for the principles and meanings elucidated by these five teachings are not only identical with those of the Tiantai school, but are also identical with those of all other schools.
