sometimes the mind and heart are shrouded in darkness; sometimes various evil thoughts are stirred; sometimes great pride arises with a resolve equal to that of all Buddhas;
sometimes inexhaustible grief is born, unable to bear seeing people; or remembering past unpleasant touches, the hair on the body stands on end; or [giving rise to] conceptualization.

Whether one is intoxicated by the dullness of pleasant objects and fails to awaken; or contemplates various subtle and excellent matters of internal seclusion; or dwells on various scattered and evil matters of external distraction;

or gives rise to a sense of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); or conceives thoughts of contentment—such various and immeasurable forms of objects that arise together with the wholesome are all termed "false and deceptive.
If one develops attachment to these states of false concentration (*mithyā-samādhi*), then immediately [one falls away].
The dharmas of devils, spirits, ghosts, and heterodox paths correspond with this, whereby one loses one's mind and becomes crazed, deluded, and inverted.
At times, various demons and malevolent spirits, knowing that the person is fixated upon those dharmas, exert their power to cause false objects to manifest.
Some may give rise to false concentration, or attain false wisdom, or possess unimpeded eloquence; some may have their physical marks and signs made upright and majestic;
some may be taught dhāraṇīs, or enter the three samādhis; some may be caused to see the Buddha-lands from nearby, or be caused to hear the sound of the sutras from afar;
some may be caused to know the good and evil of the past, or be caused to know the calamities and blessings of the future; or they may contemplate the celestial palaces, or gaze upon...
Whether through hellish powers, supernatural feats, or displays of fearlessness—all these are the delusions of Māra that mislead people; they possess no true practitioners.
The foolish and confused claim to have attained the fruits of the Path, and by this perversion they confuse and disturb the world.

Māra’s mind gives rise to weariness and detachment, yet since his body lacks true majesty and virtue, he falls into royal peril. After his life ends, he returns to fall into the māra-path, revolving in saṃsāra.
Those in the three miserable realms will never encounter a Buddha. △ Therefore, when a practitioner gives rise to wholesome thoughts, if such demonic signs appear, they should immediately repel them.
First, repelling through cessation: one should recognize that these various false and deceptive objects are empty, illusory, and unreal;

one should simply rectify one's own mind, abide in the Dharma-realm, neither accepting nor clinging, neither grieving nor rejoicing. Second, repelling through contemplation: one uses wisdom for oneself...
When wisdom-illumination contemplates the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is no object to be found apart from the mind that transcends the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
When one practices such *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, objects naturally subside and cease.
Next, it clarifies the signs produced by genuine meditation: if various wholesome states arise within contemplation, they do not [occur] as described above.
Each and every characteristic of the various false dharmas corresponds to its respective meditative concentration;
the wisdom of contemplation manifests clearly within the concentrated mind, the body becomes light, agile, peaceful, and blissful, the mental ground becomes supple, tranquil, luminous, and clear.
One’s own realized virtues become towering, filled with the joy of the Dharma, free from obscuration and affliction, and having shattered all clinging views, one attains greatness.

To be liberated from weariness with the world’s impermanence, suffering, and emptiness, seeking only the supramundane bliss of the Buddha’s Nirvāṇa, and to universally deliver all sentient beings so that they may together achieve perfect enlightenment—this is the characteristic of Right Dhyāna. It is like associating with an evil person:
it begins well but ends in evil; whereas consorting with a virtuous person becomes increasingly sublime over time. The manifestation of the signs of the false and the right is likewise: the false...
As right reception gradually declines, delusive thoughts gradually arise; as correctness prevails, afflictions gradually perish, and contemplative wisdom gradually increases.

Third, the demonstration of nurturing: if, within meditative concentration, any roots of goodness should emerge, one should employ the two methods of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) to cultivate them so that they increase.
If it is appropriate to employ *śamatha*, then cultivate with *śamatha*; if it is appropriate to employ *vipaśyanā*, then...
By cultivating this through contemplation, the roots of virtue will grow and hindrances and obscurations will naturally vanish.
Next, the manifestation of the perfected state of the sublime fruit is revealed in two parts. First, regarding the object realized by the initial mind:
when one practices with such diligence, one is able to realize and know that all phenomena are empty and lack intrinsic nature, arising entirely from the mind and being inseparable from it.
Externally there are no phenomena whatsoever; thus, the mind is signless and phenomena are also signless. Even the existence of the marks of phenomena is like an echo or a shadow.

Because one knows that all mental phenomena are empty and quiescent, one cannot apprehend any names or signs—namely, it is neither mind nor object, neither form nor emptiness, neither time nor place, neither body nor direction; it is without self and without other, and without oneness.
Without much, without great, without small, without defilement, and without purity;

transcending cultivation and realization, and severing both teaching and principle—by means of this, one cuts off afflictions, extinguishes birth and death, and awakens to and enters the unimpeded dharma-realm of rational nature. This is called the realm of the realization of True Emptiness through śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Furthermore, one knows that although the nature of the mind is empty and quiescent, it can nevertheless give rise to phenomena through the conjunction of causes and conditions.
Since phenomena have no separate substance apart from the principle, they must rely upon the principle to be established;

and since the true principle follows conditions to establish phenomenal things, form, sound, fragrance, and taste arise from within the emptiness of nature like flowers in the sky, while seeing, hearing, sensation, and cognition arise within the awakened mind just like a dream.
By perceiving that mental phenomena are entirely unimpeded through the manifestation and concealment of forms,
one immediately attains all-encompassing integration— namely, that which is both the ultimate truth and the conventional, essence and appearance, mind and form, unity and difference,
permanence and change, extinction and birth, emptiness and existence, wisdom and object, reality and expedient means, as well as essence and function. Through these, [one realizes]...

This arising of the myriad practices to deliver sentient beings and awaken to the entry into the Dharma-realm where principle and phenomena are mutually unimpeded is called the "unimpeded śamatha and vipaśyanā," the realm of realized accomplishment. Furthermore,

it is knowing that the nature of the mind is fundamentally pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, encompassing and expelling the ten voids, and manifesting as a single entity in accordance with all conditions of dependent origination.
All phenomena likewise abide as the mind, universally encompassing all without obstruction; because there is no phenomenon, whether great or small, that is not the single Dharma-realm mind,
a single small vessel can produce all food, drink, and requisites, and within a Buddha’s palace the dwellings and houses of sentient beings appear instantaneously,
while a hair-tip can contain a world-system and a mote of dust can turn a wheel-turning king’s realm— wherein the one and the many enter into one another.
By means of the broad and the narrow, the hidden and the manifest, one realizes that the mental factors (*citta-dharma*) universally encompass all things;

thus, one attains universal perfection. That is to say: the teachings and meanings universally encompass; wisdom and cessation universally encompass; the stages of practice and positions universally encompass; cause and effect universally encompass; the environment and its inhabitants universally encompass;

spatial directions universally encompass; temporal kalpas universally encompass; response and resonance universally encompass; the adverse and the favorable universally encompass; and persons and dharmas universally encompass.
By means of this perfect integration, one cuts off [delusion] and universally cultivates the realization of the dharma-realm of non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena;
this is called the "object realized through pervasive *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Next, regarding the object realized by the subsequent mind: it refers to being able to thus realize and know that all dharmas are empty, which is itself all-pervasive and all-encompassing.

This emptiness of one's own mind is all-pervasively accommodated within *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. One must apply further effort and practice to cultivate it until fulfillment is reached—just like refining gold.

By severing delusions and realizing the Truth, one transcends the ordinary and enters the state of the Sage. Through the cultivation of *śamatha*, one achieves meditative concentration (*samādhi*), transforms the basis of birth and death, and realizes *nirvāṇa*;
the fruit of this severance is called the "Well-Gone One" (*Sugata*), the Honored One whose merit is complete. Through the cultivation of *vipaśyanā*, one achieves...

Because Prajñā transforms the basis of afflictions and realizes the fruit of Bodhi-wisdom, it is designated as "Perfectly All-Knowing" (Samyaksaṃbuddha) and honored as the "Venerable One Whose Feet are Wisdom.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Knowing that all phenomena are the very nature of mind, one accomplishes the body of wisdom, awakening not through another.
And the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "Adorned with the power of concentration and wisdom, by this one delivers sentient beings."
Next, within the section on "Correct Cultivation," two gates are opened. First, the essential substance of the basis is clarified, comprising ten pairs in total:

1. Teaching and Meaning; 2. Principle and Phenomena; 3. Object and Wisdom; 4. Practice and Stage; 5. Cause and Effect; 6. Support and Manifestation; 7. Substance and Function; 8. Person and Dharma; 9.
Adverse and Favorable; 10. Response and Resonance.

Regarding the meaning of the Initial Teaching (*ādikavacana*): as for the teaching, it concerns the four evil destinies—hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and asuras—as well as the vehicles of humans, devas, the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) of Śrāvakas, the Middle Vehicle (*madhyamayāna*) of Pratyekabuddhas, and the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) of Bodhisattvas;
it comprises the Initial Teaching, the Final Teaching, the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), the Sudden Teaching, and the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpannavacana*), which is the supreme Buddhist teaching.

As for the meaning, it concerns the three paths [of rebirth] with their superior, middling, and inferior grades, as well as the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) and the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*).

The Way comprises the fivefold classification of inferior, middling, and superior, consisting of the five precepts, the ten wholesome actions, the two vehicles, the seventy-five dharmas of the Initial Teaching (which establishes characteristics), the eight consciousnesses, the ten suchnesses, and the hundred dharmas of the five stages;

the teaching that destroys appearances (consisting of four views, three emptinesses, and eighty-one dharmas); the Final Teaching (consisting of four stages, six defilements, three greatnesses, and nine appearances);
the Sudden Teaching (consisting of one hundred and eight phrases and forty-one gates); and each [of these] is beyond words.

It speaks exclusively of the true nature, the Perfect Teaching (Ekanaya), the two wisdoms, the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*), the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*), the ten mysteries (*daśaguhya*), the Tathāgata’s three bodies (*trikāya*), four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*), five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*), ten powers (*daśabala*), and so forth.

Regarding the two aspects of principle and phenomena: "principle" refers to the original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*) of the six realms, the partial emptiness of the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*, and the Dharma-nature of the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*).

The nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dharmatā*) is the wondrous true suchness-nature (*tathatā-svabhāva*) of the Ultimate Teaching (*paryantavāda*); the true suchness free from words (*nirabhilāpya-tathatā*) of the Sudden Teaching (*tongjiao*) is the supreme emptiness of ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*);

the nature of the perfectly interfused and unobstructed Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-pariniṣpanna-avyāghāta-svabhāva*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is the Buddha-realm, the One Vehicle, and Buddha-nature (*buddhatva*).

As for phenomena (*vastu*), there are the contaminated five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the six realms of existence, and the uncontaminated five aggregates (*anāsrava-pañca-skandha*) of the four noble ones; even in the Small Teaching (*hīnayāna*), there are likewise contaminated [phenomena].
Furthermore, there are the bodies and lands of the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) of the Initial Teaching; the conditioned untainted five aggregates of the Final Teaching;

the unconditioned untainted five aggregates of the Sudden Teaching; and the bodies and lands of the inexhaustible five aggregates of the Tathāgata’s Reward Body, Response Body, and Dharma-nature Body, which are the perfectly interfused *dharmadhātu* according to the Complete Teaching.

Third, regarding the wisdom of objects: as for the objects, there are the sufferings of oppression resulting from the karmic retribution of the three evil paths—superior, middling, and inferior—as well as the inverted transgressions;

and there are the joys of the appropriate and pleasing karmic retribution of the meditative virtues of the three paths—lower, middle, and upper. Furthermore, there is the partial truth of *nirvāṇa* according to the Four Noble Truths of the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*);

the two truths of the Final Teaching (*Niṣṭhāyāna*); the three truths of the Sudden Teaching (*Aksobhyayāna*); and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the Perfect Teaching (*Paryantayāna*), which is perfectly interfused and inexhaustible.
The Tathāgata of the Dharma-realm possesses the wisdom of the four nirvāṇas: the contemplation of the habitual minds of evil karma in the three miserable realms;

the contemplation of the outflowing wholesome minds of the three paths; the contemplation of the four truths of the śrāvaka’s outflow-free wisdom; and the contemplation of the natural wisdom of the pratyekabuddha’s contemplation of dependent origination.

In the Initial Teaching (śāstra), there is the contemplation of the two emptinesses through the preparatory, fundamental, and subsequently attained wisdoms. In the Final Teaching, there is the contemplation of the three truths, wherein the provisional and the real are non-dual.
The wisdom that penetrates obstructions, the contemplation of the true nature of the sudden teaching, the wisdom of the ultimate emptiness beyond words, the contemplation of the perfect dharma-realm,
the ten inexhaustible wisdoms, and the two, three, four, and five wisdoms of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the four stages of practice: in the stage of action, those who commit the five heinous crimes fall into the Avīci Hell; those with pure emotion and no thought fall into the Uninterrupted (Avīci) Hell; those with nine parts emotion and one part thought fall into the Interrupted Hells;

those with eight parts emotion and two parts thought fall into the Hungry Ghost realm; those who commit the ten evil deeds down to seven parts emotion and three parts thought fall into the Animal realm;

those who give rise to the three poisons down to six parts emotion and four parts thought fall into the Human realm; and those who cultivate the goodness of precepts down to five parts emotion and five parts thought [attain the stage of understanding].

Those who are clear-headed and intelligent have six perceptions and four feelings; those who cultivate dullness through the practices of asuras, such as the earth-dwelling rakshasas and their kind, have seven perceptions and three feelings;
those such as the powerful ghost-kings have eight perceptions and two feelings;

and the immortals and celestial beings who practice dhyāna and contemplation—stopping in mountains and seas, maintaining mental images to solidify their forms and transcend to the ninth stage—have nine perceptions and one feeling.

When one contemplates the single principle of the realm of thought (*citta*), one practices the six matters of contemplation through the four *dhyānas* and eight *samādhis*, until thought becomes purely insentient.

In the abbreviated teaching for the Two Vehicles, there are the three trainings of precept, concentration, and wisdom; in the extensive teaching, there are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. In the Initial Teaching, there are the six perfections and ten thousand practices; in the Final Teaching, there are the four faiths and five practices.
In the Sudden Teaching, the three natures are all empty and both types of selflessness are simultaneously discarded. In the Perfect Teaching, these are inexhaustible.
One encompasses all, and all enters into one. In the Tathāgata’s stage of awakening others, the eight cold and eight hot hells,
the three riches and three obstructions of the hungry ghosts, the four classes and four births of animals, the four continents and four castes of the human realm,

the yakṣas categorized by the three types of practice, the asuras ranked by their stages, the sages listed in ten kinds, and the heavens divided into the three realms, are all subsumed within the Lesser Beginning.
In the teachings, there are five stages— provisional, preparatory, seeing, cultivation, and ultimate— which differ only in terms of the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena;

furthermore, there are six stages— faith, abiding, practice, direction, ground, and so forth— which likewise differ in their gradual, sudden, or perfectly integrated nature, culminating in the Buddha’s stage of wondrous enlightenment alone.

Regarding the five aspects of cause and effect: as for the causes, there are the ten types of evil karma of the ten habitual practices created through the three paths of the three miserable realms (the lower, middle, and upper grades);
and the ten types of good karma of the ten habitual practices created through the three paths [of the human realm] (the lower, middle, and upper grades).

There are also the various adornments of concentration, wisdom, merit, and knowledge—from the beginning to the end of the seven stages of expedient means of the two vehicles, through the three sages, the four stages of application, up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment within the Buddha-realm. As for the effects, these range from the hells of Jambudvīpa to Avīci.
In the interim, they undergo the suffering of the six intersecting retributions: being cut and sawed, frozen and parched, and scorched;

as hungry ghosts, they encounter insects and beasts, taking on the forms of malevolent spirits with smoke and flames from their mouths, oppressed by hunger and thirst; as animals, they become objects of consumption to repay past debts, subjected to riding, whipping, staves, blades, chopping blocks, and boiling;
and as asuras and others in the three lower paths, they experience the fundamental cravings of the lower, middle, and upper grades.

The fruit of practice (*śikṣā-phala*) is the retribution for good karma; in the teachings of the Small Vehicle, it refers to the four fruits beginning with *srotāpanna* realized through the stages of seeing, cultivation, and realization, which are perfected from beginning to end.

The ten stages (*bhūmi*), such as the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), represent the Tathāgata’s great awakening (*mahābodhi*) in a single moment of correspondence, wherein the unsurpassed bodhi is brilliantly manifest.
This constitutes the fruit of practice. Great Parinirvāṇa, in which meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and samādhi are fully possessed, is the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*).

Furthermore, regarding the six aspects of the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya* and *sambhoga*): "environment" refers to the transformation land of the black karma of the three miserable realms; the transformation land of the white karma of the three paths; the pure transformation land of the two vehicles;
the inferior enjoyment land of the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*); and the superior enjoyment land of the Final Teaching (*nītārtha-yāna*). As for the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*):...

The Dharma-nature Land; the Land of the Unobstructed Dharma-realm of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao); the Land of the Transformation Body of the Tathāgata for the three evil paths through their evil karma;
the Land of the Transformation Body for the three good paths of the two vehicles; the Land of the Inferior Enjoyment Body of the Initial Teaching (Shijiao);
the Land of the Superior Enjoyment Body of the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao); the Dharma-nature Body of the Sudden Teaching (Dunjiao); and the Unobstructed Dharma-realm of the Perfect Teaching.
The Four Bodies of Tathāgata Dhātugarbha.

Phonetic Glossary.
*Bo* (pronounced *bǔ*; to strike with the hand). *Méng* (pronounced *méng*; dark, obscure, and lacking clarity). *Yè* (pronounced *è*; the palate within the mouth). *Bó* (pronounced *bá*;

a drought deity, two or three feet tall, bare-bodied with eyes on the crown of the head, moving like the wind). *Yàn* (pronounced *yǎn*; a demon that causes nightmares during sleep). *Xié* (pronounced *xiē*; a venomous insect that stings). *Zhàzhījiāluó* (a class of beings belonging to Maheśvara).
*Yakṣa* (translated here as "valiant and strong," or "fierce and evil"). *Rākṣasa* (translated here as "swift," or "terrifying"). *Cāmuṇḍā* (formerly translated as...).

The "jealous woman" (īrṣyā-strī) is a female spirit who serves as a servant. *Piśāca* (translated here as "one who devours vital energy"; in the Liang dynasty it was called a "mad ghost"). *Dhyāna* (translated here as "meditative concentration," where calmness and insight are in equilibrium).

*Ṛṣabha* (pronounced *dī*; a vigorous ram three years old). *Varāha* (pronounced *zhì*; a pig). *Mārjāra* (pronounced *jìng*; Meng Kang says: the *xiāo* bird eats its mother; the *mǎng* beast eats its father). *Śarabha* (pronounced *shāng*;

when this bird dances, there will be heavy rain). *Sammila* (pronounced *mǐn*; to close together). *Kicaka* (translated here as "the ghost that raises the dead"). *Samādhi* (in Chinese, "right concentration"). *Mī* (pronounced *mì*; quiet speech; peace).
Śamatha (translated as "stopping"). Vipaśyanā (translated as "contemplation"). Puh-po (phonetic transcription of *pu-thu-fu*, referring to the ground).

Oṃ āḥ hūṃ hrīḥ (the first three syllables—Oṃ, Āḥ, Hūṃ—correspond to the bodies, speech, and minds of the Buddhas Vairocana, Amitābha, and Akṣobhya; the latter two syllables, Hrīḥ, correspond to the mind and form Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva).

Akṣobhya (phonetic transcription; in Sanskrit *akṣobhya*, in Chinese "Immovable"). Cīra (phonetic transcription of *jin*; ashes remaining after fire). Māra (here translated as "slayer"). Guǎihuá (phonetic transcription of *jiao-hua*; meaning "deceitful and treacherous"). Xiá (meaning "familiarity through play"; phonetic transcription).
Qià (to moisten). Jí (pronounced jí; to be emaciated). [Bìng + xí] (pronounced xī; slight pain). Xī (pronounced xì; to rest). Sāo (pronounced sāo; to scratch with the hand).
Liè (pronounced liè; severe cold air). Zhēn (pronounced zhēn; a stone for pounding silk).

(Virtuous Leader, *Wénxián wǔjiàoyí*, Volume Five) I humbly pray that in every lifetime you may constantly invite the thousand Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma; that in birth after birth, Guhyapāda may forever subdue the hosts of māras to protect the Teaching;

that calm abiding and insight remain balanced, and the relationship between cause and fruit remains unclouded; that all present calamities and illnesses be eliminated, and that your roots of goodness flourish ever anew.
May the harmony between husband and wife flourish like the resonance of zithers for a hundred years; may descendants propagate their excellence like orchids and iris for a thousand generations;
may material generosity be inexhaustible, and may the family receive an abundance of auspicious blessings.
(Recorded at the Ciyun Meditation Hall) *Xianshou Wujiaoyi*,
Fascicle Six. Compiled by the Śramaṇa Guanding,
who continues the Dharma, of the Ciyun [Monastery] on the banks of the Qingshui River, Zhejiang.

Seventh, regarding essence (*tǐ*) and function (*yòng*): as for essence, there is the body that is the retribution of suffering from the three lower realms due to the performance of superior, middling, and inferior evil karma;

the body that is the retribution of happiness from the three paths [of humans, devas, and śrāvakas] due to the performance of inferior, middling, and superior wholesome karma; the fivefold dharma-body of the two vehicles;

the body of the conditioned, untainted *parinirmita*-transformation five aggregates according to the Initial Teaching; and the body of the unconditioned, untainted *parinirmita*-transformation five aggregates according to the Final Teaching.
The sudden teaching is the body of the dharma-nature of non-arising; the perfect teaching is the infinitely interpenetrating and inexhaustible body.
Regarding the three or four bodies of the Tathāgata’s functional manifestations: in the hells, they ascend blades and swords; as hungry ghosts, they swallow copper and chew iron;

among animals, their scales overlap as they devour one another, the strong subduing the weak and bearing heavy loads while pulling carts, committing various evils; and as asuras, they are arrogant and inverted, contending with the devas.

Those who contend for power observe the five precepts; those in the heavens cultivate the eight meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*); those of the Two Vehicles exert themselves to sever the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and realize Lesser Nirvāṇa;

Arhats possess the three knowledges (*vidyā*), the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and unimpededness; in the Initial Teaching, one gives rise to the four great vows and cultivates the practices of the six perfections (*pāramitā*), culminating in the manifestation of the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics; in the Final Teaching, one establishes and cultivates the six perfections in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*).
Extensively giving rise to the myriad practices to transform all sentient beings, they exercise great compassion to the point of manifesting the eighty-four thousand exquisite marks and signs;

through the sudden teaching of detachment from characteristics, they cultivate all practices with the wondrous power of non-action, giving rise to various transformations, powers, and masteries that are like space, without limit or boundary. In the Perfect Teaching, by severing one thing, everything is severed.
He performs all practices until he manifests as many marks as there are atoms in ten lotus-treasury world-oceans;
each and every one of these marks pervades the entire Dharma-realm, and their karmic functions are likewise so. This is the inconceivable transformation of the Tathāgata’s three wheels of activity.
The Dharma of the Eight Persons refers to: the human realm; the three paths of fire, blood, and blades; the asura realm; the human path; the heavenly path;

those of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha vehicles with determinate or indeterminate natures; the stages from beginning to end, from sudden to perfect; the initial mind and subsequent minds of all ranks of bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas;
the superior, middling, and inferior grades of the three evil paths; the lower, middling, and superior grades of the ten wholesome paths; and the Four Noble Truths of the Small Vehicle.

The twelve links of dependent origination; the fifty-one factors and one hundred dharmas of the Initial Teaching’s Dharma-character school (Xiangzong); the eighty-one dharmas of the Emptiness school (Kongzong);
the single mind and two gates of the Final Teaching; the single true nature of Suchness of the Sudden Teaching;
and the ten unspeakable and inexhaustible dharma-gates of the Perfect Teaching, including the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, eighteen unique qualities, and so forth.
Regarding the nine cases of transgression and conformity: Transgression leads to hell—such as [the story of] Bhadra; increased pride leads to the animal realm—such as the deer king Puṣya;
lack of compassion leads to the hungry ghost realm—such as the yakṣa Śreṇika; reciting half a verse leads to the asura realm—such as Bhañji, Khaṇḍa, Citra, and Rāhu;
humans have the six heretical teachers, the ten seers, Caṅkī the butcher, and others; and among devas, there are Maheśvara, the Unconscious Heaven, and the two [forms of] Maheśvara.
The six groups of bhikṣus from beginning to end; the Brahmin Niṅ-jién (Nirgrantha); Lū-kia-têng-ga (Rudraka);
Po-sou (Vatsa); Wu-yen (Anavatapta); the Śrotriya Brahmin; the Buddha as Devadatta; those who follow the rules; the hell-being who received light;
the son of a heavenly king who pulled the fire-chariot; the animal, the Bodhisattva-deer king; the golden lion; the dragon girl; and the hungry ghost who spoke incantations.
The Buddhalands open their gates of teaching; the Asuras manifest great power through illusory arts; the humans possess the fourfold assembly as their Dharma kin;
the devas have the World-Protectors, Śakra, and Brahmā; the two vehicles include five hundred arhats who are perfected from beginning to end both gradually and instantaneously;
and there are Vimalakīrti, Mahāmati, Kṣitigarbha, Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, and others, such as the Buddha Bhaiṣajyaguru.
Da. Tenth, regarding "response and resonance" (*ganying*): when there is resonance, those of the same class within the six realms of existence arise together;

likewise, those of the same class among the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), as well as those of different classes—the ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the six realms—whether at the beginning or end, whether gradual or sudden, and whether their faculties have matured or they are beginners on the path of training (*śaikṣa*). And...
Other categories include the two vehicles, the six realms, and the nine realms of sentient beings; those who respond through the same activities as the six realms;
and the four noble bodies: the two vehicles with their four fruits and four stages of approach, the Bodhisattvas, and the Tathāgata.

Regarding the Tathāgata, there is the gradual and sudden perfection of the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood, the five wisdoms of the Tathāgata, and the Buddha’s five eyes and ten bodies.
Among these ten pairs, the first serves as the general overview while the subsequent ones gradually become more concise.

The first means that when the Tathāgata speaks the teaching (*deśanā*) which expresses the principle (*tattva*), there is no phenomenon (*dharma*) that is not exhausted; since phenomena consist of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit, and both practice and fruit are included within the expressed principles.
Second, although the expressed [phenomena] are numerous, they do not transcend the category of "things" (*vastu*).

Regarding the principle of suchness (li-ji-xing) and the principle of non-existence of phenomena (xiang wu-fa), there is nothing that is not subsumed within these three principles; they encompass the eight [stages] below, so let us set them aside for now.

Within those matters, nothing is excluded from the four categories of object (jing) and wisdom (zhi). When wisdom contemplates the object, there arises the practice of cultivation (zao-xiu) and the stages accomplished thereby (cheng-zhi wei).

Fifth, the five stages traversed before reaching the ultimate are collectively categorized as the cause (yin); when the ultimate is reached, it constitutes the fruit (guo). Sixth, within the fruit, there are many dharmas.

There is nothing that does not emerge from the seven aspects of the "supported" (the environment) and the "supporting" (the beings). Within the seven aspects of the supporting, there is that which does not emerge:

the essence and its function. The essence refers to the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*; the function refers to the *nirmāṇakāya*. Among these eight functions, there is naturally a distinction between the Dharma and the person:

the Dharma constitutes the person, and through the person, one comes to know the Dharma. Ninth, within the Dharma, there is both inverse transformation and conformative transformation. Tenth, within conformative transformation, there is naturally the interplay of response and resonance (*ganying*). If one relies on the latter...

If one subsequently opens [the previous categories] into two, then the phenomena become even more numerous; that is to say, if the fruit-aspect is divided into the dependent and the primary, the causes are likewise so, resulting in four.
Within both the dependent and the primary, there are both essence and function. Regarding the essence within the primary, there are the Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, and so forth;

regarding the function, there is the manifestation of transformation according to what is appropriate. Regarding the essence within the dependent, there is the Dharma-nature realm; regarding the function, there is the response to things according to circumstances.

Since the gate of manifesting results is thus, the gate of causes follows the same analogy, thereby forming eight [categories]. Within the primary essence and function, there are further distinctions between persons and dharmas;
as with the support (*āśraya*), it likewise becomes sixteen. Furthermore, regarding persons, there are both inverse and direct transformations, and the dharmas are likewise so;
this thus constitutes thirty-two [categories]. Since the inverse and direct actions of persons must necessarily evoke a response, they should be treated inversely.
When the response of transformation is initiated, Vāsuki and others respond; when the response of conforming to transformation is initiated, Mañjuśrī and others respond.

Such is the principle of human resonance and the principle of Dharma resonance. When these are accumulated, they total sixty-four. Thus, by mutual observation and successive progression, they become manifold.

Yet this remains an explanation based on sequential order; if one were to discuss their opening and closing according to the principle of perfect interpenetration (*yuanrong*), they would become inexhaustible.

Furthermore, these ten pairs do not exist only across the ten realms; rather, within a single realm, upon any given phenomenon, these ten pairs are present—just as a single lotus leaf or a single atom possesses all ten characteristics, such as teaching and so forth.
Furthermore, taking one pair from among these ten pairs of teachings and meanings, it contains the remaining nine pairs;
likewise, the nine pairs of principle and phenomenon (*li-shi*) and so forth also contain the remaining nine pairs of teaching and meaning and so forth. Thus, there are one hundred gates.
Within each gate, there are the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*) that it contains, resulting in one thousand gates. Taking any one of these one thousand gates, it likewise contains [all others].
One thousand [units] amount to one million, just as one thousand coins together constitute a single causal origin (*nidāna*).
If one coin is taken as the primary unit, then possessing one thousand others is likewise the case; thus, it becomes "a thousand times a thousand.

If one takes the ten [realms] possessed by each as an analogy for the ten realms that possess them, then the ten dharma-realms also become one million dharma-realms. As the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "In a single thought-moment, when a mind of anger arises, a hundred..."

When the gate of ten thousand hindrances opens, a single thought is not anger; from this, one hundred thousand Dharma-gates arise. Within these one hundred thousand gates, each and every one possesses the six aspects in perfect fusion:

the principle and phenomena correspond, such that "one" possesses many names (the identity of principle and phenomenon); the totality of the many is not a single name (the difference of principle and phenomenon);

they do not obstruct one another (the non-contradiction of principle and phenomenon); they do not confuse one another (the non-intermixture of principle and phenomenon); and they are distinct from one another (the differentiation of principle and phenomenon).

The mutual establishment of characteristics is called "logical formation" (*yukti-siddha*); each abiding in its own fundamental nature is called "logical dissolution. The unification of all things into a single dharma is called "totality of phenomena" (*vastu-sāmānya*);

the distinct manifestation of all dharmas is called "particularity of phenomena" (*vastu-viśeṣa*). The non-differentiation of many types is called "identity of phenomena" (*vastu-samāna*); the differentiation of each as distinct is called "diversity of phenomena" (*vastu-bhinna*).

The accomplishment through various conditions is called "phenomenal completion" (*vastu-niṣpatti*); not departing from its own position is called "phenomenal dissolution" (*vastu-vināśa*). These are further categories such as the meanings of other teachings.
The nine pairs and the ten dharma-realms possess hundreds, thousands, and even millions of the six aspects; one should understand them all through this analogy.
Such inexhaustible and perfectly interfused dharmic characteristics all serve as the objective basis for the three contemplations. As the Sūtra says:
"If a person wishes to fully understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should contemplate the nature of the dharma-realm: everything is created solely by the mind."
Next, the contemplative methods (dharma-gates) that rely upon [the ultimate] are explained in three stages.
First, regarding the contemplation of "emptiness and the severance of marks" (*śūnyatā-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-vipaśyanā*), four propositions and ten gates are briefly opened therein.
Within the first proposition, the contemplation of "reducing form to emptiness" (*rūpa-śūnyatā-pratyāgamana-vipaśyanā*) is further divided into four gates.
First, the gate that form is not "emptiness of annihilation": form is not identical to emptiness of annihilation, because form in its entirety is true emptiness.
Second, the gate that form is not "true emptiness": blue and so forth are not the principle of true emptiness, because blue, yellow, and the rest have no intrinsic substance.
It is not because all things are empty.

Regarding the three gates of "form is emptiness" and "emptiness is form": through the gate of "form is emptiness," one brings form back to emptiness; yet within that emptiness, there is necessarily no form.
The above three gates have completed the process of using dharmas to distinguish them from deluded emotions.
The four forms are themselves the gate of emptiness; all phenomena that are form are necessarily not different from true emptiness, because they lack intrinsic nature.
Just as it is with form and emptiness, so it is with all dharmas.
The second sentence clarifies that the contemplation of emptiness as form (*śūnyatā-rūpa*) also has four gates:
1. The gate of emptiness not being illusory form: severed emptiness is not identical to form, because true emptiness (*bhūtakoṭi-śūnyatā*) is necessarily not different from form. 2.
The gate of emptiness not being substantial form: the principle of true emptiness is not blue or yellow, because emptiness is necessarily not different from blue or yellow.
The three emptinesses are not empty of form; the door of emptiness is that which is relied upon rather than that which relies, for it must serve as the basis for that which relies.
Thus, the previous three doors have also completed the selection of phenomena from among mental objects.

The four emptinesses are themselves the gateway to form; for whatever is true emptiness is necessarily not different from form, because this principle of the selflessness of phenomena is neither annihilation nor extinction.
As it is with emptiness and form, so it is with all phenomena.
The third phrase is the contemplation of the non-obstruction between emptiness and form: it means that the entire substance of form is entirely true emptiness;
form is identical with emptiness, yet form is not exhausted, while true emptiness is entirely no different from the dharma of form; emptiness is identical with form, yet emptiness is not concealed.
Being unobstructed and unhindered, they constitute a single-flavored dharma.

The fourth phrase is the contemplation of the cessation of all extremes and non-reliance, which means that this observed true emptiness cannot be said to be identical to form nor not identical to form, nor identical to emptiness nor not identical to emptiness; all phenomena are thus ineffable.

This ineffability itself cannot be grasped, for it is utterly detached and beyond reliance. Words fail to reach it, and the arising of thoughts or mental movements deviates from the essence of the Dharma.

Among the first four lines, the first two lines—comprising eight gates—all exclude emotional affliction (*kleśa*) to reveal understanding (*prajñā*). The third line—comprising one gate—marks the culmination of understanding and the transition toward practice.
The fourth line—comprising one gate—perfectly establishes the essence of practice; through understanding, practice is perfected, and as practice arises, understanding is transcended.

Taking one pair from among the ten previously established pairs—namely, the pair of principle (*li*) and phenomenon (*shi*)—and applying it to these ten gates of the contemplation that takes them as its support, and since within that pair of principle and phenomenon the remaining nine pairs such as teaching (*jiao*) and meaning (*yi*) are likewise each endowed with these ten gates of contemplation, this constitutes one hundred gates.

Since this is the case for the pair of principle and phenomenon, the same applies to the other nine pairs such as teaching and meaning; thus, they also each possess one hundred gates. Therefore, there are [one thousand gates].
Among the thousand gates, taking any one of them also contains a thousand; it is likewise with the others, such that there are one hundred thousand.
One possesses many names, which constitutes the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*); many are not a single name, which constitutes the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

These do not contradict one another. Names being identical, their characteristics do not intermingle; names being distinct, their common characteristics are established. Characteristics being established, each abides in its own place.

The stage is named "the characteristic of destruction. These six characteristics and one million dharma-gates are all for the purpose of contemplating the ultimate emptiness and the transcendence of characteristics.

As the *Xingkong juexiang guan jing* (Sutra on the Contemplation of the Ultimate Emptiness and Transcendence of Characteristics) says: "The nature of dharmas is fundamentally empty and quiescent; there is neither grasping nor seeing. That the nature of dharmas is empty is itself the Buddha; it cannot be apprehended through thought or deliberation."

Second, regarding the contemplation of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai guan*): when principle and phenomena are fused such that existence and non-existence, as well as the favorable and the adverse, interpenetrate, there are ten gates.

First is the gate of "principle pervading all phenomena" (*li bian yu shi men*): this means that the principle, which is without limits, is entirely present within phenomena, which possess parts; by means of that...
Because the ultimate truth (*tattva*) is indivisible, every single atom is perfectly complete in its principle.

It is like a great ocean that is entirely present within a single small wave; at that time, the ocean does not become small, yet it is not hindered from pervading all waves with its entire essence, nor does the ocean become something other [than itself].
Therefore, the *Phenapiṇḍopama-sūtra* states: "For example, the *dharmadhātu* pervades all things, yet it cannot be perceived as being 'all'."
This clarifies that the single nature is entirely contained within the five natures.
Furthermore, it says, "The Tathāgata’s wisdom reaches everywhere," which clarifies that the One Vehicle pervades the Three Vehicles.

Moreover, it says, "When the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he universally perceives all sentient beings within his own body attaining perfect enlightenment, and even universally perceives all sentient beings entering [nirvana]."

Nirvana is of a single nature, namely, the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). This clarifies that the principle is universally pervasive within phenomena; thus, when one phenomenon is realized, all phenomena are realized.
Second, regarding the gate of phenomena being pervasive within the principle: phenomena that possess limitations are entirely identical to the undivided principle, because of the phenomenon.
Because that which lacks intrinsic nature accords with reality, each and every subtle atom pervades the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Just as when a single small wave completely encompasses the great ocean, that wave is not the ocean itself, yet all waves simultaneously encompass it and each is not the ocean alone;
therefore, the *Samudgata-parivarta* states: "The liberation of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all buddhas is entirely dependent upon the dharma-realm."
"The Dharma-realm has neither increase nor decrease" clarifies that the five natures are entirely contained within the one nature.
Furthermore, it says, "There is not a single sentient being who does not possess the Tathāgata’s wisdom," which clarifies that the five vehicles are universally encompassed by the One Vehicle.
Moreover, it says, "For example, just as empty space is neither formed nor destroyed, so too is Bodhi: it is without marks and yet not without marks; it is neither one nor not one."
Because phenomena are universally identical to principle, it is said that there is nothing at all that is established.
Third, the gate of phenomena being established based on principle: this means that phenomena have no separate essence and must depend on principle to be established;

since all dependent originations lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is through the absence of intrinsic nature in phenomena that principle is established. This is like perceiving the form of waves as they are gathered from the substance of water.
The verse of Bodhisattva Vana states: "The mind is like a skilled painter, capable of painting all worlds; the five aggregates all arise from it, and there is no phenomenon that it does not create.
The verse of Bodhisattva Bodhimukha states: "The nature of phenomena is fundamentally without birth, yet it manifests as having birth."
There are four matters that can manifest the gateway to principle (*tattva*): because phenomena (*dharma*) are grasped by means of principle, phenomena are empty while principle is real.
Because phenomena are empty, they are able to manifest the real principle; just as the empty characteristics of waves allow the reality of water to appear. As the *Yāma-gāthā* says:
"When one discriminates these aggregates, their nature is fundamentally empty and quiescent. Because they are empty, they cannot be extinguished; this is the meaning of non-arising."—Sentient beings.
Since this is so, it is likewise for all Buddhas; both the Buddhas and the dharmas of the Buddhas have no self-nature whatsoever.
As stated in the *Sumeru-śikhara-gāthā*: "To realize that the self-nature of all phenomena is non-existent—thus understanding the nature of phenomena is to see Vairocana."

Fifth, the gate of subsuming phenomena by means of principle (*li*) means that once phenomena are fully constituted by encompassing principle, the nature of principle manifests and phenomenal characteristics are entirely exhausted;
for apart from true reality (*tattva*), not even a fragment of a phenomenon can be found. It is like water subsuming waves, wherein the characteristics of the waves are entirely exhausted.
As the *Xianxing pin* (Chapter on Manifestation) states: "Suppose all sentient beings were to attain perfect enlightenment within a single thought-moment..."
There is no difference between not attaining perfect enlightenment and so forth. Why? Because bodhi is without marks (*animitta*).

If there are no marks, then there is neither increase nor decrease. As the Sūtra says: "Because all the ignorant do not know the single dharma-realm as it truly is, they give rise to views of error, claiming that the realm of sentient beings increases or that the realm of sentient beings decreases. All of this reveals the principle of equality.
In its nature, there is no dharma that possesses superiority or inferiority.

The six matters are able to conceal the gate of principle; that is to say, as true reality follows conditions to form phenomenal dharmas, it causes the phenomena to manifest while the principle remains unmanifest.
This is because these various phenomenal dharmas are in opposition to principle, just as when water forms waves, the movement manifests and the stillness is concealed.
The opening verse states: "All the discourses spoken in the world are merely conceptual constructions; not a single dharma has ever entered the Dharma-nature of the Dharmakāya.
A sūtra says: "The Dharmakāya circulating through the five paths of rebirth is called a sentient being."

The seventh is the gate of truth as being identical to phenomena (*dharmatā-tattva-yathābhūta-mukha*). This means that whatever is the ultimate truth is necessarily not external to phenomena, because the principle of the selflessness of dharmas (*dharmanairātmya*) is not distinct from form (*rūpa*).
It is like water being identical to waves: the entire substance is in motion. As the *Sumeru-gāthā* states:

"When one observes all dharmas, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is non-existent; their characteristics of arising and ceasing are merely spoken of as provisional designations. (From the *Dàpǐn Bōrě Jīng Huíxiàng Pǐn*).
It is said that the dharma-nature does not contradict the characteristics of phenomena, and it is further said that there is no suchness outside of wisdom for wisdom to enter;
these all reveal that principle is itself the phenomenon, and thus although empty, it is not severed.
The eight categories of phenomena (*dharmas*) are precisely the gateway to principle; that is to say, the phenomena of dependent origination necessarily lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because they lack intrinsic nature, their entire substance is *tathatā* (suchness). It is like waves being water: there is no movement that is not moist. As the *Sumeru-gāthā* states:

"The actions of all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) inevitably and swiftly return to exhaustion; because their nature is like empty space, it is said that there is no exhaustion. This is from the "Dedication" chapter.
It is said that "the characteristics of phenomena do not violate the nature of reality," and it is further said that "there is no wisdom external to suchness by which one could realize suchness.
Both statements reveal that phenomena are themselves the principle; thus, although they exist, they are not eternal.
The ninth is the gate of truth as non-phenomenon: it is the principle within phenomena, yet it is not the phenomenon itself.

This is because truth differs from delusion, because that which is supported is not the support, and because reality is not the unreal. Just as moisture is not motion, so too is true wisdom. As the verse of True Wisdom says:
"In reality one sees reality; in unreality one sees unreality. Such ultimate understanding is therefore called Buddhahood.
The fourth dedication states: "Within the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*), one demonstrates conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) without destroying the nature of the unconditioned.

This refers to the irrational gate of the ten matters of phenomena; it means that while the matters are entirely rational, they are constantly irrational because their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) differ from their nature (*dharmatā*).
Therefore, that which is able to rely upon it is not its support; being empty, it is not substantial; like motion, it is not moist.

As the *Gāthā on the Forest of Shame and Remorse* says: "Just as form and non-form, these two do not become one; likewise, the characterized and the uncharacterized, saṃsāra and nirvāṇa—these distinctions are each different.
The *Chapter on Dedication* says: "Within the realm of the conditioned, one demonstrates the unconditioned dharma, yet does not extinguish it."
It destroys the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

These ten superior meanings share a single dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*): viewed from the perspective of principle (*li*) toward phenomena (*shi*), there is formation and destruction, as well as integration and separation;

viewed from the perspective of phenomena toward principle, there is concealment and manifestation, as well as identity and difference, opposition and conformity, and simultaneity without obstruction. Mastery over these ten constitutes the "total ten."
Non-identity constitutes differentiation; mutual non-contradiction constitutes sameness; the absence of mutual confusion constitutes difference; the collective fulfillment constitutes completion;
and abiding in the fundamental position constitutes destruction. Thus, although all ten pairs above are entirely unimpeded, for now they have been elucidated by way of principle and phenomenon.

Furthermore, within these ten gates of the contemplation upon the supported [object], one takes up the gate of "the principle pervading all phenomena. This contains the ten pairs previously mentioned regarding the substance of the supported object.

Moreover, within this gate of "the principle pervading all phenomena," there are further contained the nine other gates—such as "phenomena pervading the principle" and so forth—each possessing the aforementioned ten pairs of dharmas, thereby constituting one hundred gates. Since the principle thus pervades all phenomena, the same applies to the remaining gates, such as "phenomena pervading the principle" and so on.

The nine gates each possessing one hundred are likewise thus, forming one thousand gates; taking one from within those one thousand, it likewise possesses one thousand, and the remainder are all likewise so, thereby forming one million.
One containing many is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*); many that are not one are the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*);

each being without difference is the characteristic of sameness (*tulya-lakṣaṇa*); not being identical is the characteristic of difference (*bheda-lakṣaṇa*); collectively accomplishing [an effect] is the characteristic of accomplishment (*niṣpatti-lakṣaṇa*); not departing from its position is the characteristic of non-separation (*aviyoga-lakṣaṇa*).
These various inexhaustible dharma-gates of the interfusion of characteristics are all the contemplative aspect of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena. As the *Sūtra* says:
"Just as gold and the color of gold are in their nature without distinction, so too are the Dharma and the non-Dharma; their essential nature is without difference."

Regarding the third contemplation, the Universal Containment (*sarvākāra-saṃgraha-vipaśyanā*), the phenomena are harmoniously integrated with principle, universally encompassed, unobstructed, interpenetrating, and sovereign.
Briefly, ten gates are opened: 1.

The Dharma-gate of Principle Being Like Phenomena: This means that since phenomena are empty, there is nothing their nature does not exhaustively pervade; the essence of the nature of reality is truly real.
There is nothing that does not manifest; thus, phenomena are not distinct from the principle, for phenomena are entirely the principle itself.

Therefore, the inexhaustible characteristics of phenomena are themselves the inexhaustible dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Consequently, the entire body of the dharma-realm is simultaneously manifested within every single atom, pervading all without obstruction.

The second point concerns the gate of reality as it accords with principle: because all phenomena (dharmas) are not different from principle, phenomena accord with principle and are thus universally pervasive.
Consequently, a single atom becomes omnipresent throughout the Dharma-realm; just as this is true for one minute particle, so it is for all phenomena.

The third is the gate of phenomena and principle being mutually inclusive: because all phenomenal dharmas are not identical to the underlying principle, they preserve their original singular nature while being able to extensively contain others—just as a single minute particle, though its form is not large, can encompass and contain boundless worlds of the dharma-realm and other such dharmas;
as it is with one particle, so it is with all dharmas.

The Fourth Gate: The Unobstructed Interpenetration of the Particular and the Universal (Reopened as the Second). This refers to the fact that phenomena and their underlying principle are neither identical nor distinct;
thus, these particular dharmas do not depart from a single location while simultaneously pervading the entirety of all lands within the atoms of the ten directions.

While pervading the entirety of all lands within the atoms of the ten directions, they do not move from their original position. Thus, they are both distant and near, both pervasive and stationary, without obstruction.
Non-obstruction.

Fifth, the Gate of Non-obstruction between the Vast and the Narrow (a further opening of the third): This refers to how phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*) are neither different nor identical, such that this single atom of a phenomenon does not destroy the single atom while being able to extensively contain the oceans of lands of the ten directions and extensively contain the dharma-realm of the ten directions.
Yet, although these atoms are not large, they are simultaneously broad and narrow, simultaneously large and small, without obstruction or hindrance.
This is the sixth gate, the Gate of Universal Pervasiveness and Unobstructed Containment (combining the previous second, third, fourth, and fifth gates).

It means that when this single atom, in relation to all those [other phenomena], is universally pervasive, it is therefore broadly containing; thus, when this single atom pervades all those phenomena, it simultaneously subsumes them all once again.
All phenomena reside within a single atom; furthermore, because they possess vast capacity, they are all-pervasive.
Thus, when this single atom encompasses all those phenomena, it simultaneously and without obstruction pervades within its own single atom and within all phenomena.

This is the seventh gate of inclusion without obstruction (the reverse of the sixth gate), which means that these [all phenomena], in relation to that single phenomenon, by entering into the other, are...
Because this involves the inclusion of others, when all of these are entirely contained within a single dharma, that single dharma is in turn included within all;
since including others is itself the act of entering into them, when that one dharma is subsumed within all,
it causes all to constantly enter into that one dharma simultaneously and without obstruction.

The Eighth Gate: The Unimpeded Interpenetration (incorporating the preceding sixth and seventh gates). This refers to the relationship between a single dharma and all dharmas, wherein there is inclusion and penetration;
generally, there are four permutations: First: One includes all, and one enters all.
Second: All include one, and all enter one. Third: One includes one, and one enters one. Fourth: All include all, and all enter all.
"Everything" means that when this single dharma correctly subsumes all those things and causes all those things to enter into this one,
it simultaneously causes all those things to subsume this single dharma and enables its own oneness to enter into all things; furthermore,
when all those things correctly subsume this one and cause this single dharma to enter into all those things, it simultaneously causes this one [to do the same].
The Dharma encompasses all those [phenomena] and enables all those phenomena to enter into this single [principle].

Just as the first two phrases involve the inclusion and the hidden-manifest (yin-xian), so too do the remaining latter two phrases involve inclusion and entry. The interaction between the subject and object is simultaneous and unimpeded;

thus, the nine aspects reside within the gate of non-obstruction (the reverse of the eighth gate). That is to say, when all [phenomena] are viewed in relation to a single phenomenon, there is both inclusion and entry.
There are four propositions: first, one inclusion of one; second, one inclusion of all; third, all inclusion of one;

and fourth, all inclusion of all. This means that when these all-encompassing dharmas correctly include another single dharma, they cause that other single dharma to enter into that one [inclusion]; furthermore, that single dharma is correctly included therein.
At all other times, it causes the inclusion of all others; that one *āyatana* is included within this totality of all phenomena, and that one includes all *āyatanas*.
Since these two propositions are thus established, the remaining two are likewise so. The characteristics of inclusion and being included exist simultaneously without obstruction.
The Tenth Gate: Universal Integration and Non-obstruction (which, in the near sense, subsumes the eighth and ninth gates, and in the far sense, universally subsumes the preceding nine).
This means that all and one are universally simultaneous, such that each and every one mutually faces the others, each possessing the two sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) mentioned previously:
First: One encompasses all; one enters all; all encompass one; all enter one. Second: All encompass one; all enter one; one encompasses all; one enters all.
One entrance includes one; the third includes one; each individual entrance includes all entrances; the fourth includes all; all entrances include one;
and all entrances include every entrance. That is to say, this single dharma correctly includes all others, and all other entrances are included within this one.
When about to enter that [state], it causes all those [others] to do so as well.
When the remaining one and the remaining one are subsumed into all those, and all these dharmas are correctly subsumed into the remaining one and the remaining one;
when all these are about to enter into that single dharma, it in turn causes that single dharma to subsume all the others,
and all those others to enter into that one, which is about to enter into all these— this constitutes the first two [stages].
Since this is so for the first phrase, the same applies to the latter two phrases; they correspond simultaneously and are universally fused in an inexhaustible manner.
Thus, the ten meanings above arise from one another to form ten gates. Principle is the foundation of phenomena, and because principle manifests as phenomena, there is the first gate.
Phenomena arise in dependence upon principle, and because phenomena pervade principle, there is the second gate. It is not merely a matter of principle and phenomena alone.
Since the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) also contain both principle (li) and phenomena (shi), and since phenomena contain both principle and phenomena, there are three gates.

Because two of these [the second and third] are exclusively pervasive, there is a fourth gate; because among the three [the first, second, and third], only one [the first] is all-encompassing, there is a fifth gate;

because the second and fourth are exclusively pervasive while the third and fifth are exclusively containing, there is a sixth gate; and because the sixth is both pervasive and containing, it is established as such by means of a single [attribute].

Because one is viewed from the perspective of many, there is a seventh [category]; because many are viewed from the perspective of one, the sixth is that one which can enter and subsume, while the seventh is that many which can subsume and cause entry.
Because both one and many together function as the agent of entry and the agent of subsumption, the eighth is that both are capable of doing so.

Because both many and one together function as the object of subsumption and the object of entry, the ninth is that neither the six, seven, one, nor many possess the relationship of agent and object across the eighth and ninth categories.
Because each is mutually lacking, there is the eleventh gate, "the many aspects," in which subject and object are simultaneously fused; this constitutes the general intent of the first two gates.

Since these two are capable of establishing the subsequent eight gates—which encompass both the non-obstruction of principle and phenomenon as well as the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena—the meaning of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena is thereby established, and it is subsumed under the category of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena.

The Ancient Worthies, based on these ten meanings, further opened them as the Ten Mysterious Gates: 1. The Gate of Simultaneous Mutual Fulfillment and Correspondence; 2. The Gate of Unobstructed Freedom between the Vast and the Narrow; 3.
The Gate of the Mutual Interpenetration of the One and the Many without Confusion; 4. The Gate of the Sovereign Mutual Identity of All Dharmas; 5.
The Gate of the Simultaneous Accomplishment of the Secret, the Hidden, and the Manifest; 6. The Gate of the Subtle Interpenetration and Stable Establishment.

7. The Gate of the Realm of Indra’s Net; 8. The Gate of Manifesting the Dharma by Relying on Phenomena to Generate Understanding; 9. The Gate of Establishing the Distinctness of Dharmas Despite Temporal Separation;
10. The Gate of the Perfect Clarity and Endowment of Virtues through the Mutual Relationship of Principal and Associate.

First, regarding the Gate of Simultaneous Fulfillment and Correspondence: the ten meanings, such as the teaching and so forth, correspond simultaneously to form a single dependent origination, devoid of distinctions such as before and after or beginning and end.
Because they are fully present, sovereign, and interpenetrating without confusion, the verse in the "Chapter on Sublime Adornment" states:
"The inexhaustible ocean of all dharma-gates converges within the single dharma of the site of enlightenment."
The second is the gate of unimpeded mastery over breadth and narrowness: ten pairs of phenomena may be broad or narrow;
within a single phrase, one unfolds boundless teachings, extending to great bodies and lands that penetrate without interior, while even the smallest atom or hair-pore contains all without exterior.
Thus, there is universal containment, unimpeded and sovereign. As Māyādevī said: "My body..."
Although its physical dimensions do not exceed its original state, it has in fact already transcended all worldly measures; being equal to empty space, it is able to contain everything.
In the *Saptasaptati*, Sudhana praises the pavilion, saying: "Without moving from its original location, it is able to reach all Buddha-fields.
In the "Ten Abodes" chapter (*Daśabhūmika*), it says: "The countless mountains of the Vajra-perimeter can all be placed within a single hair."
Duan further states that the Buddha could not exhaustively expound even a single phrase of the Dharma throughout immeasurable kalpas, and so forth.
Third is the "Gate of the Mutual Inclusion of the One and the Many without Confusion":

within each of the aforementioned meanings, according to any single gate, all dharmas of cause and effect, principle and phenomena, are fully subsumed; yet, although the one contains the many, it remains one.
It is not that there are merely many; within those many, each single one is to be contemplated according to the principle above.

Because the power and function of the one and the many arise through mutual dependent origination, they penetrate and interpenetrate one another; thus it is said they are "mutually inclusive. Yet because their individual characteristics are not destroyed, it is said they are "not identical.
This is the case in every single gate [of contemplation]. Therefore, a verse in the Sūtra says: "With a single Buddha-land, filling..."
The ten directions enter into one direction without remainder, yet the original characteristics of other worlds are not destroyed; it is because of incomparable merit that this is possible.
The "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra" states: "All worlds enter into a single hair-pore, and a single hair-pore enters into all worlds.
The "Chapter on the Ten Practices" states: "One is able, within each and every samādhi, to universally enter into countless worlds."
Through samādhi, immeasurable and boundless lands are all made to enter together into a single atom.
Fourth, regarding the gate of the sovereign interpenetration of the characteristics of all phenomena:

because the ten pairs of phenomena above—where one is all and all is one—are perfectly interfused and sovereign, the ten bodies are clearly manifest while mutually functioning, and the six positions remain distinct without confusion.
Furthermore, another sutra states: "The merit of a single thought-moment of a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment is profound and vast, with no limit or boundary;

even if a Tathāgata were to explain it in detail for an entire kalpa, he could not exhaust it. How much more so the merit and practice of the various pāramitās and stages (bhūmis) fully cultivated over infinite, immeasurable, and incalculable kalpas.
It further says: "One may take the body of a sentient being and transform it into the body of a buddha-field," and yet...

One does not destroy the bodies of sentient beings by taking the body of a buddha-field (*kṣetra*) to become the body of a sentient being, yet one does not destroy the body of the buddha-field either.
As the *Acintyadharmamukhaparivarta* states: "The Buddhas know that all Buddha-speech is the speech of a single Buddha.

And as the verse from the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* says: "The one is many, and the many are one; the meaning follows the text, and the text follows the meaning. In this way, all things proceed through mutual transformation.
This should be explained for those who have attained this stage of non-retrogression.

Regarding the fifth gate, the "Gate of the Simultaneous Manifestation and Concealment of the Secret": it refers to the aforementioned ten meanings, wherein this [the one] fully encompasses that [the many], making the former manifest and the latter concealed;

and that [the many] fully encompasses this [the one], making the latter manifest and the former concealed. Thus, the one encompasses the many, the one manifests while the many are concealed, and the many [encompass the one].

The inclusion of the one and many, the manifestation of the one and the concealment of the many—thus, this mutual inclusion of the one and many, their simultaneous concealment and revelation, are accomplished at once without mutual obstruction.
Though these secret masteries differ from one another, they are not confused; therefore, it is said that concealment and manifestation are accomplished simultaneously.
Because the essence has no sequence, it is said they are "accomplished together," each attaining its own place with sovereign mastery.
Because it is unimpeded, the *Guhyaka-sūtra* states: "In this world one enters into meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), while in other worlds one arises from samādhi;

through the faculty of the eye one enters into meditative absorption, while through the object of form (*rūpa*) one arises from samādhi; within a male body one enters into meditative absorption, while within a female body one arises from samādhi;
within a single atom one enters into meditative absorption, while at the tip of a single hair one arises from samādhi. It further says: "The ten directions..."

Because the world has conditions, [the Buddha] comes and goes, enters and emerges, to deliver sentient beings; sometimes one sees a Bodhisattva entering right concentration (*samādhi*), and sometimes one sees a Bodhisattva arising from that meditative state.

It is further said that within those worlds of the ten directions, he manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment, the turning of the wheel of the true Dharma, and entry into *nirvāṇa* moment by moment, manifesting the distribution of relics to deliver sentient beings. As the *Yama-gāthā* says:
In all places throughout the ten directions, it is said that the Buddha is here; some see him in the human world, while others see him dwelling in celestial palaces.

The "Ten Samādhis" chapter states: "Some see the Buddha’s body as being seven cubits in measure, some see the Buddha’s body as being eight cubits in measure, some see the Buddha’s body as being nine cubits in measure, and so on, until some see the Buddha’s body as being unspeakably unspeakable [cubits] in measure."
Regarding the sixth gate, the subtle containment and establishment of the magnitude of the trichiliocosm: as previously described, within a single thought-moment, all dharma-gates— beginning and end,
simultaneity and succession, anteriority and posteriority, direct and inverse order, and so forth— are fully present and vividly manifest within that single thought-moment.
Nevertheless, they manifest simultaneously and in unison, appearing with complete clarity, just as a bundle of arrows appears when their heads are aligned;

for a single [entity] can contain many dharmas, and all dharmas are likewise thus, which is why it is said they are "mutually inclusive. Because the characteristics of the one and the many are neither destroyed nor confused, they are said to be "established.
As the Sūtra says: "In a single thought-moment, the Bodhisattva descends from Tuṣita Heaven into his mother’s womb."
Furthermore, it is revealed that the dissemination of the *śarīra* (relics), the long endurance of the Dharma, and all the sentient beings who are benefited are all fully manifested;
again, it is said that within a single pore, immeasurable Buddha-fields abide in vast tranquility;
and again, it is said that within a single atom, subtle lands all abide therein.

The seventh is the gateway of the realm of Indra’s net (*indrajāla*). Among the aforementioned meanings, the essence and characteristics are sovereign, manifesting through mutual concealment and appearance in infinite layers.
It is like the jeweled net covering the celestial palace of the Lord of Devas: within a single bright jewel, the myriad images all appear;
every jewel is likewise so, reflecting one another’s shadows, and those shadows again reflecting shadows, without end. This is the tenth [aspect].
This alone receives its name from a metaphor; if established according to the actual phenomena (*dharma*), it should be called the "Inexhaustible Gate of Multiple Layers of Mutual Reflection.
As the Sūtra says: "All worlds—vast, immeasurable, coarse or subtle, disordered, inverted, or upright;
whether entering, moving, or departing—are as diverse as a celestial net (*indrajāla*). These infinite varieties throughout the ten directions appear before one's eyes for direct perception."

Their wisdom is entirely clear and lucid. The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "The Buddhas know all the various phenomena within the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), like the Indra-net, exhaustively and without exception.
The *Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta* states: "Within the space of a single minute hair-tip, there are unspeakably many Samantabhadras;
it is the same for every single hair-tip, and so on, pervading the entirety of the Dharma-realm."
Within a single hair-tip of the world-systems, the number of lands is immeasurable and cannot be fully described; as is the measure of space, so it is at every single hair-tip.
Furthermore, it is said that within a single atom, lands are unspeakable in number, and as it is for one, so it is for all.
These unspeakable Buddha-lands are reduced to atoms in a single thought-moment, and those thought-moments are themselves unspeakable in number.
Recalling that all which was thus shattered is likewise so: within these atoms are unspeakably many buddha-fields. The "Chapter on Samādhi of Samantabhadra" states:
"Within all the lands manifested by the Buddha’s body, and within every single atom of all those lands, there are buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds;
and within each such field, there are buddhas as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds."
Before each and every Buddha, there are Bodhisattvas such as Samantabhadra, numbering as many as the atoms within an ocean of worlds.
Regarding the eighth gate, "The Gate of Generating Understanding by Relying on Phenomena to Reveal the Dharma":

the various phenomena mentioned previously, according to whichever single one they rely upon, reveal many dharmas—namely, that which is the basis and the realization, the dharma and the person, the principle and the phenomenon, and so forth—all such gates of dharma are revealed accordingly.
A single matter is precisely the vision of the inexhaustible Dharma-realm; because the Dharma-realm is inexhaustible, the dharmas within it are likewise inexhaustible.
Thus, according to each single matter, there are many dharma-gates. This is not a case of relying on this [single matter] to represent something else separately. As the Sūtra says:

"From the dharma that transcends the three realms, from the profound dharma of skillful means, and from the dharma-gate of non-action, one produces offerings surpassing all celestial requisites to make offerings to the Buddha."
