Clouds of all precious lotuses born from roots of goodness dedicated to non-arising, clouds of all solid fragrances, and clouds of all pure ornaments, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, were used to make offerings to the Buddha.
Furthermore, it is said that Maitreya Bodhisattva approached the pavilion, snapped his fingers, and the gate opened; he then commanded Sudhana to enter, and Sudhana entered.
He saw that the pavilions were vast and immeasurable, equal to empty space;
furthermore, within them he saw hundreds of thousands of myriad exquisite pavilions, each adorned and identical to empty space, without mutual obstruction and without confusion.
In one location, Sudhana saw all locations, and in all locations, everything was exactly as it was there.
Regarding these views and so forth:

the ninth section, "The Gateway of the Distinct Formation of Dharmas Separated by Ten Time-Periods," concerns these various composite meanings which manifest simultaneously throughout the ten time-periods.
Because dharmas and time are inseparable, they are spoken of as "ten time-periods," which refers to the three periods of time.

Each [of these] has its own past, present, and future, which are termed the nine time-periods (*navadhva*). However, these nine time-periods mutually interpenetrate and are subsumed within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*);

the former nine are the particulars, while the single thought-moment is the whole. Because the whole and the particulars are discussed in combination, it is called the "ten time-periods" (*daśadhva*).

The differentiation of these ten time-periods is termed the "separation of dharmas," yet their mutual presence constitutes their "differentiation-in-identity. Thus, the Jin translation says: "The past..."
"In immeasurable kalpas, the future is placed within the present; now, those immeasurable kalpas of the future are turned back and placed within the past.

Regarding the conduct of Samantabhadra, it is said that within the past, the future is seen, and within the future, the present is seen; the three periods of time are mutually perceived, each clearly understood.
Furthermore, it is said that immeasurable and innumerable kalpas, when resolved, are but a single thought-moment. This is stated in the "Chapter on the Merit of Arousing the Mind."
"Immeasurable eons are but a single thought-moment, and a single thought-moment is immeasurable eons. The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states:
"One eon enters many eons, and many eons enter one eon; long eons enter short eons, and short eons enter long eons," and so forth.
Regarding the "Ten Gates of the Perfect Clarity and Endowment of Principal and Retinue":
in the preceding section on the essential substance (*vastu*), if one is cited, it immediately becomes the principal situated in the center, while the others become the retinue surrounding it.

Because they function as the leader or the follower without confusion or obstruction, it is said that the principal and retinue are mutually hidden and manifest; because the principal and retinue shine upon one another, it is said to be "perfectly clear" (*pariniṣpanna*).

Because the one and the many are subsumed within the dependent origination of mutual connection, it is said to "possess excellence," as stated in the Sūtra: "One direction serves as the principal, while the ten directions serve as its retinue;

the same applies to all other directions. Furthermore, in the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs," the Bodhisattva Viśvaghoṣa emerges from between the Buddha’s eyebrows together with immeasurable attendants—this refers to the person and their retinue. In the "Chapter on Vairocana," the *Dharmadhātu-sūtra* is elucidated.
With *sūtras* as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field serving as their retinue, they constitute the "Retinue of the Dharma" as described in the chapter on the manifestation of the retinue;
furthermore, with the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of light rays emitted from between the Buddha’s eyebrows serving as their retinue, they constitute the "Retinue of Light.
Thus, within each and every dharma, there exists its own respective retinue.
Now, furthermore, taking one single dharma from among the ten previously mentioned, we shall clarify how it possesses the ten gates.

First, regarding the gate of simultaneity (*yugapat-mukha*): as in the *Avataṃsaka*, a single lotus petal or a single atom possesses the ten pairs—such as the teaching and so forth—in simultaneous correspondence, complete and perfect; it likewise possesses the remaining nine gates and their respective sub-gates.
Because the teachings and so forth contained therein are comprehensive, the *Avataṃsaka-gāthā* states:
"Within every single atom of all the atoms of the Flower Treasury World, one perceives the entire Dharma-realm; if even a single atom possesses this, how much more so a single petal?"
Second, the gate of breadth and narrowness: these lotus petals universally pervade the entire Dharma-realm yet do not destroy their original positions.
Thus, division is non-division, and non-division is division; breadth and narrowness are sovereign, unobstructed, and unhindered. As the *Ten Samādhis Chapter* states:
"There is a single lotus flower that reaches the limits of the ten directions, yet it does not hinder what can be seen outside of it. Therefore, it is either exclusively broad, or...
It may be boundless, or its limits may be clearly defined; it may be both expansive and contracted, or both expansiveness and contraction may be simultaneously obliterated;

it may possess all four of these preceding states because it is the object of understanding, or it may transcend all five because it is the object of practice—the subsequent cases are all to be understood according to this principle.

Furthermore, this expansiveness and contraction is also termed "purity and intermixture": because it universally pervades the Dharma-realm, it is pure and singular without a second, never destroying its original nature.
In terms of their positions, there is no obstruction to the integration of the myriad practices;

this is the general rule. Regarding the "Gate of Mutual Accommodation of the Three Phases": when these flowers and petals have unfolded, they universally enter into all phenomena, thereby encompassing all things and causing them to enter within themselves.
Since this simultaneous unfolding and encompassing is without obstruction, they are thus fused and integrated. Alternatively, there are four [aspects].

Regarding the six phrases, contemplate them as follows: The *Ten Stages Sūtra* (*Daśabhūmika-sūtra*), in the chapter on the Ten Concentrations (*Daśa-vyākaraṇa-parivarta*), states: "World-systems of three thousandfold great thousands, as numerous as atoms, all enter the body of this bodhisattva;
the body of this bodhisattva also enters all those world-systems. The *Lokottara-parivarta* (Chapter on Transcending the World) states:
"One enters the bodies of all sentient beings into one's own body without obstruction, and uses one's own body to enter the bodies of all sentient beings."
If the unimpeded functions and so forth are analyzed in relation to both the one and the all, they are subsumed within four permutations for each:
namely, the one entering the all, the one entering the one, the all entering the one, and the all entering the all; the same mutual inclusion applies to the others as well.
Regarding the gate of the mutual identity of the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa-samāveśa-mukha*): this single flower-petal sets aside its own self and becomes identical with others;

its entire substance is entirely those other phenomena, while it constantly subsumes others as its own self, causing all those others to be identical with its own essence. The mutual identity of the one and the many is thus indistinguishable and without obstruction.
The six phrases concerning the distinctions between the sphere of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā*) are the same as before.

Regarding the fifth, the gate of concealment and manifestation: when the flower is able to encompass that [the petals], one is manifest and many are concealed; when all are encompassed by the flower, one is concealed and many are manifest.

Manifestation and manifestation do not coexist; concealment and concealment do not occur simultaneously. Concealment and manifestation, as well as manifestation and concealment, occur at the same time without obstruction.
When fully encompassed, both are merged; whether retained or forgotten, both are established. The enumeration of these phrases is the same as before.
Sixth, the gate of subtlety: within these flower petals, all phenomena, such as subtle lands and so forth, manifest clearly and simultaneously.
Seventh, the gate of the net: it means that within each and every flower petal and within each minute atom, boundless lands appear.
Within an ocean of lands, there are further oceans of lands as numerous as motes of dust; within those motes of dust, there are again oceans of lands.
Thus, layer upon layer, they are inexhaustible, beyond the sphere of conceptual thought and mental calculation.

The eighth is the gate of relying on phenomena (*vastu*). To see these flower petals is precisely to see the inexhaustible dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). As the *Inexhaustible Dharma-Realm Sūtra* states:
"These flower canopies and so forth arise from the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."
Regarding the ninth, the gate of the formation of differences: this very flower, having already pervaded all places, further encompasses all times.
Since each of the three periods [of past, present, and future] has three [sub-periods], these are subsumed into a single thought-moment; thus, there are ten periods of time.
Because time has no separate substance apart from the flower, it is established by means of the flower; since the flower is unimpeded, time is likewise so.
The tenth is the gate of primary and attendant [elements]. This means that these flowers and petals, by their very nature, cannot arise in isolation;
they must be surrounded by immeasurable retinues. As the Sūtra says: "This flower has as its retinue as many flowers as there are atoms in ten worlds."
If it is so with the raising of a flower, it is likewise with a single mote of dust and other such matters. If this is true for phenomena, it is equally true for all other teachings and meanings.
Thus, the significance of these ten gates is profoundly deep and far-reaching; were it not for parables, how could they be fully understood?
They manifest vividly and simultaneously, like mustard seeds and a jar coexisting in their entirety, or like a drop merging with the many—just as in an empty room, [all reflections appear at once].
The thousand lights, appearing and disappearing together, are like a crescent moon in the autumn sky; their layered reflections are like pearls hanging from a celestial net (*indrajāla*).
Moment by moment, they are perfectly integrated, resembling the passage of a world through a single night's dream. These gates of Dharma are tiered like clouds rising in the vast expanse of space;
the principal and its attendants are all-pervasive, like stars surrounding the North Star. They are mutually identical, like a hundredfold reflection.
Specifically, by means of a single mirror—vast yet narrow, and harmoniously integrated—one reflects images across a thousand *li*.
As for the sequence: first, the "Simultaneous Gate" (*yǒngshí mén*) is placed at the beginning of the nine gates because it is the totality;

second, within the "Distinct Gates," the "Gate of Vastness and Narrowness" (*guǎngxiá mén*) is distinguished first, as this serves as the basis for the subsequent distinct gates, following from the matters of the first two gates.
Because the principle (li) is all-pervasive, it gives rise to the other eight gates. To begin with, regarding phenomena (shi): because the principle is all-pervasive, it is "broad" (*guǎng*);
because it does not destroy the characteristics of phenomena, it is "narrow" (*xiá*). Thus, it constitutes the beginning of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wu'ài*).

Third, regarding the non-obstruction of the broad and the narrow: that which is pervaded is manifold, for one takes its own self and looks toward that multiplicity; thus there is the mutual containment of the one and the many. When they mutually contain one another, both entities coexist. However—

4. Because their powers and functions interpenetrate: since this can contain that, that is immediately this; and since this pervades that, that is immediately this. Thus, there is the gate of mutual identity (*xiāngjí mén*). 5.

Because they mutually encompass one another, there is a mutual presence of concealment and manifestation: when encompassing the other, the other is visible, which constitutes the gate of mutual entry (*xiāngrù mén*);
when encompassing the other, the other lacks substantiality, which constitutes the gate of mutual identity (*xiāngjí mén*). Thus, they are encompassed.

Although the Buddhas exist, they cannot be seen; thus, there is the gate of concealment and manifestation. These three [gates] all arise from the mutual inclusion of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) because they are distinct gates of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Mutual inclusion is like two objects reflecting one another; mutual identity is like waves and water merging;

and concealment and manifestation are like fragments of the moon reflecting each other. Through these six, all others are encompassed simultaneously, and that which is encompassed by them is itself encompassed.
1. Because it is likewise so, there is the subtle mutual containment; 2. because of the layering of mutual inclusion, there is the inexhaustible Indra’s net; 3.
because once the net is established as such, each single element is itself the entirety of the inexhaustible, there is the manifestation of the Dharma by relying on phenomena; 4.
since the eight preceding gates are all that which is supported, and the supported dharmas have already been shown to be fused, one next examines that which supports them.
Since the time-periods that serve as the basis are likewise [tenfold], there are ten distinct temporal periods. This is established by the fact that all phenomena (dharma) are thus;

therefore, whichever one is cited becomes the primary [factor]. Because dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) functions through association, it possesses companions; thus, there is the "primary with its retinue" (sādhika-saparivāra).
These ten gates of mystery share a single dependent origination that is unimpeded and perfectly interfused; as such, each individual gate encompasses all others.

Furthermore, these ten mysteries are established according to the previous principles and likewise possess three meanings: First, in accordance with the previous principle, each single gate is opened to manifest as ten.
This is illustrated by taking the "phenomena conforming to principle" gate as an example: phenomena, in their conformity to principle, simultaneously and fully possess manifold meanings and gates.

Therefore, [the gates are opened as follows]: the gate of simultaneous universal correspondence according to principle; the gate of the narrow opening into the broad due to the extensive abiding in the one;

the gate of mutual containment where one phenomenon universally accommodates all; the gate of the identity of phenomena through the relinquishing of self to accord with the characteristics of others according to principle;

the gate of the concealment and manifestation of phenomena according to principle because the subject and object follow conditions; and the gate of opening [to unity] because all things are equally subsumed within principle.

Subtle matters are also subsumed within the gate of the "multiple layers of Indra's net" (*indrājāla*); matters are also fully present and inexhaustible, which is the gate of "relying on phenomena" (*vastu-ālambana*).

According to principle, they penetrate through ten ages, which is the gate of "possessing ten ages"; according to principle, they bring forth their retinues, which is the gate of "possessing the principal and its attendants.
Just as it is with one gate regarding phenomena in accordance with principle, so too are the other nine gates opened to the profound mystery. This is based upon...

Because each meaning within the ten gates is fully complete, they are opened out into the Ten Mysterious Gates (*daśa-guhyaka*). Third, based on the previous ten gates, they are either opened or closed and established as ten:
namely, because the first three comprehensively establish all gates, phenomena and principle are mutually identical;

thus, there is the gate of breadth and narrowness—phenomena are broad because they pervade principle, and principle is narrow because it conforms to the smallness of phenomena—and the gate where phenomena contain both principle and phenomena.
Therefore, there is: the fourth, the gate of subtlety; the fifth, the gate of non-separation wherein being at one place is identical to being omnipresent;

the sixth, the gate of identity between the extensive and the narrow; the seventh, the gate of identity between the two aspects of the extensive and the narrow; the eighth, the gate of mutual interpenetration and inclusion;

the ninth, the gate of mutual interaction wherein each acts as both subject and object through the manifestation and concealment of phenomena; the tenth, the gate of Indra’s net; and the eleventh, the gate of sameness.

At that time, the "Gate of Complete Endowment" (Juzumén) serves as the primary heading for ten gates, including the "Gate of Having a Principal with its Retinue" (Youzubanmén), which reveals that within the temporal [gate] there are ten temporal periods;

since all phenomena are thus, there is the "Gate of Relying on Phenomena" (Tuoshimén). Because these meanings are mutually inclusive within the ten gates, they are established as the Ten Mysterious Gates (Shixuan).
Third, each of the aforementioned ten gates is further opened into ten: the first is the "Relying on Phenomena" gate, and the second is...

The mutual identity of phenomena (xiāngjí) is established through ten gates: first, the subtle fourfold division; second, the ten periods of time; third, the five returns; fourth, breadth and narrowness;
fifth, mutual inclusion; sixth, the formation of hidden and manifest; seventh, the opening of the principal and the attendant; eighth, the belonging to the Indra’s Net; and ninth, simultaneity.
These are each opened up as a distinct "mystery" because their meanings are individually complete within these ten gates.

Taking one principle from among the ten gates of contemplation previously established—such as the gate of "principle-as-phenomenon"—and equipping it with the ten successive profound gates subsequently established;
furthermore, within this gate of "principle-as-phenomenon," one includes the other nine types of contemplative gates, such as "phenomenon-as-principle" and so forth.
Since each gate possesses its own ten successive profound gates, there are thus one hundred gates. As it is with the gate of "principle-as-phenomenon," so it is with the others.

The nine gates, such as "phenomena according to principle," each possess a hundred [aspects], thus forming one thousand gates. Within these one thousand gates, taking any single one also possesses one thousand [aspects];

all others follow this same pattern, thus forming one million. Furthermore, by applying the ten layers of the "Mysterious Gates" (*xuanmen*) that can manifest [the truth] to the ten types of contemplative gates previously manifested, they likewise form one million. Moreover, by applying the ten "Mysterious Gates" of the dependent [to the basis]...
Within one gate, there are nine simultaneous gates; the remaining nine gates likewise each possess the other nine gates, such as those of breadth and narrowness.
Thus, there are one hundred gates. Within each of these gates, there are ten pairs of dharmas—such as the teachings upon which they rely and their meanings—which constitute one thousand dharma-gates.
Taking one from within these one thousand, it likewise possesses one thousand others, and the same applies to all the rest.

Thus, there are one million [categories]. If one applies the principle of the "gates of the dependent" (*āśraya-mukha*) to the "dharmas that are depended upon" (*āśrita-dharma*), these also constitute one million.

Furthermore, by cross-referencing the ten gates of contemplation (*daśa-vipaśyanā-mukha*) with the ten paired dharmas (*daśa-pratipakṣa-dharma*), the formation of one million meanings can be understood through this analogy. In summary: 1. That which universally encompasses all is the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). 2.

Each individual [phenomenon] according to its own kind is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). 3. According to principle, they are all identical and thus constitute the identical characteristic (*tulya-lakṣaṇa*). 4. They manifest in accordance with conditions (*pratyaya*).
The distinctness of each individual entity is the characteristic of differentiation; their formation through the harmonious combination of various conditions is the characteristic of formation;

and their dissolution as each returns to its own state is the characteristic of destruction. Therefore, when one clearly realizes this perfect manifestation, one constantly enters the realm of the dharmadhātu’s multilayered profundity.
Question: What causes and conditions allow these phenomena (*dharmas*) to be thus interpenetrating and unobstructed? Answer: The causes are too extensive to describe in detail;

briefly, ten categories may be cited: first, because they are manifestations of mind alone; second, because phenomena have no fixed nature; third, because of the mutual dependence of dependent origination;
fourth, because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is harmoniously interfused; fifth, because they are like illusory dreams; sixth, because they are like reflections.

1. Because it is manifested; 2. because the seven causes are without limit; 3. because the realization of the Buddha-fruit is ultimate; 4. because of profound meditative concentration and great function;
5. because of supernormal powers and liberation.
Regarding the first point, "manifested solely by mind": all phenomena are manifested from the true mind, just as the entirety of the great ocean water [is manifested].
Fifth, because all phenomena are nothing other than the single mind, the characteristics of magnitude and so forth revolve according to the mind and thus enter into non-obstruction.
Sixth, as for the lack of a fixed nature in phenomena: since they are manifestations of mind alone, arising from conditions, they possess no fixed nature or fixed characteristics.
Because it is free from the small yet not definitively small, it can contain the vast void with room to spare, for it shares the "greatness" of being without exterior;
because the great is not definitively great, it can enter into minute particles without interval, for it shares the "smallness" of having no interior.
Thus, if a single atom is equal to the vast void and contains a broad world-system as vast as that void, what difficulty could there be? (The Ten Abodes)
The chapter states: "The countless mountains of the Vajra-encircling range can all be placed upon a single hair-tip;
one who wishes to know that the greatest possesses the characteristic of the smallest is a Bodhisattva who has thus first resolved their mind.

1. Because it is not fixed as one, it can be all many; because it is not fixed as many, it can be one; because it is not fixed as a side, it can be the center; because the center is not fixed as a center, [it is the ultimate].
Therefore, it can be understood that in each and every instance—whether regarding limits and continuity, brevity and prolixity, stillness and turbulence, and so forth—the same principle applies.

Third, regarding the mutual dependence of the characteristics of dependent origination: within the great Dharma-realm, the meanings and gateways of the ocean of dharmas of dependent origination are immeasurable;
however, according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), ten gateways are briefly cited here to explain the preceding meaning.

First, the meaning of the distinctness of each condition: within the Great Dependent Origination (*mahā-pratītyasamutpāda*), when various conditions are compared with one another, it is essential that their substance (*svabhāva*) and function (*vṛtti*) be distinct and not confused;
only then does dependent origination come to be established. If they were confused, the fundamental dependent origination would be lost and dependent origination would not be established.
This means that each condition maintains its own single position. As the Sūtra says: "Within the many there is no single nature, and the single..."
There are not many [distinct entities].
The meaning of "mutually pervasive and mutually supportive" refers to the fact that these various conditions must pervasively correspond with one another for dependent origination to be established.
Just as one condition pervasively corresponds to many conditions, each of those many conditions is entirely identical with that one; therefore, this single [condition] possesses all the many.
First, if this single condition were not complete, then the many would lack their support and the principle of dependent origination would not be universally established;
thus, each and every one must individually possess all others. As the Sūtra says: "Know that through the one there is the many, and know that through the many there is the one."
The meaning of the unimpeded coexistence of the three is as follows: any single condition must possess the preceding two [aspects] to constitute dependent origination;
for it must abide in its own nature in order to be able to universally respond, and it is only by universally responding to multiple conditions that it becomes one.
Therefore, there are six propositions regarding the unimpeded, fused integration of the one and the many: first, the entire substance abides [in its own place], which is exclusively...
1. Or [the one] pervades the many as its entire substance; 2. Or both exist together; 3. Or both are simultaneously negated; 4. Or they are merged as a whole; 5.
Or they are entirely separated—all of these can be understood through reflection. As the Sūtra says: "All dharmas have no basis; they arise solely from combination.
△ This concludes the three preceding sections, which collectively clarify the fundamental principle of dependent origination.

Fourth is the meaning of the mutual inclusion of distinct entities (*bhāva-viśeṣa-praveśa*). This means that because the functional powers of the various gates mutually support one another and reciprocally influence each other, each possesses both the sense of having complete power and the sense of having no power at all;
it is only through this that dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is established. As the *Dilun* says: "Because causes do not produce [results], they arise from conditions;
because conditions do not produce [results], they arise from their own causes. △ If each were to possess only power and lack the absence of power, then...

There would be the fault of multiple fruits arising from each individual [cause], because they would each produce [a result] separately. Alternatively, if each were individually powerless, there would be the fault of no fruit at all;

for if they are equally not conditions, none would arise together. Therefore, in dependent origination, it is essential that they rely upon one another, possessing both power and powerlessness, just as if one condition were missing, everything would fail to be established; the same applies to the others. Therefore, a single [condition] is capable...
That which possesses unity has the power to sustain many, whereas that which depends on unity and consists of many lacks such power; it must enter into the one.
Since that which possesses unity necessarily does not coexist with that which possesses multiplicity, there is no single entity that does not encompass the many.
Furthermore, since that which possesses multiplicity necessarily does not coexist with that which lacks unity, there is no multiplicity that...
They do not enter into one another. △ As it is with one supporting many bases, so too is it with many supporting one base; reflect on this by reversing the above.

△ As it is when one looks toward many—where there is both support and supported, where the former has full power and the latter lacks it, where the many are constantly contained within the one, and where the one is secretly entered by the many, being simultaneous and unobstructed—so too should it be understood when the many look toward the one. △
Contemplate how both "coexistence" and "mutual extinction" are non-obstructive in these two phrases.
Fifth, the meaning of the mutual identity of distinct entities: when various conditions are compared, they mutually appropriate one another’s entire substance;

thus, the meanings of having substance and lacking substance are established only through dependent origination. If even one condition were missing, the others could not arise, and therefore the principle of conditions would be destroyed.
When this single condition is obtained, it causes all things to become that which arises and that by which they arise; thus, the meaning of "condition" is finally established.

Therefore, because the single condition is that which can give rise to and can accomplish [the effect], it possesses substantiality (*savastuka*); whereas because the multiple conditions are that which is given rise to and accomplished, they lack substantiality (*avastuka*).

Since a single entity possessing substantiality cannot coexist with many entities possessing substantiality, and many entities lacking substantiality necessarily do not coexist with a single entity lacking substantiality.
For these reasons, there is no "one" that is not manifold, nor is there a "manifold" that is not one. △ Since this is so for the one and the many, it is likewise for the manifold and the one;

reflect upon this by reversing the above. △ Just as when looking from the one toward the many, there are cases where the one has substance and the many lack it, and thus the one can subsume the other to be identical with itself, or abandon itself to be identical with the other, such that they are simultaneously unimpeded—so too should one know it is when looking from the many toward the one.
Reflect on this according to what was stated previously. △ One may also see that the two phrases "both existing" and "both extinguished" are mutually unimpeded by reflecting upon them.

The meaning of the sixth point, the "mutual fusion of essence and function," is that the various conditioned phenomena must have their powers and functions interact and their entire essences merge before they can constitute dependent origination.
Therefore, there are also six phrases regarding perfect penetration; first, because the essence has no non-function, it cites the entire essence.
First, when function is fully employed, there is only the principle of mutual inclusion (*xiāngrù*) without mutual identity (*xiāngjí*);
this is because function is never without its essence, so when one brings forth the function as the entire essence, there is only mutual identity without mutual inclusion.

Second, when the function that returns to the essence does not obstruct the function, and the essence that constitutes the entirety of the function does not lose its essence, then both are preserved without obstruction; thus, both inclusion and identity manifest with sovereign freedom.

4. The essence of the total employment of all functions vanishes, and the function of the total embodiment of the essence perishes; neither identical nor entering, they are a perfectly interfused single flavor. 5.
These five combined with the preceding four lines constitute a single unimpeded dependent origination where all exist together. 6.

These six, having extinguished the preceding five lines, are beyond dependence and transcend words, merging silently into the ocean of the same nature. △ These three gates above clarify the meaning within the first gate, that of distinct entities.
The principle is concluded.

Seventh is the meaning of the mutual inclusion of identical entities (*samatā-svabhāva-praveśa*). This means that the "many-ones" belonging to a preceding condition are non-different in essence from that single condition;
therefore, they are called "identical entities. Furthermore, because this single condition should correspond to many conditions, there exists this "many-one."

Since those many conditions that ought to be mutually related are already identical and interpenetrating, this "one" and "many" must likewise possess mutual identity and interpenetration. Now, first we shall clarify their mutual interpenetration:
it is said that one condition possesses the power to sustain the many, while the many lack the power [to sustain themselves] and thus rely upon that single condition.

Therefore, the one can encompass the many, and the many consequently enter into the one. One entering the many and the many being encompassed by the one should be understood as the reverse of the above.

The single essence of the fundamental unity can produce many unities, causing one to encompass many. Just as it is with the multiplicity of space within a single [entity], so too is it with the singularity of space within the many.
Other meanings and other phrases should all be considered according to this precedent.
The ninth meaning, "the simultaneous fusion and non-obstruction," means that, as before, essence and function are doubly fused, thereby entering into mastery;

it likewise consists of six phrases, which should be understood according to the preceding model. △ These three sections above complete the analysis of the principles within the second section, the Section on the Identical Substance.

The tenth is the meaning of the perfection of identity and difference (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-pariniṣpatti*). This means that by synthesizing the preceding nine gates into one great dependent origination, many gateways of meaning are simultaneously fulfilled;
thus, there is the gate of simultaneity (*yugapat-mukha*), because by abiding in one, all are universally responded to.

There is the gate of mastery over breadth and narrowness (*vistṛta-saṃkucita-vaśitā-mukha*), because it functions according to both essence and utility. There is the gate of mutual inclusion and entry (*anyonya-anupraveśa-mukha*), because distinct essences are mutually compatible.

The gate of subtle differentiation (sūkṣma-viśeṣa-mukha) being identical with the gate of concealment and manifestation (gūhana-āviṣkaraṇa-mukha): furthermore, taking functional mutual entry (kārya-anyonya-anupraveśa) as manifestation, one takes essential identity (svabhāva-ekatva) as concealment;

likewise, the entry of manifestation into concealment is also thus. Furthermore, taking mutual entry through different entities (bhinnasvabhāva-anyonya-anupraveśa) as manifestation, one takes mutual entry within the same entity (ekasvabhāva-anyonya-anupraveśa) as concealment;
likewise, the identity of the manifest and the difference of the concealed is also thus. Furthermore, by means of the different entities, mutual entry carries...
The gate of the mutual entry of identical substance and characteristics, which is like a net of Indra, exists because this great dependent origination is itself the unimpeded Dharma-realm;

the gate of manifesting the Dharma by relying on phenomena exists because it is manifested within time; and the gate of primary and attendant elements exists because they are mutually inclusive and interrelated.
△ This tenth gate, the "Gate of Perfect Fulfillment," clarifies its meaning by means of the third gate mentioned above.
Principle. △ Therefore, one should know that for dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) to arise, it must necessarily possess these ten meanings; if any are lacking, it is not established.

△ As the Sūtra says: "The Bodhisattva skillfully contemplates the dharma of dependent origination, understanding the manifold within a single dharma, and understanding the single within the manifold"—all such statements convey this same meaning.
Fourth, regarding the interpenetration of phenomena and principle (*dharmatā*): if one considers only phenomena, they obstruct one another and cannot be immediately interfused;

if one considers only principle, it is of a single flavor and there is nothing with which to interpenetrate. Now, however, phenomena and principle are interpenetrating, possessing this non-obstruction:
when a single phenomenon that is not different from principle fully encompasses the nature of principle, it causes those many phenomena that are not different from principle [to likewise do so].

Regarding phenomena, according to the principle of their dependence, all are manifested within a single [phenomenon]. If the principle were not fully encompassed within that one, there would be the fallacy of the ultimate truth having spatial limitations.

If the principle were fully encompassed within that one, yet many phenomena did not manifest in accordance with that principle, there would be the fallacy of phenomena existing outside of the principle.
Now, since the principle is entirely and fully encompassed within a single phenomenon, how could many phenomena not likewise be manifested within that one?
The *Huazang* (Flower Treasury) Chapter states: "Within every single atom of all the Flower Treasury Worlds, one perceives the Dharma-realm;
this Dharma-realm is precisely the phenomenal Dharma-realm.
This is the general purport; specifically, it also encompasses the ten gates of the Mysterious Portal.
First, since the ultimate truth is in perfect correspondence with all phenomena, encompassing them without omission, it is the simultaneous and complete fulfillment of all gateways and all dharmas.

Second, because phenomena accord with reality, they can both contain [all things] as they do and pervade extensively according to reality without destroying their specific characteristics; therefore, there is "extensiveness."

The Gate of the Unobstructed Interfusion of the Narrow, the Pure, and the Mixed: Furthermore, because their nature is eternally equal, they are "pure"; because they universally encompass all phenomena, they are "mixed.
Since these three principles pervade all manifold things, a single thing follows the principle to pervade within all;

and since the principle pervading all is entirely present within a single thing, all things follow the principle to reside within that one thing. Thus, there is the mutual containment of the one and the many.
Section: The Four Truths. Since the Four Truths are not separate from all phenomena, a single phenomenon is itself the Truth, and the Truth is itself all phenomena.
Therefore, this one is precisely that entirety of phenomena, and the entirety is precisely this one; the reverse may be understood accordingly.
Therefore, there is the gate of mutual identity and sovereignty.

Fifth, because the absolute truth is fully present within each particular phenomenon without partiality, when this [phenomenon] is manifest, that [truth] is said to be hidden, and when that is manifest, this is hidden;
thus, there is the gate of concealment and manifestation.
Sixth, because the principle of universal inclusion encompasses all phenomena and brings those dependent entities instantaneously into a single [reality], there is the "subtle gate.

Seventh, because this is the principle of total inclusion, it can manifest everything; that principle of total inclusion is identical to this, and thus manifests instantaneously. This is its manifestation.
At that time, both the manifesting subject and the manifested object appear therein; at this time, both the manifesting subject and the manifested object likewise appear within that [other].
Because they are thus layered upon one another without end, there is the "Imperial Net" (Indra-jāla) gate, for True Suchness (Tathatā) is ultimately inexhaustible.
Eighth, because phenomena and principle are identical, any single phenomenon that is mentioned is itself a true Dharma-gate; hence there is the "Gate of Relying on Phenomena" (*toshi-mon*).

Ninth, because True Suchness (*tathatā*) is omnipresent, it is fully present throughout days and nights, years and eons; thus, its presence during a day is no different from its presence during an eon.
Hence there is the "Gate of the Ten Times Being Differently Established" (*jisse-i-jō-mon*); for if even time is formed by phenomena, how could phenomena ever dissolve time?
Is it not integrated? Tenth,
because this phenomenon is identical with principle and is never obstructed by its constant mutual correspondence with all other phenomena, there is the "Gate of Master and Retinue."
Therefore, the single principle is harmoniously integrated, and the ten gates are fully present.

Regarding the fifth point, "matters like illusions and dreams": it is just as a magician can transform a single object into various illusory things, or various objects into a single thing, and so forth.
As the sutra says: "Or manifesting a brief moment as a hundred years," and so on; all such things [are like this].
Because the phenomena of karma are produced as illusions, they are without obstruction regarding identity or difference. △ Regarding the phrase "like a dream": it is like what is seen in a dream;
though vast and seemingly having moved far away, time has passed for a long duration without even a moment having elapsed. Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* says:
"In a dream one thinks years have passed, yet upon waking it is but a brief instant. Therefore, although time may be immeasurable, it is subsumed within a single kṣaṇa. Know this.
Time, place, and so forth are all as sovereign as a dream.
Regarding the manifestation of all phenomena as being like reflections, there are briefly two meanings:

first, all things possess a nature of luminous clarity because they are produced by the mind; second, they are manifestations of conceptualization, just like reflections. By virtue of the former meaning...
Therefore, by virtue of the latter meaning, they are that which manifests, and by virtue of the former meaning, they are that which is manifested;

thus all phenomena are mutually like reflections, just as mirrors reflect one another without their original characteristics being destroyed. As the Sūtra says: "Though distant objects and near objects both cast reflections, the reflections do not themselves possess distance or proximity according to those objects."

Regarding the seven causes being immeasurable: this refers to the fact that when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas were formerly in the causal stage, they constantly cultivated the contemplation of dependent origination, the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), great vows, dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*), and practices in accordance with the *dharmadhātu*, as well as other immeasurable and sublime causes;
therefore, the fruits now arisen possess these very same unimpeded qualities.
The realization of the fruit of Buddhahood by the eight [Buddhas] is attained through the profound nature of reality (tathatā), whereby they obtain the functional activity of suchness.
Therefore, one is all, without any obstruction. As the Sūtra says: "With a single Buddha-land filling the ten directions, the ten directions enter into one without remainder;
yet the original characteristics of the worlds are not destroyed. It is because of incomparable merit that this is possible.

The ninth is the great function of profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This refers to the power of the various great *samādhis*, such as the Ocean-Seal (*Sāgaramudrā*) concentration, which causes great dharmas to manifest within a small space with unimpeded mastery. As the "Chapter on the Excellent Head" (*Bhadramukha-parivarta*) states:

"Entering into as many *samādhis* as there are atoms, one gives rise from each atom an equal number of concentrations; yet those atoms do not increase by even one, while universally manifesting what is difficult to fathom."
Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of lands, it is said that the forms and appearances of sentient beings differ from one another, and their karmic actions and voices are likewise immeasurable;
all such things can be manifested through the majestic spiritual power of the Sea-Seal Samādhi (Sāgaramudrā-samādhi), and so forth.
The ten supernormal powers and liberations refer to the power of the ten supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) and the inconceivable liberations (*vimokṣa*).
By virtue of these, even small places manifest as large without any obstruction or doubt. As stated in the "Chapter on Inconceivable Dharmas" among the ten kinds of liberation:
"Within a single atom, one establishes all the Buddha-dharmas of the three periods of time," and so forth.
Therefore, among the ten [aspects] above, citing any single cause is sufficient to enable those dharmas to interpenetrate, merge without obstruction, and function with sovereign ease.

△ Among the ten, the first six universally take the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as their causal characteristic of virtue; such is the natural law (*dharmatā*). The latter two are both matters of functional activity (*karma-vyāpāra*), whose meaning extends to both cause and effect.
The seventh concerns the sense of initiating cultivation, extending to both the characteristic of virtue and functional activity. The eighth concerns the fruit.
Because virtue is exclusively the characteristic of virtue. Question: Regarding the ten preceding profound gates (*xuanmen*), do they pertain to the function of virtue universally or specifically?
Are they opened or closed? Answer: The ten preceding gates pertain to both the characteristics of virtue and its functions; they are universal rather than specific, and unified rather than separate.

From the perspective of the Buddha, the function is also a characteristic of virtue, because it is the functioning of virtue. From the perspective of sentient beings (*jī*), the characteristic is also termed a function, as it causes [the realization of] that function.

Because the characteristics are known, their function is the simultaneous fusion of both defilement and purity; since the function of these characteristics can both defile and purify, the characteristics and the function are not divided into two separate entities.
By means of the ten causes mentioned above, the ten pairs of doctrinal meanings and so forth are made to be perfectly interfused through the ten gates such as "simultaneity" and the rest.
Inexhaustible.
These one million gates of the six profound aspects are all characterized by universal inclusion and containment. As the *Sūtra on the Contemplation of Universal Inclusion* states:
"To understand the infinite within the one, and the one within the infinite, and to realize their mutual arising—this shall bring about fearlessness."

Nevertheless, these three contemplations can be practiced wherever one encounters them; just as with the mind’s arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, they can be applied to the body’s walking, standing, sitting, and lying down;
to the primary retribution of birth, aging, sickness, and death; to the secondary retribution of formation, abiding, decay, and emptiness;

and even to the two periods of daily life, clothing and food, and the six sense organs encountering their objects—within all such phenomena, one may cultivate contemplation, for fundamentally they are not separate from this Dharma-realm.

However, those taught through the gradual method practice the contemplation of sequential arrangement (*xingbu guan*); those taught through the sudden method practice the contemplation of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong guan*); and those taught through the perfect teaching practice the contemplation of non-obstruction (*wuai guan*).

Furthermore, beginners practice the contemplation of sequential arrangement; those who have practiced for a long time practice the contemplation of perfect interfusion; and those with advanced minds practice the contemplation of non-obstruction. Moreover, those with dull faculties practice the contemplation of sequential arrangement;

those with sharp faculties practice the contemplation of perfect interfusion; and those with mature faculties practice the contemplation of non-obstruction—all according to their respective capacities.
The distinction between phenomena and non-phenomena exists separately;

through the perfection of the contemplation of true emptiness, one severs the obstacle of active manifestations and realizes all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*), attesting to the principle of the merging of appearances.

Through the perfection of the contemplation of the unobstructed reality of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), one severs the obstacle of seeds and realizes spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*), attesting to the functioning of the dharma-realm as the interdependent origination of fused appearances and conditions.

Through the contemplation of pervasiveness (*zoubian guan*), one completes the severance of the obstacles of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and achieves unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna*), thereby realizing the single true, unobstructed Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Furthermore, based on the principle of the contemplation of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the two teachings of the Small and Initial [Vehicles] are established;

based on the principle of the contemplation of non-obstruction, the two teachings of the Final and Sudden [Vehicles] are established; and based on the principle of the contemplation of pervasiveness, the three teachings of the Identical, Distinct, and Perfect [Vehicles] are established.
Furthermore, it is through the two teachings of the Small and Initial [Vehicles] that one can fully articulate the principles contained within the Contemplation of True Emptiness;
it is through the two teachings of the Final and Sudden [Vehicles] that one can fully articulate the principles contained within the Unobstructed Contemplation;

and it is through the three teachings of the Identical, Distinct, and Perfect [Vehicles] that one can fully articulate the principles contained within the Universal Contemplation. Therefore, the teachings and contemplations proceed together without contradiction.
Just as a person cannot function if either their eyes or feet are missing, there has never been a case where there was teaching without contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
This is explained in the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā-mukha* and within the *Huayan Xuanzan*.
As for why there are only these five gates, they correspond to the three periods of time—the basis for practice—and the teachings expounded according to those modes of contemplation.

Furthermore, the "ten modes" refer to the modes of transformation; the "doctrinal essence" refers to the methods of transformation; and the "doctrinal essence as received" refers to the teachings themselves.

The "three contemplations" refer to the contemplations that can be cultivated. Such meanings as these are scattered throughout the texts of the Tripiṭaka; now, based on the various major treatises of the Hossō school, I have briefly recorded this essential outline.
If one can understand this, one will have grasped more than half of the fundamental tenets of the Hossō school.
For those who wish to investigate this in detail, they should consult the *Huayan*, *Yuánjué*, and *Qǐxìn Xuántán Shùchāo*, as well as the *Jiàozhāng* and other such works;
I shall not elaborate further here.
This concludes the sixth fascicle of the *Xiánshǒu Wujiàoyí*.

(Virtuous Leader, *Wénxiū Wùjiàoyí*, Scroll Six) I humbly pray that each of the six aspects and ten mysteries may be fully opened and realized without end, and that through the three contemplations and four dharma-realms, one may enter them in ever-deepening layers of interpenetration.
May all things in the past, present, and future be fulfilled according to one's wishes; now and hereafter, may every single matter accord with the heart’s desire.
(Recorded at the Ciyun Meditation Hall) Regarding the *Origins of the Compilation of the Ritual Manual of the Five Teachings*:
The *Ritual Manual of the Five Teachings* is the standard for the Buddhas’ preaching of the Dharma and the scale for the successive patriarchs’ analysis and interpretation. As for the teachings...
Wisdom and principle are severed [from delusion] by means of this; all things emerge from this. The stages of practice and the causes and effects of fruition do not depart from this.

By means of this, the One Vehicle accomplishes the three types of enlightenment; by means of this, the Mahāyāna ascends the three paths; by following this, the Three Vehicles transcend the three realms;

and by relying on this, humans and devas pass beyond the three miserable destinies. Thus one knows that apart from this, there is nothing with which to polish and illuminate the self-substance. To depart from this...
Without this, there is no means to transform and guide sentient beings. Outside of this, there is no means to propagate the Buddha-dharma.
Apart from this, there is no means to transmit and uphold the ancestral seal. Without reaching back to this, there is no means to serve as a bridge for the末代 (final age).

Turning one's back on this, there is no means to provide relief for those in times of famine. Therefore, this single work is truly an essential scripture within the Dharma-gate. Alas! Among the teachings and sections of the various patriarchs...
The many meanings in this volume are so vast that beginners are struck with awe, not knowing where to turn. When I first entered the study, I was already concerned about this.

Since the summer of the Gengzi year, I have had the honor of receiving the *Qingliang Xuantan* (Profound Discourses on Qingliang) from my late teacher; I have subsequently transcribed the *Xianshou Jiaoyi* (The Rituals of Xianshou’s Teachings) and am now reciting it.
In the spring of the *xinchou* year, I happened to find a copy of the *Wujiaoyi* (The Ritual of the Five Teachings) by Xianshou at a bookstall.

Upon examining it, I found it to be the original version by Master Daoxian Qian of Western Sichuan. It also follows entirely the three sections—*Zongqu*, *Yili*, and *Jiaoyi*—of Huayan’s *Zhongjiaoyi*.

I compiled the commentary and sub-commentary into eight fascicles and presented them to my late teacher. The teacher said, "This is the *Qingliang Jiaoyi* (the Ritual of Qingliang), not that of Xianshou."
The teachings of Xianshou constitute the ritual of the primary instruction. Since the *Huayan Xuanji* (Profound Record of Huayan) is already extant, why labor over this further?

Thereupon, he again bestowed upon me the *Xianshou Jiaozhang* (Treatise on the Teachings of Xianshou). I immediately transcribed it and divided it into two sections: "Classification of the Teachings" (*Fen jiao*) and "Distinctions of the Doctrinal Basis" (*Kaizong suoquan*).

Upon reaching this point, I first learned of the distinction between the Xianshou school and the Qingliang school. During the Renyin year, while reading the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), I noted that the Xian family possessed these teachings.
There was no contemplation; there was nothing to be severed and nothing to be realized. He then took these points to seek a definitive resolution from his former teacher.

The teacher rebuked him for not yet understanding the perfect meaning (*yuan-yi*) of the Xianzong (Xianshou) school, despite having explained it through the five teachings (*wu-jiao*). He then instructed him by means of three chapters.

In the spring of the Gui-mao year, he again compiled a single volume combining the temporal rituals as interpreted by the two patriarchs Xianshou and Qingliang, along with Dushun’s *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*, and sought verification therein.
The former master said: "When you, Master Guan, compiled the *Sijiàoyí* (Outline of the Four Teachings), you recorded the meanings rather than the texts.
Now that you have compiled the *Wujiàoyí* (Outline of the Five Teachings), you have taken both text and meaning; this may truly be called a success.

It cannot be compared to the ancients who recorded only the *Huánhuán* or recorded only the *Jiāozhāng*. You should investigate it further; therein lies inexhaustible, wondrous significance. (Year of Yi Si)
One year, a fellow student who was studying *Vijñaptimātra* at Lianju Temple told me that Qingliang’s presentation of the ten schools of Buddhism seemed erroneous.

I did not respond to him at the time. Later, I re-examined various commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka*, *Śraddhotpāda*, *Prajñāpāramitā*, and *Caryāpraṇidhāna*, as well as Guishan’s extensive and abbreviated commentaries on the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* and Yuanjue, and the *Zhen weishi liang* by Gao Yuan.
Only then did I come to understand Qingliang’s establishment of the [school of] Non-... (text fragmentary).

There have been some errors. However, because later students are superficial, they read that [text] but not this one, which has led to much criticism. In the summer of the Bingwu year, I re-edited the *Jiaoyi* (Rituals of Teaching).

I integrated the expedient means of the *Sanzhang zhang* (Chapter on the Three Jewels) into the section on Contemplation (*guan*), and incorporated the distinctions made in the *Canyuan quan* (Commentary on the Source of Chan) into the section on the School (*zong*).

Furthermore, I included the five gates of emptiness-nature from the *Yuanjue shu* (Commentary on Perfect Enlightenment) and the benefits for the capacities of beings from the *Jiaoyi zhang* (Chapter on the Meaning of Teaching).

The "Resolving Obstacles" (Tongfáng) section of the *Huìxuán jì* is integrated within the teachings; the "Emergence and Disappearance of the Three Illuminations" (*Chūmò sānzhào*) of the *Huìxuán jì* is integrated within the "Pointing to the Return" (*Zhǐguī*);
and the "Explanation of Intent" (*Shuōyì*) of the *Cányuán quán* is integrated within the "Timing" (*Shí*). Regarding these, I sought confirmation from my former teacher.

The teacher nodded his head and said: "The essential points of your house are now finally complete. Compared to what I perceived previously, your understanding of the teachings and contemplation is like the stars in the heavens."

The essential points of the school’s doctrine are its eyes and brows; the stages of realization and verification are like reflections in a mirror; and the meaning of the emptiness of nature and characteristics is as clear as fruit held in the palm.
In the year Dingwei, my teacher passed away. I shut myself in my room for several years, refining and polishing the text again and again.

I compared each passage one by one to ensure that no essential meaning was omitted. Where there were omissions, I supplemented them; where the phrasing was harsh, I made it smooth; where the order was inverted, I rearranged it; and where there were errors, I corrected them.
I further edited and extracted one fascicle, *The Primer for Opening the Ignorant Regarding the Five Teachings*, which I recite daily as a regular practice.

In the spring of the Geng-cheng year, I arranged a single-sheet diagram titled "The Chart of Realization and Certification in the Five Teachings" for the convenience of others' study. In the winter of the Ren-zi year, the Venerable Tianxi Jingchun arrived;

he also requested the *Five Teachings Ritual* along with the *Primer for Opening the Ignorant* and the "Chart of Realization and Certification" to verify their correctness. The Venerable joined his palms and exclaimed, "Xianshou!"

Regarding the acquisition of this person by my family: it was like the dispatching of an envoy by Vairocana Buddha. From the spring of the *guichou* year to the winter of the *jiayin* year, the ten-fascicle draft of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* commentary was completed.
In the autumn of the *yimao* year, the six-fascicle draft of the *Wujiaoyi* (The Ritual of the Five Teachings) was finalized and lectured upon once.
From the winter of the *yimao* year to the summer of the *wuwu* year, the forty-eight-fascicle annotated edition of the *Wujiaoyi* was produced. Thus the writing was finished.

On the day of the fourth quarter of the middle month of autumn in the Gengshen year of the Kangxi era, the consecrated practitioner Xufa Shi inscribed this postscript to the *Wujiao yi* (The Ritual of the Five Teachings) by Xianshou.
Long ago, when the World-Honored One first attained perfect enlightenment and the ten bodies were initially fulfilled, he exclaimed: "How marvelous! All sentient beings..."
All possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata; yet, due to the clinging of delusive thoughts, they do not realize them.
Because sentient beings cling through delusive thoughts, the Tathāgata manifests speech within that which is beyond speech:

first, to fulfill his own original intent and reveal that every person possesses these virtues and marks; second, because the capacities of beings differ—some sharp and some dull—he establishes various teachings.

Regarding the partial and the perfect, there are differences in the methods of guidance. Since the Great Teaching gradually spread to the East, those in this land who divided the schools and categorized the teachings have not been uniform.
It was only the Great Master Zhiyi of the Chen and Sui dynasties who, by means of the five periods and eight teachings, categorized and interpreted the sacred scriptures of a single lifetime;

his work remains preeminent. Subsequently, when the Patriarch Xianshou arose in the Tang Dynasty, he categorized and interpreted them by means of the five teachings, which was likewise most excellent.

Furthermore, the two schools of Tiantai and Xuanzang have galloped side by side throughout the land. Yet, those who study the Tiantai tradition sometimes criticize the Xuanzang school for having "teaching but no contemplation.
Conversely, those who study the Xuanzang school maintain that because the names of the five teachings are not confused, the meaning of contemplation is naturally revealed;
thus, all capacities are gathered and the principles are perfectly complete. My master, Ciyun Fazhi, and my elder brother Bai Ting, sighed deeply and said: "The Tiantai..."

The four teachings of our school are originally found throughout the great Mahāyāna scriptures; later generations compiled them into a collection known as the *Sijiao yi* (The Ritual of the Four Teachings) so that people might easily understand them.
The five teachings of our school likewise exist within various sections of the canon, though they have simply not yet been formally compiled.

Therefore, having tasted the divine essence of the teachings and contemplations and cast off the vulgar habits of relying on mere "traps and snares" (metaphors for external means), I have compiled this *Wujiao yi* (The Ritual of the Five Teachings), which sets forth the stages of severance and realization according to these five teachings.

The general and specific aspects of the three periods, the distinctions among the six schools, and the perfect and gradual modes of the three contemplations—how orderly and brilliant they are, like the sun and stars!
How excellent it is that he has established this as a unified system of discourse. As the Elder Tianxi said:
"That Vairocana Buddha sent you here was the meritorious achievement of the Patriarch Xianshou. Once the book was completed, in the autumn of the Jihwei year, he passed through Ciyun.
I visited my elder brother Bai, who brought out [the texts] for me to examine; the entire Tripitaka was as clear to him as pointing at one's own palm. I was moved by this experience.

Nowadays, those within the realm who study the teachings of the Xianjia (賢家) school are few; I regret that there is no complete collection of their works, making it difficult for people to gather and study them together.

Even though I have read the *Jiaoyi* (教義), the *Zhuangyan Dacuo* (華嚴大鈔), and other such texts, my sighs of profound lamentation only increase. Hereafter, I know that those who honor these teachings will be as numerous as the clouds.

The succession of the lineage is as numerous as rain; it all depends on this very point. Why worry that delusive thoughts will not be destroyed, or that the realization of the ten-fold body of perfect enlightenment will not be fulfilled?
I have urgently encouraged [the donors] to first have the six volumes of the *Wujiaoyi* (Five Teachings Ritual) carved for printing.

As for its commentary in forty-eight volumes, these shall await subsequent carving. Consequently, having received the pledge forms for the fundraising, I request that we begin with the humblest and thus compose this postscript.
Respectfully inscribed by the younger brother Qingzhu at Donggao under the bright moon.
